articles.title: ‘I Can’t Mislead People’: Ukraine’s Spy Chief Warns Russia Can Fight Through 2028
articles.body:
Russia may have enough resources to continue its war against Ukraine through 2027 and 2028, while preparing intensified attacks on the country’s energy infrastructure during the coming autumn and winter, Ukraine’s military intelligence chief said.
Oleg Ivashchenko, head of Ukraine’s Defense Intelligence Directorate (HUR) made the assessment in an interview with the state-run Ukrinform news agency.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“We do not rule out that Russia will have enough resources to wage war against Ukraine in 2027 and 2028,” he said.
Ivashchenko said Ukraine and its international partners must work together to restrict Russia’s access to the equipment and materials needed to sustain its military production.
Ivashchenko said sanctions must be effectively enforced, adding that Ukrainian intelligence knows which countries supply Russia with electronic components, machine tools, and specialized chemicals. He said numerous intermediary companies have emerged to deliver goods that are later used by Russia’s war machine.
The intelligence chief also said public dissatisfaction with the war was growing inside Russia, although it remained unclear whether it could develop into a significant protest movement.
According to Ivashchenko, more than 60% of Russians now oppose the war, a trend he attributed to worsening economic conditions and heavy battlefield losses. Russia’s contract recruitment model had largely exhausted itself, with regional governments increasingly unable to finance the payments offered to new recruits.
China Asks Ukraine Not to Strike Vladivostok During Forum
Ivashchenko has estimated that Russian forces lose an average of 1,200 to 1,400 personnel a day, with the figure sometimes rising to 1,500, including soldiers killed or seriously wounded.
Russia preparing combined winter attacks
Ivashchenko also warned that Russia was preparing combined attacks involving ballistic and cruise missiles, jet-powered Shahed drones, and new loitering munitions.
He said Ukrainian intelligence had information about the facilities Russia intended to target, the weapons it planned to use, and the approximate timing of potential strikes.
“I can’t please you and I can’t mislead people. As the head of intelligence, I have to speak objectively. People have to understand this, and our country has to prepare for this.”
According to him, Russia’s primary objective is to reduce Ukraine’s military potential and long-range strike capabilities. Russian forces are targeting ammunition storage sites and attempting to destroy Ukrainian defense production facilities, he said.
Energy facilities and thermal power plants are expected to become increasingly frequent targets as colder weather approaches, Ivashchenko said.
He also reported a significant increase in the use of jet-powered Shahed-type drones. Russia could deploy groups numbering 120, 300, or even 500 drones in a single day, while simultaneously launching ballistic and cruise missiles.
Ivashchenko said Russia was also introducing new loitering munitions that combine features of jet-powered drones and cruise missiles. He identified the weapons as the Banderol and Dan-T, saying they could travel at speeds of 500 to 700 kilometers per hour (about 310 to 435 mph), and be launched from either air or ground platforms.
The weapons use artificial intelligence and machine vision to improve accuracy and operate with greater autonomy, making them less dependent on external guidance and more difficult to counter.
He said their warheads weigh more than 130 kilograms (286 pounds), significantly heavier than those carried by Shahed or Geran-type drones, which he put at between 50 and 90 kilograms (110 and 198 pounds).
Ballistic missiles, particularly Iskander and Zircon missiles, remain among the most difficult targets for Ukrainian air defenses to intercept, Ivashchenko said. Countering them requires advanced missile defense systems and an adequate supply of interceptor missiles.
“The enemy is adapting. And our task is to adapt faster.”
Ivashchenko said military intelligence was working directly with Ukraine’s Air Force by providing information about potential threats. He added that securing sufficient numbers of PAC-3 interceptor missiles for Patriot air defense systems remained a priority for President Volodymyr Zelensky, his office, Ukrainian diplomats, and intelligence officials.

articles.title: Russo-Ukrainian war, day 1657: Ukraine’s newly appointed top commander wants to break with a Soviet-inherited system
articles.body:
Exclusive
Team news
Vacancy: deputy editor-in-chief.
Military
Ukraine's new top commander is pushing to unwind a Soviet-inherited command model mid-war. He wants combat-tested sergeants to have real authority. Ukraine inherited a system where officers decided everything and sergeants were senior soldiers with no ladder of their own.
Russia deploys missile brigade to Belarus as fears grow over new threat to Kyiv. The move comes as Russia steps up aerial attacks on Kyiv from the north and Belarus allows Moscow to use its territory to help guide strikes against Ukrainian targets.
Some ten robot boats. Five hundred Russian air sorties. One very lopsided hunt. Missions that once took a night now stretch to five days, and Russia keeps its fleet hidden, a naval drone unit commander says.
Ukrainian drones took Ryazan's blending unit after knocking out two of its four crude units. Satellite imagery in August showed half the plant's primary distillation capacity already out of action.
Ukraine's drone forces say they hit 58,465 Russian targets in August, nearly 1,900 a day. Three named campaigns did the strategic damage. Most of the volume is small front-line hits.
Intelligence and technology
Ukrainian AI targeting module placed third among 60-plus entries in NATO contest. NATO and Ukraine ran the challenge through their first jointly staffed body.
Ukrainian university and the Flamingo missile-maker opened an engineering course. On the first try, zero of 150 passed. Even students who scored well on the university entrance exam flunked the physics round.
Ukraine's Brave1 says it can down Russia's Banderol missiles with cruising speed 650 km/h for less than what they cost, and has destroyed at least four. In July, Ukrainian troops downed Banderols with Swedish Bofors L70 anti-aircraft guns designed in the late 1940s.
Ukraine has 67 companies working to shoot down Russia's jet-powered drones en masse, Zelenskyy says. Only three to five have real results. He called the whole air-defense push "Plan B" to diplomacy's "Plan A".
China calls itself neutral—but its fiber ends up in the drones that hit Ukraine. The papers, reviewed by Western governments, trace drone-grade material straight from a Chinese state firm to a sanctioned Russian plant.
International
Ukrainian journalist asks Trump's envoy to his face whether he was disgusted to sit across from "international criminal" Putin. Witkoff wouldn't answer directly. Earlier, Russia's FSB put a $400,000 bounty on Ukrainian journalist Dmytro Gordon.
Humanitarian and social impact
Russia burns occupied Zaporizhzhia nuclear plant's last-resort generators as everyday power, Ukraine says. Off-site power has been gone since 20 August, and the plant has cut its running generators to two to stretch the fuel that is left.
"Now on the 1,657th day": Ukraine's crews restored power to over 900,000 homes last week as Russia keeps striking grid before winter. Crews brought it back to 596 settlements, most of them in Odesa and Donetsk.
Kyiv stockpiles food and water as Russia's new aerial tactics threaten a brutal winter. Russia has already targeted food storage around Kyiv, while Ukraine's limited air defenses struggle to stop ballistic missiles and faster drones.
Political and legal developments
Russia's FM says war must end so there is "no more Nazism" in Europe. Russian occupation official already said what that means: erasing Ukraine and stopping its aid. The collaborator put it plainly: "denazification is re-Russification".

articles.title: Russia deploys missile brigade to Belarus as fears grow over new threat to Kyiv
articles.body:
Russia has deployed units of its 101st Missile Brigade to Belarus, a formation equipped with the Oreshnik intermediate-range missile system, according to Ukraine’s military intelligence chief Oleh Ivashchenko, Ukrinform reports.
Russia has been ramping up missile and drone attacks on Ukraine in recent weeks, including increasingly frequent strikes on Kyiv from the north, launched from Russian territory close to Belarus. Russia used Belarusian territory to launch its 2022 invasion of northern Ukraine, while Belarus is now allowing Russia to use its territory to support drone attacks. The latest deployment could give Moscow another launchpad for strikes deeper into Ukraine or potentially against targets in Europe.
Belarus not preparing to enter war, but threat remains
Ivashchenko said in an interview with Ukrinform that Ukraine currently assesses the military threat from Belarus as low and sees no signs that Belarus is preparing to directly enter the war.
But he said Kyiv is concerned by the growing Russian military presence in Belarus and the role Belarusian territory is playing in Russian attacks on Ukraine.
“Units of the 101st Missile Brigade of the Russian Armed Forces, which are equipped with the Oreshnik missile system, are also deployed on the territory of Belarus,” Ivashchenko told Ukrinform.
The Oreshnik is a Russian intermediate-range ballistic missile system that Moscow has presented as a new weapon capable of striking targets deep inside Europe. Russia first used an Oreshnik missile against Ukraine in November 2024, striking the city of Dnipro.
Oreshnik has been stationed in Belarus
Russia has maintained Oreshnik missile systems in Belarus since at least December 2025, when Belarusian leader Aliaksandr Lukashenka said an Oreshnik system had been placed on combat duty there as part of expanded military cooperation with Moscow.
The system is capable of carrying nuclear warheads, although Russia has used Oreshnik against Ukraine in a non-nuclear strike. Ukrainian intelligence has previously said the deployment is aimed in part at increasing pressure on Europe and NATO by shortening the missile's flight time to European targets.
The Oreshnik systems in Belarus remain under Russian control rather than Belarusian command, according to Ukrainian intelligence.
Nuclear-capable but carrying concrete: Expert explains Russia’s Oreshnik is psychological weapon, not military one
Belarus allows Russia to use its territory to guide drone strikes
Ivashchenko also said Belarus has allowed Russia to deploy radio-signal repeaters that help guide Russian Shahed-type attack drones toward Ukrainian civilian and critical infrastructure targets.
“If Belarus did not give such permission, this indicates that Minsk no longer controls Russia’s activities on its own territory,” he said, according to Ukrinform.
The use of Belarusian territory to support Russian attacks has stopped short of Belarusian forces directly entering the war, but it demonstrates Minsk's growing role in enabling Russia's military operations.
That cooperation makes the prospect of Russia using Belarusian territory for additional military capabilities less remote, particularly as Moscow expands its forces and intensifies attacks on Kyiv from the northern direction.
Renewed concern over a northern Russian offensive
The comments come as Russian strikes on Kyiv have intensified in recent weeks, while Ukrainian officials have increasingly warned about the possibility of another Russian offensive from the north toward Kyiv and Chernihiv.
There is no reported Russian ground offensive from Belarus underway. But the northern direction remains a major concern for Ukraine because of the precedent set in 2022, when Russian forces crossed from Belarus and advanced toward Kyiv before withdrawing in early April.
For now, Ivashchenko assesses the military threat from Belarus as low. The deployment of Russian missile forces nevertheless adds another significant Russian weapons capability to Belarus, while leaving open questions about how Moscow could use the territory in a future escalation.

articles.title: An unmanned army: Hezbollah terrorists are using UAVs to hold off  Israel’s superior forces
articles.body:
In late August, Israel resumed active strikes on positions held by the Shiite movement Hezbollah inside Lebanon — a response to FPV drone attacks against Israeli soldiers. Cycles of escalation keep repeating themselves in the region: despite ceasefire agreements between Israel and the Lebanese government, Hezbollah fighters continue to attack Israeli forces, and Jerusalem’s response results in civilian casualties, leading to further rounds of fighting. Importantly, Hezbollah’s countermeasures against the IDF now involve the use of fiber-optic-guided drones of the sort developed on the battlefield in Ukraine. The use of this relatively accessible, highly effective technology allowed Hezbollah to retain its ability to fight in the face of Israel’s undeniable military superiority.
What is happening in southern Lebanon
On Aug. 27, following an attempted drone attack on IDF troops near the Ali al-Taher ridge, Israeli aircraft carried out a series of strikes on facilities belonging to Hezbollah near Nabatieh. Military warehouses are reported to have been hit; a woman was killed, and other civilians were injured.
Two weeks earlier, three Israeli soldiers had been severely injured by a drone strike in the same area, and the airstrikes carried out in retaliation for that incident killed not only Hezbollah fighters and commanders, but also at least 11 civilians, including women and children (according to the Israeli side, some of them were relatives of the killed militants).
Similar “cycles of escalation” have accompanied the talks on conflict settlement in southern Lebanon in recent months — negotiations that are themselves part of the broader process of ending the conflict between the U.S.-Israeli coalition and Iran.
The Lebanese theater of operations is one of the key topics in the negotiations. Back in 2024, Israeli authorities announced their intention to “dismantle the terrorist infrastructure” and “liberate” Lebanon from the influence of Hezbollah, which remains Iran’s most valuable and dangerous asset on its “external perimeter.”
Israel’s stated goal in Lebanon is to free the country from Hezbollah’s influence
On Oct. 1, 2024, Israeli forces launched a ground operation into Lebanon aimed at limiting the Shiite movement’s combat capability — the third such war in recent decades (the first two being in 1982 and 2006). A ceasefire was reached at the end of November 2024.
Then, on March 2, 2026, Hezbollah resumed rocket fire on Israeli territory following the death of Iran’s supreme leader Ali Khamenei in a missile strike by the U.S.-Israeli coalition. In response, the IDF continued its ground operation in Lebanon.
A ceasefire was announced on April 16, but fighting continued yet again. With U.S. mediation, an agreement between the Israeli and Lebanese governments was signed on June 26, providing for a partial withdrawal of IDF units from several areas in the south of the country while maintaining an Israeli presence until Hezbollah is disarmed.
Hezbollah leader Naim Qassem refused to recognize the agreement and stated that armed resistance would continue. Notably, the particularities of the Lebanese political system make it impossible to implement any settlement agreement with Israel without the support of the Shiite community.
Drones vs. IDF
At the current stage of the war in southern Lebanon, fiber-optic-guided FPV (first-person view) drones have become Hezbollah’s main means of countering Israeli forces. As many as 33 incidents involving Israeli military deaths and injuries in southern Lebanon were recorded from March to July 2026, with FPV drones used in more than half of them. By some estimates, they have curtailed Israel’s offensive capabilities by up to 80%.
Observers note Hezbollah appears to be in the early stage of what is known as a reconnaissance-strike loop: drones first conduct aerial reconnaissance, followed by launches of fiber-optic FPV drones at identified targets. If the use of drones can be scaled up and incorporated into a strategy for countering Israeli forces, this would create a long-term threat with no clear solution.
In a sense, Hezbollah has successfully exploited a gap in Israeli operational capability that stems less from technological asymmetry than from differing speeds of adapting doctrine to technological progress in warfare.
Hezbollah is successfully adapting to technological progress in warfare
Notably, before the April 16 ceasefire, videos of drone attacks showed hits on static objects or combat vehicles, and despite the agreement, on April 26 a Hezbollah FPV drone struck a tank, killing one Israeli soldier and wounding six others, and more drones came close to successfully attacking an Israeli helicopter that had arrived to pick up the wounded.
It appears that drones have become central to the attrition strategy Hezbollah has adopted against Israeli forces. Speaking with The Insider, Israeli military expert David Gendelman notes the similarities between the southern Lebanese theater of operations and the battlefield in Ukraine:
“FPV drones have proven to be an extremely cost-effective weapon on the Russian-Ukrainian front, which is why millions of them are now being used there, partially replacing the roles of artillery, anti-tank guided missiles, and air power. And this is happening in a symmetric war between two regular armies. Such weapons will be all the more effective in the asymmetric war that Hezbollah is waging against Israel’s regular army.
The Russian and Ukrainian armies are world champions at countering FPVs, with years of experience, and they still suffer several hundred casualties from them every day, because just as there is no wonder weapon, there is no counter-wonder-weapon either. There is a set of partial solutions, in both troop training and technical means, that reduces losses but does not bring them to zero.
The same is true of other types of weapons for which no ‘wonder shield’ has been found either. FPVs are no exception. Just as artillery, anti-tank guided missiles, small arms, and other battlefield tools remain with us, FPVs are here to stay too — this is now a new reality we have to live with.”
Hezbollah’s rocket and missile stockpiles — mostly short- and medium-range ones — have shrunk from roughly 100,000 to 25,000 since 2023, and drones have proven to be an extremely flexible and effective alternative, well-suited for use by small combat cells operating within a decentralized command structure.
Comparing the active periods of fighting in Lebanon from October to November 2024 and from March to July 2026, Hezbollah’s use of FPV drones for attacks on Lebanese territory rose from 0 to 214 cases (21% of all attacks), and the use of conventional suicide drones rose from 21 cases (6%) to 244 cases (24%).
In attacks on Israeli territory, the use of FPV drones rose from 0 to 16 cases (1% of all attacks), and suicide drones from 176 (14%) to 343 (31%). According to calculations by the Israeli research center Alma, from the announcement of the ceasefire on April 16 through June 21, 2026, Hezbollah carried out more than 1,163 attacks, with 637 involving the use of various drones.
Why the IDF was unprepared for drone warfare
The first serious incident involving Hezbollah drones occurred on Oct. 13, 2024, when a Sayad-107 suicide drone struck a dining hall at a Golani Brigade base in Binyamina. Four soldiers were killed, and more than 50 were injured. The drone approached the target from the Mediterranean Sea, evading detection by Israeli air defense systems. Still, Hezbollah’s systematic shift to FPV drones as a primary weapon is likely linked to the collapse of the Assad regime in Syria in December 2024, which disrupted the supply route of traditional missiles. So far, Israel has not found a reliable answer.
David Gendelman points out that the resulting asymmetry in drone use and countermeasures is explained primarily by organizational differences between the two sides:
“The experience of the Russian-Ukrainian war was studied by both Hezbollah and the Israel Defense Forces. The difference was that Hezbollah, as a relatively small, non-bureaucratic structure, adopts and masters innovations like FPVs quickly and doesn’t need a large quantity right away to start carrying out attacks.
For the IDF, the main issue wasn’t so much adopting FPVs themselves, which was also happening, but countering FPVs. And that is a far more labor-intensive process, because protective measures need to be introduced everywhere, tactics need to be changed everywhere, budgets and man-hours need to be allocated to everyone for this, and time and resources are limited. On top of that, the war has continued on multiple fronts since 2023, diverting resources to other urgent matters. Plus they had to deal with the traditional bureaucracy of regular armies and large organizations in general.
As a result, by the start of the latest war with Hezbollah, the Israeli army had spent several years studying Ukraine’s experience and writing recommendations on implementing the lessons learned, but they had adopted practically none of the tactics against FPVs — and only began doing so once the war had already started.
Hezbollah sporadically used FPVs, including fiber-optic ones, in 2024, and even in this current round of hostilities in 2026 the daily number never exceeded a few dozen — nothing comparable to the thousands per day in Ukraine. But due to poor preparedness, even such a small number led to undesirable losses… And we had to implement rapidly, on the fly, all those measures that the army had included in the guidelines years earlier based on Ukraine’s experience, adapting them to our own conditions given differences in terrain, the theater of operations, the forces and resources of the two sides, and so on.
Protective netting, shotguns, field training for troops, countermeasure tactics, acoustic, optical, and radar warning systems, electronic warfare, and various interception tools — all of this is already being put into practice, but there are limits to what we can speed up. Developing new tools, testing available ones, approval, procurement, distribution, training, deployment — once the decision is made, things move forward, but the decision itself came years too late.”
The FPV drone threat has already resulted in operational changes. Some IDF units have shifted to operating at night, although it is known that militants are trying to equip drones with thermal imaging cameras. No changes are yet apparent at the organizational level.
What’s next
Changes in Hezbollah’s tactics show just how quickly the processes of adoption and adaptation happen in wartime. Just a few years ago, the group relied mainly on unguided rockets, anti-tank guided missiles, and classic fixed-wing drones. Now, their mass use of commercial fiber-optic drones is rendering Israeli electronic warfare countermeasures useless. The cost of these new guided munitions starts at $300–400 per unit, and many components can be 3D-printed on site or sourced from civilian-grade parts.
The conflict in southern Lebanon shows how quickly innovations are adopted during wars
Improvised munitions and a guerrilla-style organization — with drone crews hiding in mountainous terrain or residential areas — pose a challenge to the foundation of Israeli military doctrine, which is built on unconditional technological superiority over neighboring state and non-state military-political actors.
Unlike in Ukraine, in southern Lebanon FPV drones serve as a cheap weapon in a low-intensity war, preventing Israel from establishing stable control over the “buffer zone” it created, and thereby serving as a tool of pressure on Israel both within Lebanon’s domestic context and regionally, in Iran’s interests. By some estimates, there are fewer than 100 trained drone operators in all of southern Lebanon, but even this quantity allows Hezbollah to sustain its activity.
Israel is working on interceptor drones and combined systems based on laser technology and electro-optical systems, along with so-called “smart sights” for firearms that significantly increase the chances of hitting a drone. The IDF, for its part, is procuring multi-pellet ammunition and special anti-drone shotguns as a last line of defense and adopting protective netting based on lessons learned from the war in Ukraine. Overall, according to Gendelman’s assessment, due to various constraints Hezbollah will not be able to scale up its use of FPV drones to Ukraine’s level and, as the IDF rolls out various countermeasures, the threat will largely be neutralized. But it will not be eliminated entirely.

Russia Moves Oreshnik-Equipped Missile Units Into Belarus, Ukraine’s Spy Chief Says
Russia has stationed elements of its 101st Missile Brigade in Belarus, a formation equipped with the Oreshnik intermediate-range missile system, according to Ukraine’s military intelligence chief Oleh Ivashchenko on September 7.
Ivashchenko told Ukrinform that Ukrainian intelligence currently sees no evidence that Belarus itself is preparing to directly enter Russia’s war against Ukraine. Kyiv assesses the immediate military threat from the Belarusian direction as low.

However, Russia’s growing use of Belarusian territory for missile and drone-related infrastructure remains a significant concern.
“However, we are concerned that Belarus has permitted the deployment on its territory of radio-signal relay stations that guide Russian Shahed-type strike UAVs toward Ukrainian civilian targets and critical infrastructure,” Ivashchenko said.
He added: “We also note the deployment in Belarus of units of the 101st Missile Brigade of the Russian Armed Forces, which is equipped with the Oreshnik intermediate-range missile system.”
The deployment gives Russia another potential platform for positioning long-range missile capabilities closer to Ukraine and NATO’s eastern flank, even as Minsk stops short of directly committing its own forces to the war.
Ivashchenko also raised a broader question over how much control Belarusian authorities retain over Russian military activity inside the country.

Ukraine has monitored Belarus closely throughout the full-scale war because Russian forces used Belarusian territory during the initial invasion in February 2022, and Moscow has continued maintaining military infrastructure and personnel there.
In general terms, the “Oreshnik” is an intermediate-range ballistic missile with nuclear capability that travels through the stratosphere, making it extremely difficult to intercept.
It is equipped with a multiple independently targetable reentry vehicle (MIRV) system, meaning a single missile can carry several warheads that separate in flight to strike different targets, though they are not independently guided after release.
For now, Ukrainian intelligence does not assess Belarusian forces themselves as preparing for a new offensive against Ukraine.
Previously, Belarusian Deputy Foreign Minister Igor Sekreta has claimed that Minsk would use its “entire arsenal” if Ukrainian forces crossed Belarus' state border, a statement that comes amid renewed rhetoric from Belarusian officials over alleged threats from Ukraine.

articles.title: Russian missile brigade equipped with Oreshniks deployed in Belarus, Ukraine's military intelligence says
articles.body:
Units of Russian missile brigade equipped with Oreshniks deployed in Belarus, Ukraine's military intelligence says
Units of Russia's 101st Missile Brigade, which is equipped with the Oreshnik intermediate-range ballistic missile system, are deployed in Belarus, Ukraine's military intelligence chief Oleh Ivashchenko said in an interview published on Sept. 7.
The interview comes more than half a year after President Volodymyr Zelensky said Belarus already "fully or partially" hosts Russia's Oreshnik missile system, reporting that Russia has already completed "preparatory, technical work." Zelensky described the move as a major escalation risk.
The Oreshnik is a missile believed to be a modified version of the Rubezh surface-to-surface missile. Its high speed makes it exceptionally difficult to intercept and poses a significant challenge to Ukrainian air defenses. It is designed to carry nuclear warheads, but the Oreshnik missiles previously launched at Ukraine did not carry nuclear warheads.
Russian President Vladimir Putin claims it is unstoppable, a claim disputed by military experts.
The damage from the three known attacks in which Russia deployed Oreshnik has been minimal. Russia first used an Oreshnik against Ukraine in November 2024, striking the city of Dnipro. The second time Russia deployed Oreshnik was in its large-scale attack on western Ukraine, including the city of Lviv. Most recently, Russia launched an attack involving an Oreshnik missile in May on Bila Tserkva, a town about 80 kilometers (50 miles) south of Kyiv.
Speaking to the Ukrainian news agency Ukrinform, Ivashchenko also said that Kyiv is concerned about Belarus granting Moscow permission to deploy radio signal repeaters on its territory, which help adjust Russian Shahed drone strikes on civilian and critical infrastructure in Ukraine.
"And if Belarus did not grant such permission, this indicates that Minsk no longer controls Russia's activities on its own territory," Ivashchenko said, as quoted by Ukrinform.
Ivashchenko added in the interview that while Russia seeks to use Belarus' territory and its military resources for its war efforts against Ukraine, Kyiv currently sees no signs that Minsk is preparing to enter Russia's war against Ukraine. He assessed that the threat from Belarus, north of Ukraine, is low.
Belarus, ruled by dictator Alexander Lukashenko since 1994, is among Moscow's closest allies and has provided political and military support to Russia since the beginning of its full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

articles.title: Middle East Live: Israel army orders evacuation of zone in south Lebanon ahead of strikes
articles.body:
Several killed in Israeli strikes in southern Lebanon
At least 11 people were killed, including two infants, were injured in Israeli strikes on a residential building in a town in southern Lebanon early on Monday, Lebanon's state news agency reported. The Israeli army had demanded early Monday that residents of Deir Zahrani in southern Lebanon leave a specific zone ahead of strikes against Iran-backed Hezbollah. Follow our liveblog to see how the day's events unfolded.
This liveblog is no longer being updated.
Our liveblog is now closed.
Israel army says will continue to 'remove threats' after strikes on Lebanon
Israel's military said Monday it was committed to the ceasefire but would continue to "remove threats" from Hezbollah, after Lebanese state media reported overnight strikes killed at least 12 people.
The military said it had struck Hezbollah "infrastructure sites" across southern Lebanon in response to the launch of two explosive drones towards its troops, as well as "several terrorists" it said were transferring weapons.
"The claim that several uninvolved individuals were harmed as a result of the strikes is being reviewed," it said, adding that the military "will continue to operate to remove threats while remaining committed to the ceasefire agreement".
Proof of 'atrocity crimes' could be lost as Israel clears rubble in Gaza, UN expert says
A UN expert warned Monday that large-scale rubble removal in parts of Gaza under Israeli control risked erasing traces of "atrocity crimes", and preventing the recovery and identification of human remains.
Francesca Albanese, the United Nations special rapporteur on the Palestinian territories, warned in a statement that the implications of Israel's "ongoing removal, crushing and relocation of rubble in Gaza" were "profound".
"Gaza's rubble contains human remains and physical evidence relevant to the investigation of alleged international crimes, including genocide," she said, pointing to estimates from Palestinian authorities that more than 10,000 people remain buried under the debris.
The Italian-born independent expert has faced harsh criticism from Israel and some of its allies over her long-standing accusations of Israeli genocide and war crimes against Palestinians.
Wave of Israeli air strikes in south Lebanon kill 12, including two children
Israel conducted a wave of air strikes in south Lebanon killing 12 people including women and children, the Lebanese health ministry said on Monday, in an intensification of violence after a weeks-long lull.
The Health Ministry said one of the strikes hit a building, killing 11 people, including two children and four women. Eight were also wounded, including three children and a paramedic.
The ministry said that another strike on a car in the village killed a paramedic with the Lebanese Islamic Risala Scout Association and wounded two others.
The Israeli military said the strikes come in retaliation for two Hezbollah drone attacks that exploded while targeting Israeli troops in Lebanon from the area on Monday.
Hezbollah did not claim the attacks nor immediately issue a statement on the intensifying strikes around Nabatiyeh province.
Volkswagen plant to be converted for Israeli defence projects
Israeli investor Aurelius Capital and the German state of Lower Saxony are planning to take over one of Volkswagen's German auto factories to repurpose it for defence projects, Europe's largest carmaker said on Monday.
Rising demand for defence assets is seen as one of the main solutions for how European automotive firms can tackle the issue of excess capacity, also reflected by with Rheinmetall and Continental both having made efforts.
The joint statement of intent signed on Monday would see Aurelius take over the factory together with Lower Saxony, which is Volkswagen's second-largest shareholder, while the Israeli investor would become a majority-owner.
No further details were disclosed for the plans, which still need to be finalised.

Lebanese President Joseph Aoun has urged Washington and the international community to help stop Israeli attacks, with strikes in the south of the country killing at least 11 people on Sunday despite a truce and a framework deal aimed at halting the violence.
Oman says it evacuated 16 crew members of Saudi Sidr vessel attacked by Iran
Oman said it had evacuated 16 crew members from the Saudi-owned tanker Sidr, after it was attacked by Iran, according to a statement posted on X by its Maritime Security Centre.
The Sidr was one of two supertankers carrying Saudi oil that were reported hit while transiting the Strait of Hormuz last Monday.
Saudi Arabia said last Wednesday that the attack on the tanker, owned by national shipping company Bahri, had killed two Filipino seafarers.

Gulf nations cannot rely solely on the United States and other international alliances for their security and need to be more self-sufficient, Qatar's foreign ministry spokesman said in Abu Dhabi on Monday.
"We need to realise in the Gulf that having international forces in the region, having a strategic alliance with the United States, is very important, but is not enough," he told the Hili Forum in the United Arab Emirates' capital.
"Self-sufficiency when it comes to security is the only way forward. Yes, we need our partners. Yes, we need our allies. But we cannot depend on them alone for our security," he added.
Iran will reciprocate if UN nuclear watchdog adopts resolution against it, official says
Iran will reciprocate if the UN nuclear watchdog adopts a resolution against it, Tehran's Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmail Baghaei said in a press briefing on Monday.
He added that European states seeking a UN resolution against Iran were "irrational" as the war with the United States has made nuclear facilities inaccessible.
Israel accuses Hezbollah of repeatedly violating ceasefire agreement
Israel accused Iran-backed Hezbollah of repeatedly violating a ceasefire agreement in recent days, as Lebanese state media reported 11 killed in overnight Israeli strikes in a southern village.
"Repeated drone attacks. Weapons storage. Terror infrastructure. Command centres embedded in civilian areas. Hezbollah continues attempting to rebuild its military capabilities in southern Lebanon. These violations will not be accepted," Israel's foreign ministry wrote on X.
Iran warns South Korea against joining Gulf operations
Iran's Foreign Ministry spokesperson said in a post on X  that South Korea's military participation or presence in operations in the Gulf and Strait of Hormuz would be regarded as support for US "aggression" and would have serious consequences.
Iran war shows strategic alliance with the US is not enough, Qatari official says
The Iran war showed that Gulf Arab countries should not only depend on their strategic partnership with the United States for their security, Qatar's foreign ministry spokesperson Majed al-Ansari told a panel on Monday at the Hili forum in Abu Dhabi.
"We need to realise in the Gulf that having international forces in the region, having a strategic alliance with the US is very important but is not enough. Self-sufficiency when it comes to security is the only way forward," Ansari said.
At least 9 killed in Israeli strikes in southern Lebanon, state media reports
At least nine people were killed, including two children, and five others were injured in Israeli strikes on a residential building in a town in southern Lebanon early on Monday, Lebanon's state news agency reported.
US denies that Iran struck an uncrewed US military ship in the Strait of Hormuz
The US military denied that Iran struck an uncrewed American military vessel in the Strait of Hormuz, calling the claim a “total lie". A top Iranian official said Tehran plans to announce an “exclusion zone” outside the Strait of Hormuz aimed at vessels it believes are attempting to transit the waterway.
Meanwhile, Israeli strikes in southern Lebanon killed seven people and leveled a vacant hospital, according to Lebanese authorities, near an area that has become a flash point in fighting between Israel and the Iran-backed militant group Hezbollah.
Hormuz traffic dips to lowest since May after US, Iranian strikes on ships
An average of 10 commodity ships transited the Strait of Hormuz per day over the past 10 days, the lowest since May, according to shipping data on Monday, after US and Iranian strikes on tankers.
The 10-day moving average was 10 on Sunday, down from more than 15 on Friday and nearly 13 on Saturday, data from analytics firm Kpler found.
Only two vessels passed through the strait on Saturday while six went through on Sunday, mostly using the Iranian route.
Iran says it plans to announce a new 'exclusion zone' near the Strait of Hormuz
The new head of Iran's Supreme National Security Council on Sunday said Tehran plans to announce an "exclusion zone” outside the Strait of Hormuz aimed at vessels it believes are attempting to transit the waterway.
Mohsen Rezaei's comments to Iran's state broadcaster came with few details, a day after the US struck three Iranian oil tankers in response to Tehran launching ballistic missiles at US warships. Experts called the launches a dangerous escalation after Iran’s previous attacks at sea targeted commercial shipping.
The new zone should be announced in the coming days and weeks and “will begin from the line of the US naval blockade, extend toward the Strait of Hormuz, and from this side continue into the Persian Gulf,” Rezaei said. "Any ship that enters this area with the intention of passing through the Strait of Hormuz and is identified will be placed on our sanctions list.”
Oil extends gains after US and Iran strike ships
Oil prices extended gains on Monday as tit-for-tat strikes between the US. and Iran on vessels sailing in the Strait of Hormuz and other areas heightened concerns of a prolonged supply disruption from the Middle East.
Brent crude futures climbed 52 cents, or 0.54%, to $96.80 a barrel by 2354 GMT while US West Texas Intermediate crude was at $92.14 a barrel, up 66 cents, or 0.72%.
(FRANCE 24 with AFP, AP and Reuters)

articles.title: Burnham, Trump Agree to Keep Working Toward Ukraine-Russia Ceasefire
articles.body:
British Prime Minister Andy Burnham and US President Donald Trump agreed Monday to continue working toward a ceasefire between Ukraine and Russia following Washington’s latest diplomatic push to restart negotiations to end Moscow’s war.
The two leaders spoke by phone Monday afternoon, with Burnham reiterating Britain’s support for Ukraine and the recent US-led peace efforts, according to Downing Street.

Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“On Ukraine, the two leaders agreed on the need to continue working towards a ceasefire that prevented more loss of life,” the British government said in its readout of the call.
The conversation came a day after Trump envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner visited Kyiv for talks with President Volodymyr Zelensky after meeting Russian President Vladimir Putin in Moscow on Saturday.
The back-to-back meetings marked Washington’s latest effort to revive negotiations that had stalled despite several previous rounds of US-mediated diplomacy.
Witkoff and Kushner said after their meetings that they were encouraged by new ideas raised during the talks and hoped another round of trilateral negotiations involving Ukraine, Russia and the US could be announced soon.
Zelensky described his discussions with the American delegation as “very substantive,” saying they covered not only the diplomatic process but also security guarantees and Ukraine’s military and energy needs ahead of winter.

No breakthrough was announced following either the Moscow or Kyiv meetings.
The Kremlin said Monday that it did not rule out resuming trilateral talks involving Ukraine, Russia and the US, although spokesman Dmitry Peskov said it was still too early to discuss possible dates or a venue.
Peskov also declined to disclose details of the latest US proposals or identify which issues remained the most difficult.
The latest diplomacy comes as fighting and Russian attacks on Ukraine continue despite efforts to restart negotiations.
Kyiv has repeatedly said that any ceasefire must be backed by credible security guarantees and cannot simply provide Moscow with an opportunity to regroup before renewing its invasion.
Britain has remained one of Ukraine’s major European military and diplomatic supporters.
Burnham’s government recently approved the transfer of classified British intelligence and production blueprints connected to Anglo-French Storm Shadow cruise missiles to Ukraine, potentially allowing Kyiv to expand domestic production of long-range weapons.
Monday’s Downing Street statement made clear that London intends to continue supporting both Ukraine and the US-led diplomatic process as Washington seeks to determine whether Moscow is prepared to move beyond talks toward an enforceable ceasefire.
Burnham and Trump also discussed the Middle East during their call, including reopening the Strait of Hormuz, and efforts to prevent Iran from acquiring a nuclear weapon.

articles.title: Germany on its way to getting Israel's Iron Dome missile defense system
articles.body:
Germany is on its way to getting Israel’s Iron Dome missile defense system, Defense & Tech by The Jerusalem Post understands.
D&T has confirmed that the letter of intent signed by the German state of Lower Saxony, Rafael Advanced Defense Systems, and Aurelius Capital is the first step toward the European nation acquiring the Iron Dome.
The agreement, signed at the factory on Monday, will see the Volkswagen site in Osnabruck developed into a center of excellence for innovative security and defense solutions. It will combine German engineering expertise, industrial capital and quality standards.
Though it is not a signed agreement, sources who have spoken to D&T have said that the plan later down the road is for Germany to procure the famous interceptor. Germany, a key ally of Israel, currently has the Arrow 3 missile defense system that is manufactured by Israel Aerospace Industries. Berlin, like most of Europe has been bolstering its defenses as Russia continues it's war against Ukraine.
Rafael has been active in Germany for over 20 years and has established a strong presence in the country with various subsidiaries including Dynamit Nobel Defence, EuroSpike and EuroTrophy GmbH.
Yoav Tourgeman, president and CEO of Rafael Advanced Defense Systems, said that the partnership with Germany is part of a long-term relationship with the country “with the idea that the technology will be fully produced in Germany, to protect Germany and Europe.”
“The technology at the heart of this partnership is built for the defense of today, tomorrow, and well beyond. Our outstanding combat-proven technology evolves constantly in order to be ahead of the threats, so that highly reliable defense will always be provided,” he added.
Integral part of Israel’s missile defense array
Initially designed to shoot down short-range rockets, the Iron Dome has, over the past 15 years, become an integral component of Israel's multi-layered defense array.
The system’s modular architecture enables seamless integration with additional defense layers, and it can operate independently or as part of Israel’s broader air defense network that includes the the Arrow (Arrow 2 and Arrow 3) system, which intercepts ballistic missiles outside of the Earth’s atmosphere, and the David’s Sling missile defense system which is designed to intercept tactical ballistic missiles, medium- to long-range rockets, as well as cruise missiles fired at ranges between 40 to 300 km. Rafael has also manufactured the Iron Beam laser defense system, which has been operational along Israel’s northern border.
The system’s early years were defined by rapid operational learning. Iron Dome took part in a long series of conflicts and operations, from Operation Protective Edge, Operation Guardian of the Walls, Operation Breaking Dawn, Operation Shield and Arrow, Operation Swords of Iron, and Operations Rising and Roaring Lion, where it served alongside the Arrow and David’s Sling as a central pillar in the protection of Israel’s home front.
Each round of fighting was followed by a new wave of software updates, radar refinements, and interceptor improvements.
It quickly became evident that the system was a flexible defensive layer capable of handling dense salvos, more complex trajectories, and a wider range of threats. The system’s radar was upgraded to track more targets simultaneously, its algorithms became faster and more selective, and its interceptors were refined to handle longer ranges and more demanding engagement profiles.
Yet, despite its successes, the Iron Dome is not infallible.
Israeli officials have consistently noted that no air‑defense system can guarantee complete protection. Some rockets inevitably penetrate the system’s defenses, underscoring the importance of measures such as early warning sirens and reinforced shelters.
Nevertheless, the system’s high interception rate has significantly reduced casualties and property damage during periods of conflict, altering both military calculations and civilian life in Israel.
An Israeli shield over Europe
Europe has increasingly turned to Israeli air defense technology over the past decade, especially after Russia invaded Ukraine and the growing demand for rapid, combat‑proven systems.
The news comes just one week after Israel and Greece have formalized one of the largest defense export agreements in Israel’s history, a €3 billion government‑to‑government deal that will see Israel design and deliver a complete, multi‑layered national air defense architecture for the Hellenic Republic’s Achilles Shield project.
Though the Iron Dome is not part of it, the project will integrate several Israeli‑made systems into a unified national network. At its core are David’s Sling, BARAK MX, and SPYDER missile defense systems developed by the Israeli defense companies and already deployed operationally within Israel’s own air defense array.
The package also includes MMR radars produced by IAI subsidiary ELTA for air surveillance coverage and a new national command‑and‑control system developed by Rafael to integrate all layers into a single operational picture.
The agreement represents the first time Israel will supply a complete, end‑to‑end air‑defense array to another country. According to a statement released by the Defense Ministry, the architecture is based entirely on Israeli systems and incorporates operational lessons drawn from Israel’s recent wars wherein these systems played central roles in intercepting thousands of hostile aerial targets, including drones and ballistic missiles launched by Iran, Hezbollah, and the Houthis in Yemen.
Central European states have also moved toward Israeli systems, with the Czech Republic receiving the Spyder medium‑range system, Slovakia selecting the Barak MX, and Estonia contemplating purchasing the David Sling missile defense system as it bolsters its long-range air defenses and plans to invest over €1b. in a new long-range ground-based air defense system to protect strategic sites.
Germany has also purchased Israel’s Arrow 3 as a response to Russia’s war against Ukraine and the growing proliferation of advanced missile systems. Germany signed the $3.5b.Arrow 3 contract in November 2023, the largest defense deal in Israel’s history at the time. In December, the two countries signed a $3.1b. follow-up contract to expand interceptor and launcher stocks.
Arrow 3, developed by Israel Aerospace Industries (IAI), is a highly maneuverable system designed to provide ultimate air defense by intercepting ballistic missiles when they are still outside the Earth’s atmosphere.

articles.title: Danger remains real despite Israeli wins against Iranian nukes, sources tell 'Post'
articles.body:
Despite Israeli wins against Iran’s nuclear program in 2025’s 12 Day War and in early 2026, its potential danger remains real, although not imminent, multiple sources have told The Jerusalem Post.
Among the positives are that Iran is currently not operating centrifuges to enrich uranium, its 60%- and 20%-enriched uranium are not yet easily accessible, and the vast majority of its nuclear facilities were rendered inoperable by the two major rounds of airstrikes, the Post has learned.
Those are no small achievements, setting back Iran’s nuclear program in many ways even more than during “pause” periods from 2003-2007 and from 2015-2018, when large portions of Tehran’s nuclear program were frozen although not dismantled, and other portions were still being clandestinely expanded.
Despite these achievements, the potential nuclear threat remains more serious than was hoped for in the periods immediately after the wars of 2025 and 2026, the Post also understands.
Therefore, while each facet of the nuclear program has been significantly improved for Israel, a gap of concern remains.
On the one hand, the vast majority of Iran’s estimated 20,000 centrifuges have been eliminated. On the other hand, a sizable number of centrifuges have survived deep underground.
Even if only a few hundred advanced IR-6 centrifuges could be salvaged and reconnected to their cascades at some medium-term point, that would be enough, at some future undefined point in time, to secretly weaponize enough uranium for a weapon, multiple sources have told the Post.
Tehran could develop clandestine digging strategy around enriched uranium, sources warn 'Post'
Separately, Tehran could develop a clandestine digging strategy to extract its 60%- and 20%-enriched uranium from underneath the rubble and deep underground in a way that circumvents US and other surveillance, multiple sources have said.
It is public knowledge from regular satellite reports from the Institute for Science and International Security and others that the Iranian regime is constantly adding structures to hide certain areas from ongoing satellite coverage.
In these reports, the Iranians are portrayed as digging in a wide number of areas, many of which are at a distance from the primary portion of any of the nuclear facilities that were attacked.
It could take months or even years of digging underground from a distance to smuggle out the 60%- or 20%-enriched uranium. But the possibility of secretly transferring as little as one-tenth of it might be a sufficient basis for an eventual nuclear bomb, according to the sources.
IAEA has been blind to Iran's nuclear program since 12-day June 2025 war, Grossi says
Keeping tabs on all of these issues is harder than ever in some ways. The International Atomic Energy Agency remains completely blind regarding Iran’s nuclear program since at least June 2025, IAEA Director-General Rafael Grossi told the agency’s Board of Governors on Monday.
“As stated in the report, [the] agency has neither received information from Iran regarding the status of its declared nuclear material or facilities nor had access to any of those facilities to conduct in-field verification activities,” he said. “Therefore, the agency was unable to discharge its safeguards responsibilities under the NPT [Non-Proliferation Treaty] Safeguards Agreement at declared nuclear facilities in Iran.”
People familiar with the matter said they did not expect Iran to outsmart Israeli and American intelligence, but they also do not want to underestimate the Iranians’ frequently shocking resourcefulness.
According to the sources, this may mean that the crux of keeping Tehran’s nuclear program “in the box” may shift again to some extent from uranium enrichment to holding back any weapons development activities.
Although not in the spotlight as much, one of the main focuses of Israeli airstrikes on Iran’s nuclear facilities was not only the enrichment sites but also those for converting enriched uranium into uranium metal, as well as for developing hemispheres to place them on a nuclear warhead.
Absent these and other assets, even a significant volume of weaponized uranium would not really help Iran because it would be unable to launch the uranium on a missile that could reach Israeli territory from a distance of 1,000 or more kilometers.
Preventing Iran from rebuilding such weapons facilities is now one of the primary missions of Israeli intelligence, people familiar with the matter have told the Post. So far, Tehran has failed to achieve any real progress in this area.
In essence, Iran’s nuclear program has been far more damaged than some critics have said. Yet there are also potential vulnerabilities for Israel regarding the surviving remainder of the program that senior Israeli defense officials and politicians have openly acknowledged immediately after each operation.
This means that Tehran’s nuclear program has been delayed by some years in some ways, along with its ability to rebuild the parts of the program that were struck. In other ways, however, Iranian ingenuity means that Israel remains threatened, even if the danger is reduced and less imminent.

articles.title: Ukrainian journalist asks Trump’s envoy to his face whether he was disgusted to sit across from “international criminal” Putin. Witkoff wouldn’t answer directly
articles.body:
At a Kyiv press conference on 6 September, Ukrainian journalist Dmytro Gordon asked US special envoy Steve Witkoff, to his face, whether he found it repugnant to sit across a table from Russian President Vladimir Putin. Witkoff did not answer directly, saying only that settling the war means keeping relations and communication open with both sides, according to Gordon.
US President Donald Trump began his peace efforts as soon as he returned to the White House in January 2025, promising to end the war in a single day. It did not happen. Instead, Russia has only stepped up its strikes on civilians and expanded the volume and types of weapons it uses for mass terror.
“And finally, aren’t you disgusted to be sitting at the same table with an international war criminal, the butcher of the Ukrainian people, who is personally responsible for the tragedy in Ukraine?” Gordon asked.
It is a reference with legal grounding, as the International Criminal Court issued an arrest warrant for Putin in 2023 over the deportation of Ukrainian children.
The questions Witkoff would not answer
Witkoff did not provide direct answers to the questions. He only added that, in order to resolve the war, it is important to maintain relations and communication with both sides of the conflict.
According to Trump’s special envoy, he has traveled to Moscow approximately eight times, where he met with Putin and his team, and said they "have always received respect from President Putin".
In practice, however, none of these meetings resulted in anything other than an intensification of the strikes. In the winter of 2025, a specific peace plan was discussed that, at the time, consisted of 20 points.
Yet as the discussions continued, Russia intensified its terror against civilians, destroying an entire thermal power plant in Kyiv and plunging millions of Kyiv residents and people in other cities into darkness amid temperatures as low as -15°C. Now, as the US is holding its anti-ballistic missile interceptors, this scenario will likely continue this winter.
“The language of force”
“Don’t you think that Putin, the Russians, and Russia understand only one language well — the language of force?” the journalist asked.
There was no direct answer to this question either. Instead, Witkoff said that their job is to bring the two sides together and improve communication.
Earlier, there have been numerous occasions when channels of communication between Russia and Ukraine have existed. This was confirmed by Kyrylo Budanov, Head of the Office of the President of Ukraine and former intelligence chief, according to The New York Times.
Russia attempted to murder Gordon
In 2025, the Security Service of Ukraine said it had foiled an assassination attempt against journalist and media manager Gordon. According to the agency, the FSB of Russia was behind the plot to murder the prominent media figure.
According to investigators, the Russian intelligence service offered a $400,000 reward for carrying out the assassination.
As then-SBU chief Lieutenant General Vasyl Maliuk told journalists, Dmytro Gordon “triggers” Russians, while the Russian authorities regard him as Ukraine’s main “propagandist.”

articles.title: India to arm Su-30MKI fighters with hypersonic Russian air-to-air missile – report
articles.body:
India to arm Su-30MKI fighters with hypersonic Russian air-to-air missile – report
India is reportedly working on a plan to equip the Indian Air Force’s workhorse Sukhoi-30MKI fighter jets with advanced long-range Russian air-to-air missiles.
The Indian Defense Ministry is expected to consider a proposal to modify the Su-30MKI fleet to carry the Russian RVV BD air-to-air missiles, which can fly at hypersonic speeds and take out targets up to 300 kilometers away, ANI news agency reported.
The RVV BD is the export version of the R-37M missile, one of the world’s longest-range air-to-air missiles. It is designed to shoot down tanker and early warning aircraft past enemy fighter escort from long range. The Defense Acquisition Council meeting on Monday is expected to take up the proposal, the report said, citing sources.
The RVV BD is compatible with Russia’s advanced fifth-generation Su-57 fighter jet – which has already been offered to India.
Russian President Vladimir Putin is set to visit New Delhi later this week for the 18th summit of BRICS nations. A discussion on the possible sale of the Su-57 was on the agenda of the India-Russia Inter-Governmental Commission on Trade, Economic, Scientific, Technological and Cultural Cooperation held last month in Moscow.
New Delhi, which exchanged missile and drone strikes with nuclear-armed neighbor Pakistan last year, is rapidly modernizing its Sukhoi-30s. The planes have been modified to carry the air-launched version of the Brahmos supersonic cruise missile, and their avionics and electronic warfare suites are being upgraded under the ‘Super Sukhoi’ program.
The upgrades have taken on a new urgency as China has moved its J-20 fifth-generation aircraft next to the Indian border in Tibet, and is reportedly planning to transfer its J-35 fifth-generation fighters to Pakistan.
A defense acquisitions panel on Monday, chaired by Defense Minister Rajnath Singh, cleared a slew of proposals worth $11.64 billion to enhance the “war-fighting capability” of the air force, and various systems for the navy and the army.
“This upgrade is going to be formidable,” retired Air Marshal Anil Chopra told RT India.
He said India has been diversifying its defense purchases, but also maintaining strategic autonomy, despite US sanctions.
“Threats are being given to us for purchasing Russian oil and also weapon systems. We’re continuing to upgrade and use the Russian system,” he said. “Ours is a time-tested relationship.”
The Indian Air Force operates about 258 Su-30MKI – an India-specific variant of the multi-role fighter aircraft – and state-owned Hindustan Aeronautics Limited is producing 12 more at its Nashik facility to replace those lost in accidents over the years.
The jets saw action during last year’s clash with Pakistan – which India code-named Operation Sindoor – covering Indian formations and firing Brahmos missiles at Pakistani airbases.

Ukraine war latest: Drone and missile alerts sound in Kyiv amid temporary attack pause on capitals

- Kyiv shortens curfew to 1-5 am

Russian drones were reported flying toward Kyiv on Sept. 7, according to Ukrainian monitoring channels. A temporary agreement between Russia and Ukraine stipulated neither country's capital would be attacked during a visit by U.S. envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner.
The Kyiv City Military Administration declared a brief drone air raid alert on Sept. 7, as monitoring channels reported Russian drones moving in the direction of the capital. No strikes or damage in Kyiv were reported by officials at the time of publication.
A Russian attack did, however, cause damage in the surrounding Kyiv Oblast, according to the regional military administration. A private house and a car were damaged in Brovary district, while a warehouse and an enterprise were damaged in Boryspil district. No casualties were reported.
At 7:42 p.m. on Sept. 7, Kyiv authorities issued a new air raid warning for the capital, citing a missile threat and urging residents to immediately seek shelter.
The drone activity comes amid an agreement between Russia and Ukraine that neither country's capital would be attacked from midnight Sept. 5 to Sept. 8, while Witkoff and Kushner were visiting to discuss peace talks.
The two envoys arrived in Kyiv on Sept. 6 for their first visit to the Ukrainian capital after holding talks in Moscow a day earlier. The arrangement did not amount to a broader ceasefire, and Russia continued attacking other regions of Ukraine during their visit.

Russia is economically much weaker than it was at the start of the full-scale war, but likely has resources to fight for two more years, Ukrainian military intelligence (HUR) chief Oleh Ivashchenko told Ukrinform in an interview published on Sept. 7.
"The main problems facing the Russian economy are a shortage of labor resources, a growing federal budget deficit, and a deteriorating situation in the banking system," Ivashchenko told the Ukrainian news agency.
"At the same time, it still has enough resources to wage war against Ukraine. We do not rule out that these resources will last through 2027 and 2028."

Ukrainian drone strikes overnight hit a railway bridge over the North Crimean Canal in Russian-occupied Crimea, Ukraine's General Staff said on Sept. 7.
The railway bridge is located near Vladyslavivka, a village in eastern Crimea that hosts a key railway junction in the area, the General Staff said. Russia uses the railway line for military logistics, according to the General Staff.
Other targets hit overnight across Russian-occupied territories include Russian command posts in eastern Luhansk and southeastern Zaporizhzhia oblasts, an ammunition depot in Luhansk Oblast, and an automated reconnaissance system known as Grenadier in Crimea, the General Staff said.

The curfew in Kyiv will be shortened to 1 a.m. to 5 a.m. amid intensified Russian aerial attacks on the Ukrainian capital, the city's mayor, Vitali Klitschko, announced on Sept. 7.
The changes will take effect at midnight on Sept. 10, and the public transportation services in Kyiv will also be extended by an hour, according to Klitschko. He said that the working hours of restaurants, cafes, shopping malls, and other venues would remain unaffected.
The curfew reduction comes as the security situation in Kyiv deteriorates, with air raid alerts going off regularly and restricting movements within the city. Round-the-clock Russian drone attacks have targeted Kyiv for over a week, from the end of August to the beginning of September, leaving the city's residents to worry about what awaits them in the upcoming winter.
At the same time, all entertainment and sports events in open air locations or facilities without shelters will be temporarily prohibited in Kyiv, said Klitschko.

The pro-Ukrainian saboteur reportedly contacted the Atesh group, a partisan force operating behind Russian lines, and burned through wiring in a communications tower around the Russian city of Perm, roughly 1,500 kilometers (930 miles) from Ukraine, in August.
The Russian servicemember joined the Ukrainian resistance group due to his "disagreement with the country's leadership and the lawlessness he witnessed in the army," the Atesh group claimed on Telegram.
The loss of the tower reportedly disrupted data transmission in the area, leaving security personnel and Russian military units unable to maintain reliable coordination. Ukrainian drones then struck the nearby LUKOIL-Permnefteorgsintez on Aug. 21. Operations at the refinery were temporarily suspended following the strikes.

articles.title: A US-Russia deal won’t end the war. It will start the next one
articles.body:
After talks between President Putin and President Trump's representatives Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner ended, the White House called them "substantive." Putin's aide Yuri Ushakov called the meeting "substantive, constructive and exceptionally frank," adding that the US representatives "formulated a number of considerations on ways to reach a settlement."
According to Bloomberg, Putin is prepared to end the war only on Moscow's terms, and Russian demands have hardened because the Kremlin believes it holds a military advantage. Putin expects to seize the rest of Donetsk Oblast by the end of 2026, Reuters reported, citing a person close to the Kremlin: "There is no chance of reaching an agreement on the front line until Putin finishes taking the rest of Donetsk Oblast."
Witkoff has made many trips to Moscow. He arrived in Kyiv for the first time only the day after. That speaks volumes about where America's focus lies: Russia, not Ukraine.
The danger, though, is not the deal alone. Two American processes are running at once—a peace negotiated on Moscow's terms and a review that would pull US forces from Europe—and together they lower both the political and the military cost of a Russian attack on NATO. Everything below is why that convergence, not the handshake in Moscow, is the thing to watch.
Negotiating a Russian lie, not its strategic demand
Russia has long used disinformation to create strategic ambiguity, offering the West four different tales—all unpleasant, one designed to look like an "easy way out."
The first—give up Crimea, Luhansk, Donetsk, Zaporizhzhia, and Kherson—is what Trump's plan offers. But Putin's demands transcend Donbas, as both his 2024 speech and Russia's military operations show. His stated prerequisites require Ukrainian withdrawal from territory Russian forces do not even occupy, the "demilitarisation" and "denazification" of the Ukrainian government—meaning its replacement with a pro-Russian one—and Ukrainian neutrality excluding NATO.
The second: Foreign Minister Lavrov said in January that "nothing will work without settling the issue of Novorossiya"—which adds Kharkiv, Dnipropetrovsk, Mykolaiv, and Odesa.
The third, "one people, one nation," claims all of Ukraine. And the fourth—"the Russian World," the only one formalised in Russian strategic documents—encompasses the "former territories of Kyivan Rus, the Kingdom of Muscovy, the Russian Empire, the Soviet Union, and the contemporary Russian Federation." Its ultimatum of 17 December 2021 demanded that the US leave the European continent entirely.
This is what Russia is fighting for, and why the Kremlin sees an existential war: Russia becomes a Great Power or remains a pariah state. Trump is negotiating the first lie. If he intended a just and lasting peace, he would be addressing the fourth—Russia's actual strategic aim—not the one designed to look easy.
The so-called peace plan
Six months before Trump took office, I concluded his "peace plan" was a blueprint for Russian victory over Ukraine and the West. The 28-point plan published by Axios in November 2025—which alarmed European leaders, excluded NATO, and imposed demands on the EU beyond America's authority—proved the point.
The transactional logic is explicit. On 2 September, Trump said: "We want to have good relations with Russia, Ukraine, with everybody. Be great for business. Russia's got great land and very valuable land."
Asked whether Washington would pressure Russia if talks stalled, Kushner sidestepped and applied a corporate frame to the war: "In the business world, you think in terms of win-win." Of Putin, he added: "he has certain objectives... but there are different aspirations he has for his country that can also be achieved once this is concluded."
The administration does not care about peace or war, international law or the security architecture—only trade. And it has signalled that the aggressor should be rewarded, implying might makes right. This is why Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent recently blamed Ukraine—not Russia—for high fuel prices: "Ukraine has decided that they want to blow up Russian energy assets." He said it after a meeting with Russia's finance minister.
The sequence of talks
The US representatives went to Moscow first, Kyiv second—carrying the aggressor's terms to the victim, not the other way around. Since they are effectively negotiating European security, an objective team would have consulted US allies in Europe first. According to the EU Ambassador to Washington, Jovita Neliupšienė, Moscow has not abandoned its military objectives, and "the top priority remains unchanged: to provide Ukraine with everything it needs to defend itself"—implying US and European strategy are no longer aligned. We already know the US is not planning to provide Ukraine any defence aid. French, British and German security advisers were allowed to join only the final Kyiv session—informed, but not allowed to influence their own security.
It is strategically absurd to let Europe's two strategic adversaries negotiate European security—which is what happens when we insist on solving the war from within NATO and the EU rather than through a coalition of like-minded countries able to stand up to both Russia and Washington.
The military half
For Europe, the ongoing US review of its troop levels and basing matters as much as the peace process—and it is equally transactional. Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth announced the review at NATO on 18 June, framing it as a transition to "NATO 3.0," with Europeans taking on conventional defence and the US concentrating on strategic and nuclear priorities.
The Pentagon's Terms of Reference reportedly examine troop levels, basing, overflight rights, capability gaps Europeans would have to fill—and, tellingly, "the degree to which individual allies support broader US strategic priorities." The Pentagon expects four options ready by 6 November, with a decision in December. There is no reason for optimism.
There are roughly 80,000 US personnel in Europe. At the June meeting, Washington indicated it would immediately reduce the aircraft, reconnaissance drones and naval assets it would activate for Europe in a crisis. Defenders note that Congress set a floor of 76,000 and that European allies have largely filled earlier gaps. But the floor guards the headcount, not the cavalry. The assets that decide a European war—the aircraft, drones and naval power surged in a crisis—are exactly what Washington signalled it would hold back.
More troubling is a Pentagon questionnaire—sent partly in response to Europe's unwillingness to back Trump's war on Iran—asking whether governments have been "publicly supportive of US foreign policy priorities," whether they restrict US basing and overflight, and whether those restrictions could be removed. It reads as a loyalty test: the US making the size and location of its commitment conditional not on military utility but on political alignment—turning the alliance into a competition for American favour and gutting any European strategic autonomy.
Be afraid
If the USA and Russia reach an agreement, be afraid. It would mean the Kremlin has convinced the White House to give it what it wants—and that Russia is positioned to do what a growing number of European intelligence services warn of: war against NATO by 2029.
The US will want its forces out of Europe before Russia moves. Russia will await the outcome of both processes before it strikes, to reduce the risk of a US response. On my read of both timelines, the assault comes while Trump is still in office—and Russia may attack within three years. Europe will not be ready until 2035.
The two processes are not coordinated. They do not need to be. Both flow from the same transactional instinct, and both land on the same variable: Russia's calculation of whether it can attack NATO and survive the response. A deal on Moscow's terms removes the political cost of aggression—it tells the Kremlin that force sets borders and the West will ratify what the battlefield delivers. The force-posture review removes the military cost, cutting the reinforcement flow that makes an assault on NATO expensive. Lower the political cost through the "peace" and the military cost through the withdrawal, and both sides of Moscow's equation fall at once. That is the link: not a plan, but a convergence—two American processes that together make a Russian war on NATO cheaper to start.

articles.title: Ukraine’s Brave1 says it can down Russia’s Banderol missiles with  cruising speed 650 km/h for less than what they cost, and has destroyed at least four
articles.body:
Ukraine says it has found a way to shoot down Russia's Banderol jet missiles for less than the missiles themselves cost. A system from a developer in the Brave1 defense-tech cluster has already destroyed at least four of them, Brave1 said, releasing video of the intercepts.
The point is the price tag, not the kills. The Banderol is built to be cheap for Russia and expensive for Ukraine to stop, forcing Kyiv to spend scarce, costly air-defense missiles on a low-cost weapon. A counter that costs less than the target flips that math back against Russia.
A cluster developer downs four Banderols
The footage Brave1 shared shows a defender in the cluster hitting at least four Banderol missiles.
"The cost of interception is substantially cheaper than the cost of the drone-missiles themselves," the cluster said.
It added that several products capable of countering the Banderol now exist, and that it is scaling the ones that work.
Kronshtadt built the missile to bleed defenses
The S8000 Banderol is a hybrid of a cruise missile and a jet-powered attack drone, made by the sanctioned Russian firm Kronshtadt, which also builds the Orion reconnaissance drone that launches it. It flies at a cruising speed of 520 to 560 km/h and up to 650 km/h at full throttle, and carries a 114.3-kilogram fragmentation-high-explosive warhead, of which 49.5 kilograms is explosive.
The design is built for cheap mass production: it runs on a Chinese hobby turbojet sold online for about $16,000, and Ukrainian media have put the cost of a single Banderol near $100,000, Ukrainska Pravda reported. Russia has used it to strike Odesa, Kharkiv, Kyiv, and Black Sea ports.
Ukraine keeps finding cheap answers
Brave1's system is the newest in a pattern of low-cost counters. In July, Ukrainian troops downed Banderols with Swedish Bofors L70 anti-aircraft guns designed in the late 1940s. The task now is to turn scattered successes into enough deployed systems to blunt a weapon Russia is firing in growing numbers, which is what Brave1 says it is racing to do.
