articles.title: North Korea Commissions Kang Kon Destroyer That Capsized During 2025 Launch
articles.body:
North Korea has commissioned the Kang Kon destroyer into its navy, following its capsizing during an unsuccessful launch attempt last year.
The Korean Central News Agency (KCNA) reported on this.
The commissioning ceremony took place on September 6 at the port of Wonsan on North Korea’s east coast. North Korean leader Kim Jong Un attended the event.
The destroyer is the second Choe Hyon-class warship and is going to join the Korean People’s Navy East Sea Fleet.
Despite being officially commissioned only now, the ship has already been used to demonstrate its combat capabilities. In early July 2026, it carried out a mass missile launch.
In addition to the missile launches, North Korean state media showed the ship’s onboard artillery systems firing.
In May 2025, during the ceremony to launch the ship from the slipway, the destroyer lost stability and tipped onto its side, damaging its hull.
The accident was captured in satellite imagery. North Korean state media also confirmed it.
Kim Jong Un, who attended the launch ceremony, said the accident was caused by negligence and irresponsibility that could be regarded as a criminal act.
He ordered the ship’s restoration to be completed by the June plenary meeting of the Workers’ Party of Korea and those responsible for shortcomings in its design and construction to be held accountable.
Following the failed launch, North Korean authorities arrested four officials, including the chief engineer, construction manager, and project administrative manager. They also detained Ri Hyong-son, a member of the Central Military Commission, whom the state-run Korean Central News Agency (KCNA) identified as one of the officials primarily responsible for the accident.
As early as June 2, 2025, satellite imagery captured the ship being raised while in an upright position.
On June 5, the destroyer was successfully launched and sent to a shipyard in Rajin for repairs. On June 8, the ship was moved into a dry dock to complete the restoration work.
The 5,000-ton Choe Hyon-class warships are multi-purpose missile destroyers of the Korean People’s Army Navy. They are equipped with two types of vertical launch systems: larger for strike weapons and smaller for air defense missiles. The ships have a total of 74 launch cells.
The ship’s artillery armament includes a 127 mm automatic gun, as well as a close-in weapon system that visually resembles the Soviet 30 mm AK-230 and AK-630 systems.
A North Korean anti-aircraft gun system located at the stern provides the ship’s air defense. Its appearance resembles that of the Russian Pantsir-M.
The anti-ship and strike weapons are housed in transport-launch containers on both sides of the ship. They likely include eight Hwasal-2 cruise missiles capable of engaging moving targets. In addition, each side is equipped with four launchers for a North Korean equivalent of the Spike ER/NLOS missiles.
Militarnyi previously reported that North Korean authorities had instructed shipbuilders to construct a new Choe Hyon-class destroyer within one year.

articles.title: Kyiv stockpiles food and water as Russia’s new aerial tactics threaten a brutal winter
articles.body:
Kyiv is building reserves of food and drinking water to help residents during prolonged power outages and other emergencies, the Kyiv City Council said on 7 September.
The preparations come as Russia continues to target Ukraine’s critical infrastructure and food supply chains, while Ukrainian officials warn that water systems could also come under attack. Kyiv is therefore preparing for a broader range of disruptions this winter, not just power outages.
The city is preparing the reserves ahead of the 2026–2027 fall and winter season, with priority given to low-income residents and people facing difficult circumstances.
The supplies will also be available at Points of Invincibility, emergency support centers set up to provide basic services during prolonged blackouts, for people affected by emergencies, and for workers involved in emergency and other urgent response operations.
Kyiv prepares for attacks on food and water supplies as Russia makes air attacks harder to stop
Russia has increasingly targeted infrastructure connected to Ukraine’s food supply in recent months. Russian strikes have hit food warehouses and distribution facilities around Kyiv, contributing to shortages and periods of empty supermarket shelves in the capital and other parts of the country.
Ukrainian officials have also warned that Russia could target water infrastructure as part of its attacks on critical civilian systems, raising concerns about access to drinking water during prolonged disruptions.
This year, the threat is particularly acute as Russia has expanded its use of ballistic missiles and introduced faster, jet-powered Geran drones that are harder for Ukraine to intercept. Ballistic missiles can only be reliably intercepted by a limited number of air defense systems, while the faster drones reduce the time available to detect and engage them.
Russia has destroyed 90% of Ukraine’s modern commercial storage capacity. Retail logistics are being reshaped
Kyiv prepares for another difficult winter
Russia's strikes have repeatedly targeted Ukraine's energy infrastructure during previous winters, causing extended blackouts and disruptions to heating and other essential services.
Kyiv is now preparing for the possibility that attacks could again leave residents without electricity or access to essential supplies for extended periods.
Kyiv says food supply remains stable, for now
Oleh Kuіavskyi, deputy head of the Kyiv City State Administration, said the city's preparations are focused not only on accumulating supplies but also on ensuring they can quickly reach people who need them.
“Food security in the capital is not only about having the necessary reserves, but also a clear system for their distribution and delivery to those who need help most,” Kuіavskyi said, according to the Kyiv City Council.
He said Kyiv's consumer market remains stable and predictable, while the city continues to hold agricultural food fairs across its districts to help maintain access to basic food products.
Reserves could feed 25,000 people
According to the city council, Kyiv has already formed and is maintaining reserves of key food products for use if the energy system comes under severe strain.
With support from charitable and civic organizations, the city can organize hot meals for up to 25,000 people, officials said.
The city's Department of Industry and Entrepreneurship Development also plans to purchase another 20,000 food packages for use during emergencies.
The reserves are being coordinated through Kyiv's Humanitarian Headquarters, established in February 2022. The body coordinates the city administration, district administrations, municipal companies, charities, and donors, including the accounting and distribution of emergency resources.

Russia Identifies US Missile Sites in Norway It Would Target in a Military Conflict
Russia has identified US missile deployment sites and their command-and-control centers in Norway as potential targets in the event of a military conflict, following Washington’s reported deployment of a missile system capable of launching Tomahawk cruise missiles.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to Reuters on September 7, Russia’s Foreign Ministry said Moscow would pay “particular attention” to locations associated with the US missile systems, warning that the deployment had further undermined prospects for strategic stability talks between Russia and the United States.
The Russian Foreign Ministry specifically pointed to a US missile system based on Mk-41 launchers deployed in Norway. The launchers can accommodate different types of missiles, including Tomahawk cruise missiles.
Moscow claimed that missiles launched from Norway could reach a significant portion of European Russia, including Moscow. Reuters reported that US media had indicated Washington delivered the new missile launch system to Norway in August.
Russia’s Foreign Ministry said the deployment sites and command-and-control centers associated with the US systems “would become targets in the event of a military conflict.”
The ministry also argued that the deployment of US ground-based intermediate-range missile systems in Europe had effectively eliminated conditions for renewed discussions with Washington on strategic nuclear stability.
“Steps such as the deployment in Europe of US ground-based intermediate range missiles that pose a threat to the Russian Federation ‘reset to zero’—to put it mildly—the conditions for constructive dialogue with the US on strategic issues,” the ministry said, according to Reuters.
Moscow linked the Norwegian deployment to the broader breakdown in arms-control dialogue between Russia and the United States. The Russian Foreign Ministry said strategic stability talks had been curtailed under the previous US administration and described the current administration’s plans for multilateral negotiations involving China as “unrealistic.”

articles.title: Russia and North Korea open first road bridge across their shared border
articles.body:
Russia and North Korea have opened the first road bridge across their shared border, in the latest sign of the rapidly deepening ties between the two countries since the start of the war in Ukraine.
The one-kilometre bridge spans the Tumen River between Khasan in Russia’s far east and Tumangang in North Korea, along a remote and sparsely populated stretch of the countries’ shared border just a few miles from the coast.
Speaking by video link during the bridge’s opening ceremony on Monday, Russia’s prime minister, Mikhail Mishustin, said the new crossing would spur development in a range of areas, including tourism, while creating new jobs
“I am convinced that the expansion of cross-border transport infrastructure will provide a powerful impetus for the further development of trade, economic, scientific, technological and cultural cooperation,” Mishustin said.
The road bridge is named after the Soviet officer Yakov Novichenko, who is credited with saving North Korea’s founding leader, Kim Il-sung, from an assassination attempt by a pro-South Korean group.
After the opening ceremony, convoys of vehicles crossed the bridge from both sides.
Russia and the secretive North Korea regime are already connected by a railway bridge across the Tumen, as well as regular flights between Vladivostok and Pyongyang.
Ukrainian human rights groups have warned that the bridge may be intended to provide a discreet military logistics corridor between the two countries.
Truth Hounds, a Ukrainian human rights organisation, has described it as a likely future corridor for moving North Korean troops, construction brigades and military officials into Russia, while allowing Russian technology and resources to travel in the opposite direction with less risk of detection.
Ties between Moscow and Pyongyang have strengthened dramatically since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. North Korea has sent thousands of troops to Russia’s Kursk region to help Moscow repel a Ukrainian incursion launched there in 2024.
In return, Russia is believed to have provided North Korea with air-defence missiles, electronic warfare equipment, drones and spy-satellite technology, according to South Korean intelligence.
Russian and North Korean officials have also touted North Korea as a new holiday destination since the country reopened to Russian tourists in 2024, with thousands of Russians visiting its newly opened beach resorts and ski slopes since then.
Russia’s increasingly close embrace of totalitarian North Korea has raised eyebrows even in Moscow.
During an interview with the Russian broadcaster RBC last month, a reporter asked Sergei Lavrov, Russia’s longtime foreign minister, how the country had “ended up” with just “two allies – North Korea and Iran”.
Lavrov pushed back against the premise, saying there was “nothing wrong” with such company.
At the same time, some of Russia’s traditional partners have shown growing frustration with Moscow’s continuing war in Ukraine and the fallout it has caused across the region.
During a meeting in July, Kazakhstan’s president, Kassym-Jomart Tokayev, a longtime ally of Moscow, told the Russian president, Vladimir Putin, that he was hearing from leaders of many countries who questioned why Russia was still waging the war.
“The nature of the conflict isn’t entirely clear for many, including us,” Tokayev told Putin.

articles.title: IAEA has been completely blind to Iran’s nuclear program for over a year, Rafael Grossi says
articles.body:
The International Atomic Energy Agency is completely blind regarding Iran’s nuclear program and has been since at least June 2025, IAEA Director-General Rafael Grossi said on Monday.
“As stated in the report, [the] agency has neither received information from Iran regarding the status of its declared nuclear material or facilities nor had access to any of those facilities to conduct in-field verification activities,” he told the Board of Governors. “Therefore, the agency was unable to discharge its safeguards responsibilities under the NPT [Non-Proliferation Treaty] Safeguards Agreement at declared nuclear facilities in Iran.”
“Consequently, we were not able to verify their status for safeguards purposes and the associated nuclear material, and as a result, I am also unable to report in relation to the implementation by Iran of relevant provisions of the UN Security Council resolutions or the board’s resolutions of November last year and June this year,” he added.
“It is more than a year since the agency lost continuity of knowledge in relation to the previously declared inventories of LEU [Low Enriched Uranium] and HEU [Highly Enriched Uranium] enriched up to 60% U-235 at the declared nuclear facilities affected by the military attacks of June 2025,” Grossi said, citing Israel’s war with Iran last year.
“The agency’s lack of information about these facilities and associated nuclear material and our inability to conduct verification activities at these facilities is a matter of serious proliferation concern,” he said. “The situation needs to be rectified with the utmost urgency.”
Grossi called on Iran “to engage with the agency constructively in order to make possible the full and effective implementation of agency safeguards in Iran and to fulfill its responsibilities under the NPT Safeguards Agreement.”
“A return to diplomacy and negotiations aimed at finding a solution to issues related to Iran’s nuclear program is imperative, and the agency stands ready to support such efforts,” he said. “The situation regarding Iran’s nuclear program has implications for the global nonproliferation regime.”
At a press conference following his speech to the board, while using diplomatic language, Grossi belittled explanations by Iran, Russia, and China that tried to claim Tehran has not allowed IAEA inspections out of concern for the inspectors’ security in a war zone.
Ukraine has been a worse and more constant war zone, he said, adding that inspectors have still managed to carry out inspections at nuclear facilities throughout the war between Russia and Ukraine.
The IAEA Board of Governors is expected to refer Iran to the UN Security Council for further condemnation or action.
Iran has threatened the IAEA and the West with severe consequences if such a referral is made, but it remains unclear what added pressures Tehran can bring against the other parties involved given its weakened state both in military and nuclear capabilities.
As such, Iran’s main card is to continue to block the Strait of Hormuz, which is a major source of leverage that it is already exercising.
Iran refuses access to IAEA inspectors since joint Israel-US attacks
Since Israel and the US attacked Iran in June 2025, Tehran has refused to grant the IAEA access to any of its nuclear facilities, saying the agency would pass on classified information to those who attacked it.
Grossi occasionally has said solving nuclear issues by the use of force is less productive than diplomacy, but Iran has viewed his stance on US and Israeli attacks on Iran’s nuclear program in 2025-2026 as too mild and was offended that he did not condemn the attacks more forcefully.
Grossi has complained that Iran has cut off IAEA access almost completely in 2025-2026, with the exception of a visit to the Bushehr nuclear facility, which has never presented any threat. Tehran began to significantly limit access to IAEA inspectors as early as 2021.
In November 2021, Grossi cited Iran’s violation of a supposed deal from September 12, 2021, to renew IAEA access to the critical Karaj nuclear site.
Tehran had reneged on the deal, he said, and the “lack of access to the Karaj workshop has meant that the restoration of surveillance and monitoring at all of Iran’s facilities and locations in relation to the JCPOA [Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action] could not be completed. This is seriously affecting the Agency’s ability to restore continuity of knowledge at the workshop, which has been widely recognized as essential in relation to a return to the JCPOA” 2015 nuclear deal.
Iran’s IAEA obstruction predates the 2025 war with Israel
Iran has accused the US of being the first to violate the 2015 Iran Nuclear Deal. US President Donald Trump pulled out of that deal in May 2018, during his first term in office.
When Trump pulled out, Grossi said, the Mossad had provided tens of thousands of files of evidence of Iranian lying and cheating relating to the deal from when it seized Iran’s nuclear archives in January 2018.
Although Iran was complying with some significant aspects of the deal, the archives proved that the regime was also systematically seeking to hide the weapons aspects of the nuclear program from the IAEA and the West.
Currently, neither Iran nor the US is pushing for IAEA involvement until they resolve their other ongoing standoff over the Strait of Hormuz.
Israel remains concerned that whatever is left of Iran’s nuclear program after the 2025-2026 airstrikes has not yet been closed down and is not being overseen by IAEA inspectors.

articles.title: The drone war is becoming a race to adapt, rather than perfect
articles.body:
The drone war is becoming a race to adapt, rather than perfect
A soldier launches an RQ-35 Heidrun drone used for reconnaissance and artillery fire correction in the Zaporizhzhia direction in Ukraine, on Feb. 22, 2026. (Dmytro Smolienko / Ukrinform / NurPhoto via Getty Images)
Robert Brull
CEO of FibreCoat
You don't need to have followed the Ukraine war closely to recognize the central role that drones have played in the conflict.
As I write, the Russian e-commerce giant Ozon is reeling following a third day of long-range drone strikes— an indication not only of the significance of drones, but also of how the drone war has evolved.
At the start of the war, such an attack was impossible; now, as of summer 2026, drones shape almost every act as part of wider systems. But readers of this publication will know that.
What relatively few onlookers outside of Ukraine recognize is the way in which every drone innovation on one side of the conflict has prompted innovation on the other. Ukrainian recon drones led Russia to pursue jamming and short-range air defense innovation; Russian improvements in electronic warfare and air cover led to the use of expendable quadcopters by Ukraine.
On and on in this vein the war has proceeded, all the way to where we are now, where drones are mass-produced, often by 3D printers for expediency, and long-range drones are routinely flying deep into enemy territory to target oil refineries, logistics hubs, and ostensibly civilian businesses seen to be supporting the Russian war effort.
Now Russia is responding with increasingly advanced air defense systems and spoofing technology. And that has brought into focus new and increasingly sophisticated forms of technology that can protect enough long-range drones (protecting all of them is next to impossible) that some are able to penetrate those Russian defenses and carry out their missions.
Chief among these, perhaps, is chaff, a relatively old technology that has recently been brought into the 21st century.
Used on military aircraft and warships since World War II, chaff is in effect a radar countermeasure typically made of tiny aluminum-coated glass fibers.
When dispensed, it forms a large, reflective cloud or fog in which each individual glass fiber reflects a radio frequency.
These resonate, confusing enemy radar, blinding ground systems, spamming false signals, and tricking radar-guided missiles into going for the wrong target. They can create massive uncertainty across even sophisticated radar systems and make decision-making difficult. They also impose a financial cost: enemies waste ammunition aiming at the wrong target.
But technology itself is not the most important thing. Innovation, at least by itself, is not the most important thing, either. The decisive factor in Ukraine, and it will be the decisive factor in all modern conflicts, is the ability to innovate at speed.
Warfare has become a competition to learn and apply what you learn fastest. Ukraine builds a new drone; Russia replies with drone countermeasures; Ukraine tweaks the drone to overcome those countermeasures; Russia tweaks its counter-countermeasures. A system that takes ten years to develop risks becoming useless before it's even out in the field.
Why does this matter? Because wider Europe is rearming. And there's an important lesson here. The present and the future of war are being decided not by the large, established contractors who produce a small number of highly expensive platforms able to last decades, but by smaller, more adaptable, fast-moving companies.
Indeed, the use of 3D printers in Ukraine points very clearly to what matters: pragmatism, flexibility, mobility, modularity, cost-efficiency, and, of course, efficacy.
In Ukraine, technology is designed, built, sent into the field, and used; and operators on the front line then feed back to the manufacturers, who redesign the technology, rebuild it, and send it into the field to be used.
It's a virtuous, if lethal, cycle of innovation, one in which iteration is continuous and "good enough for now" is the aim of the game. You could say that this is the ultimate free market of ideas, where the most useful solutions are adopted, and those that don't are not. The Ukrainians are picking and choosing the best products for their goals in a constantly evolving marketplace.
My view is that Europe has an opportunity to support its friends in Ukraine while testing out new technologies.
It could replicate the Ukrainian model of innovation, bolster Ukraine's armed forces, and use its battlefield as a live innovation engine: testing its systems, allowing them to break, then improving them at speed.
Indeed, assuming there was Ukrainian approval, Europe should consider allocating a portion of its budget towards battlefield testing.
At the very least, we should be more humble in how we think about modern warfare and seek to learn the many lessons that have been learned so painfully by Ukraine in its attempt to hold off their Russian aggressors.
First among these is that the aim of the game is to adapt, not perfect: to iterate quickly rather than build complex systems slowly. New chaff innovations may be the latest chapter in this technological contest. But it won't certainly be the last.
Editor's note: The opinions expressed in the op-ed section are those of the authors and do not purport to reflect the views of the Kyiv Independent.

articles.title: Ukraine develops technology to shoot down Russian Banderol missile drones

Ukraine develops technology to shoot down Russian Banderol missile drones

articles.title: Sanctioned Russian ship Lady Mariia, tied to arms shipments, attacked by drones in the Mediterranean Sea
articles.body:
The Russian roll-on/roll-off cargo ship Lady Mariia (IMO: 9220641), which is under U.S. and Ukrainian sanctions, was attacked by drones in the Mediterranean Sea, according to the head of Ukraine’s Institute for Black Sea Strategic Studies, Andrii Klymenko, who reported that the vessel had been heading toward Syria.
Klymenko published footage of the attack, while a longer video was posted on the Telegram channel of Russian opposition commentator Alexander Nevzorov. The footage shows drones dropping munitions onto the vessel, with a fire breaking out after one explosion. Nevzorov claimed the Lady Mariia was hit 12 times and suggested that the drones had been launched by Ukrainian forces from the territory of Libya. He added that the ship was carrying Iranian weapons and armored vehicles intended for Russia.
Klymenko also hinted that the drones had been launched from Libyan territory, writing: “And it wasn’t us. Those were some nice, unknown drones from Libyan territory. What do we have to do with it?”
Ukrainian authorities have not officially commented on the attack. The number of hits, the origin of the drones, and the nature of the cargo on board have not been independently confirmed. The Ukrainian outlet UNITED24 Media also noted that claims about Iranian weapons and a Libyan launch point were based on Nevzorov’s reporting and had not been independently verified.
According to the vessel tracking platform Starboard Maritime Intelligence, the Lady Mariia left St. Petersburg in early August. The vessel passed through the Strait of Gibraltar on Aug. 29 and then called at the Algerian port of Oran. It later headed east across the Mediterranean. On the evening of Sept. 5, the Lady Mariia stopped transmitting its AIS (Automatic Identification System) signal.
Starboard Maritime Intelligence data also shows that since the spring of 2020, the Lady Mariia has made three calls at the Syrian port of Tartus and three at the Iranian ports of Bandar Abbas and Khorramshahr. The platform also recorded two calls at the Libyan port of Al-Buraika.
Ukraine’s military intelligence agency (HUR) lists the Lady Mariia among the vessels that have been used to transport military cargo and weapons for Russia.
The ship is owned by the Russian company MG-Flot LLC, formerly known as Transmorflot. In May 2022, the U.S. imposed sanctions on Transmorflot and vessels linked to it. The Lady Mariia, which was previously named Stella-Maria, was also placed under U.S. restrictions. Ukraine imposed sanctions on the Lady Mariia on May 23, 2026.
According to HUR, MG-Flot is linked to Astrakhan businessman Dzhamaldin Pashayev, who built his business around the Port of Olya in Russia’s southern Astrakhan Region. The port is seen as one of Russia’s key logistics hubs for the International North-South Transport Corridor, which connects Russia with Iran.

articles.title: IAEA says Iran blocking nuclear inspectors as Hormuz threats mount
articles.body:
IAEA chief Grossi told the Board of Governors that Tehran had provided no information on declared nuclear materials and inspectors had no on-site access, as Iran's parliament speaker threatened US energy assets with retaliatory strikes and the IRGC warned vessels off the southern Hormuz corridor.
The UN's nuclear watchdog said Iran had provided no information about its declared nuclear materials or facilities and that inspectors had no on-site verification access, as Tehran threatened retaliation against South Korea if Seoul joined Gulf maritime operations and Iran's parliament speaker warned US energy assets across regional waters faced reciprocal strikes.
IAEA Director General Rafael Grossi told the agency's Board of Governors that Iran was not meeting its Non-Proliferation Treaty safeguards obligations and called for constructive engagement to restore full oversight.
Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmail Baghaei dismissed the IAEA reports as instruments of Western political pressure and warned Tehran would take countermeasures if a new resolution referred Iran's nuclear file back to the UN Security Council.
He attributed restrictions on IAEA inspectors to US and Israeli strikes on Iranian enrichment infrastructure.
Grossi also argued that Western efforts to revive UN Security Council oversight implicitly validated Iran, China and Russia's position that the snapback sanctions mechanism was illegal. "It is a mistake to test what has already been tested," he said.
Hormuz corridor near completion
Baghaei said bilateral talks with Oman on a temporary safe transit corridor in the Strait of Hormuz were near completion and would likely be registered with the International Maritime Organisation within days.
"We can now say that talks between Iran and Oman have reached their final stage," he said.
However, the IRGC Navy's political deputy said safe passage through the US-designated southern corridor was practically impossible.
"Any vessel entering this corridor will no longer be safe from strikes once it reaches the area of Khasab, Oman," the official, identified as Mohammadi, said.
He said the IRGC maintained continuous intelligence and operational monitoring of vessel movements across the Persian Gulf, the Strait of Hormuz and the Sea of Oman.
Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council, announced the establishment of an "exclusion zone" outside the Strait of Hormuz, extending from the US naval blockade line into the Persian Gulf.
"Any ship entering this area without Iran's permission and coordination will have its details — along with the names of its owner and charterer — registered and placed on Iran's sanctions list," he said.
Parliament speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf separately warned on social media that US oil and gas assets across regional waters were exposed to retaliatory strikes.
South Korea warned
Baghaei warned South Korea that any military presence in Gulf operations would be treated as direct support for US aggression.
He framed the warning in diplomatic terms, noting that Iran-South Korea relations spanned more than 64 years and were based on mutual respect.
"The military presence of any other country or its participation in operations in the Persian Gulf and the Strait of Hormuz will be regarded as direct support for the perpetrators of this aggression and will have serious consequences," Baghaei said.
South Korea's foreign ministry said Seoul was in close contact with the international community over the situation in the Middle East and was working to help restore stability and ensure free passage through the strait for all vessels including its own.

articles.title: Ukraine Strikes Deep Into Russia, Hitting Airfield, Major Oil Refinery and Air Defenses
articles.body:

Ukraine Strikes Deep Into Russia, Hitting Airfield, Major Oil Refinery and Air Defenses
Ukrainian forces struck the Rostov-on-Don airfield, the Ryazan Oil Refinery, and three Russian air defense assets during an overnight operation in Russia on September 6, with fires reported at both the airfield and refinery.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine on September 6, Ukrainian forces targeted the Ryazan Oil Refinery in Russia’s Ryazan region. A fire was recorded at the facility, which the General Staff said is involved in supplying the Russian armed forces.
The Ryazan refinery is one of Russia’s largest oil-processing facilities, with a design capacity of around 17 million metric tons of crude per year. It produces gasoline, diesel fuel, aviation kerosene, and other petroleum products.
Fire Point, a Ukrainian defense manufacturer, said its FP-1 drones struck equipment at two major primary crude-processing units at the refinery.
The company reported hits on the distillation columns of the ELOU-AVT-6 unit, the refinery’s largest primary processing unit with an annual capacity of 8.5 million metric tons, as well as equipment at the AVT-3 unit, which has a capacity of 3.1 million tons per year.
Together, the two units account for more than 77% of the refinery’s primary oil-processing capacity, according to Fire Point.
Separately, Ukrainian forces struck the Rostov-on-Don airfield in Russia’s Rostov region. The General Staff reported a fire in the area of the facility but said the extent of the damage was still being assessed.
Three Russian air defense assets were also hit in the Rostov region—a Podlet radar station and two Pantsir-S1 surface-to-air missile and anti-aircraft artillery systems.
The Podlet radar is designed to detect low-altitude and small aerial targets, including drones and cruise missiles. The Pantsir-S1 is a short-range air defense system combining surface-to-air missiles with 30 mm automatic cannons to engage aircraft, helicopters, drones, and precision-guided weapons.
The strikes were part of a broader overnight Ukrainian drone operation that targeted at least 14 Russian regions, as well as temporarily occupied Crimea and areas over the Black and Azov seas. Russia’s Defense Ministry claimed 258 Ukrainian drones were intercepted, while Moscow and the surrounding region were left untouched under a temporary airspace arrangement during US envoy visits.

articles.title: China calls itself neutral—but its fiber ends up in the drones that hit Ukraine
articles.body:
Shipping documents show how a Chinese state company kept supplying Russia's drone factories with the raw material used in its long-range attack drones, Politico reported. Chinese parts have been recovered from downed Russian drones before. These records are the first to show the raw material shipped straight to the factory—a sanctioned arm of Russia's nuclear giant Rosatom.
Russia's mass-produced attack drones run on parts sourced worldwide that keep slipping past Western export controls, and Ukrainian cities take the hits almost nightly. Kyiv has spent the war naming the foreign suppliers behind that hardware, one component at a time.
What the documents show
The papers trace 46 metric tons of carbon-fiber chemicals from Jilin Chemical Fiber Group to Alabuga-Volokno, a Rosatom subsidiary in Tatarstan. The exporter disguised the cargo under a customs code meant for civilian fibers like nylon, said weapons expert David Albright, who studies Russia's drone production. That precursor, polyacrylonitrile, is the raw ingredient for the light carbon fiber in Russia's Shahed-type attack drones.
Drones of that type killed at least 15 people at a shopping mall in central Ukraine in August. Albright estimated the load could yield enough for as many as 1,300 kamikaze drones. The Kyiv-based Ukrainian Security and Cooperation Center, a think tank close to Ukraine's government, gathered the documents and shared them with Western governments. The US House Select Committee on China judged them legitimate, and Ukraine confirmed their authenticity.
Why Beijing can't plead ignorance
Alabuga-Volokno has faced Western sanctions since 2023 from the US, UK, EU, Ukraine, and others. Jilin faces none. Albright said the documents would let the State Department sanction the Chinese supplier. Serhii Kuzan, who heads the Ukrainian center, called China arguably the main and only source of these composite materials.
Former US officials rejected any idea that Beijing was unaware.
"The idea that Chinese state-owned enterprises can hide things from the Chinese government just doesn't wash," said Dennis Wilder, a former CIA deputy assistant director for East Asia and the Pacific.
Denials and a summit
Rosatom claimed it works in full compliance with the law. China's embassy in Washington called the evidence an attempt to "smear and scapegoat China," saying Beijing has never supplied lethal weapons.
The disclosure lands as US President Donald Trump prepares to meet Xi Jinping in Washington this month. In late August, Xi told Vladimir Putin their ties were set to strengthen.

articles.title: Ukraine has 67 companies working to shoot down Russia’s jet-powered drones en masse, Zelenskyy says. Only three to five have real results
articles.body:
Ukraine now has 67 companies working to shoot down Russia's jet-powered drones en masse, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said. He gave the number at a Kyiv press conference alongside US presidential envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, Ukrinform reported.
Most of those firms are still chasing the problem, and only a few have working systems. The race matters because Russia's jet-powered Geran drones fly too fast for the mobile gun teams that once downed the slower models. Russia has sharply expanded the jets' use over the summer, launching them by day as well as by night and driving air-raid alerts over Kyiv almost hourly.
Prototypes outnumber proven interceptors
"Today, we have about 60 companies in Ukraine already working on intercepting jet-powered drones, and doing so on a mass scale. To be precise, there are 67," Zelenskyy said.
He added that three to five have shown real results, and the next step is mass production.
Zelenskyy calls it all "Plan B"
Zelenskyy framed the entire defensive build-up as a fallback.
"All this defense is 'Plan B,' though right now it is very relevant. 'Plan A' is to accelerate diplomatic possibilities as much as possible, to reduce escalation from Russia," he said.
He spoke as the US envoys pressed a peace push in Kyiv, with no breakthrough announced.
He also called anti-ballistic defense Ukraine's weak point, saying he would raise it in upcoming meetings in Norway and Canada, and that the US plans to increase production of Patriot interceptors next year while Germany expands its own output under existing licenses.
Ukraine needs the interceptors to down Russian ballistic missiles that come several times per week. Each Russian attack on Kyiv costs the city budget about $12 million. More than four thousand buildings in Kyiv have been damaged by Russian strikes, with each attack adding to a repair bill the city carries alongside the human losses.

articles.title: Russia Deliberately Fired Kh-101 Into Poland to Test NATO’s Red Lines, Ukraine’s Intelligence Chief Says
articles.body:

Russia Deliberately Fired Kh-101 Into Poland to Test NATO’s Red Lines, Ukraine’s Intelligence Chief Says
Ukraine’s military intelligence believes that a Russian Kh-101 cruise missile that struck Poland on July 30 was deliberately directed into NATO territory as part of Moscow’s effort to test the Alliance’s response to a potential armed attack.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to an interview with Ukraine’s military intelligence chief Oleh Ivashchenko published by Ukrinform on September 7.
“The trajectory of the missile differed from the trajectory of the group of missiles launched at Ukrainian territory from the very beginning of its flight, which indicates the deliberate nature of the actions,” Ivashchenko said.
He said Ukrainian intelligence possesses materials indicating broader aggressive intentions by Russia toward Europe and assessed the July incident as an attempt by Moscow to test NATO’s “red lines” regarding collective defense in the event of an armed attack against an Alliance member.
Ivashchenko said Russia has been unable to achieve its objectives in its war against Ukraine and is therefore considering escalating its confrontation with countries on NATO’s eastern flank in an effort to pressure European governments into reducing military support for Kyiv.
Ukraine’s military intelligence is tracking Russian violations of NATO members’ airspace, including Poland, Romania and the Baltic states, as well as military provocations near NATO borders, sabotage against European critical infrastructure, false-flag operations, cyberattacks and disinformation campaigns.
Ivashchenko warned that Russia is expected to further increase pressure on NATO’s eastern flank to test the response of Alliance members and portray them as unwilling to enter into an open confrontation with Moscow.
According to him, such actions are also intended to increase psychological pressure on European countries and ultimately undermine their military assistance to Ukraine.
Earlier, Poland announced it would temporarily restrict air traffic along its eastern border from September 10 to December 9 to give its air defense systems greater freedom to respond to potential Russian threats.

articles.title: US to pull air defences from Iraqi Kurdistan in September exit
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
US to pull air defences from Iraqi Kurdistan in September withdrawal
The United States will withdraw all its forces and air defence systems from Iraq by 30 September as planned, Iraqi government security adviser Qasim al-Araji said on Sunday.
Al-Araji said the US withdrawal from Iraq would include air defence systems stationed in the Kurdistan Region, including Patriot and C-RAM systems that have played a key role in intercepting Iranian drone and ballistic missile attacks.
Speaking to reporters in Baghdad, Al-Araji said US-led international coalition forces would leave Iraq completely by the end of September, in line with an agreement reached between Baghdad and Washington.
"On 30 September, coalition forces will withdraw completely from Iraq, and this is the implementation of the agreement between the previous government and the international coalition," he said.
Baghdad and Washington reached an agreement in September 2024 setting a deadline of the end of September 2026 for concluding the international coalition's mission against the Islamic State group (IS) in Iraq, following months of talks between the two sides.
Al-Araji said Prime Minister Ali al-Zaydi's government was proceeding with the agreement and that the US had expressed its readiness to withdraw by the agreed date.
He said the withdrawal would include all coalition air defence systems deployed in the Kurdistan Region, adding that the phased removal of troops and equipment had already begun.
The systems have served as an important security shield for the Kurdistan Region against repeated Iranian attacks.
A Kurdish official in Erbil separately told The New Arab that coalition forces would withdraw completely along with the air defence systems.
The official said the Kurdistan Regional Government had expressed concern that their removal could leave the region vulnerable to repeated Iranian attacks and potentially result in casualties.
The regional government had sought guarantees from Baghdad that Iranian attacks would not resume following the US withdrawal and that any renewed attacks would be stopped, the official said.
However, the official said neither the federal government nor the Kurdistan Regional Government currently had clear assessments of what the security situation would look like following the withdrawal.
Al-Araji also linked the withdrawal to efforts to bring weapons held by armed factions under state control.
"The issue of regulating weapons will be discussed after the coalition forces withdraw," he said. "A comprehensive mechanism will be agreed to place all weapons under state control."
He pointed to progress in talks between the Iraqi government and armed factions over the issue.
"The talks are going very well, and there is a positive understanding. The committee of the Coordination Framework, under the direct supervision of the prime minister, is continuing its work to resolve this issue," he said.
The comments come as several powerful Iran-aligned Iraqi factions resist government efforts to bring their weapons under state control, with some demanding the withdrawal of foreign forces as a condition for doing so.
Under the timetable agreed by Iraq and the United States, US forces are due to withdraw from their remaining bases and conclude their military mission in Iraq by 30 September 2026.
Despite the reduction in its military presence, the United States has said it will continue cooperating with Iraqi forces on training, intelligence sharing and counter-IS operations through bilateral arrangements that do not require a large-scale military presence.
No official figures have yet been released on how many US troops or other international coalition personnel have already left Iraq.

articles.title: Chinese State Firm Secretly Sent Russia 46 Tons of Carbon-Fiber Materials for Strike Drones
articles.body:
- Category
- World
Chinese State Firm Secretly Sent Russia 46 Tons of Carbon-Fiber Materials for Strike Drones
A Chinese state-owned company supplied Russia with materials needed to manufacture hundreds of strike drones, according to internal Russian shipping records obtained by POLITICO on September 4.
The documents, which have also been reviewed by Western governments, offer evidence to date that a Chinese state-controlled company has continued supplying a sanctioned enterprise linked to Russia’s military-industrial complex.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Shipping and customs records show that earlier this year, the Chinese company sent 46 metric tons of carbon-fiber-related chemicals to a subsidiary of Russia’s state nuclear corporation Rosatom. According to POLITICO, the shipment was declared under a customs classification typically used for materials such as nylon and polyester.
The Rosatom subsidiary develops critical components for strike drones used by Russia in attacks against Ukraine, including a strike on a shopping mall in central Ukraine in August that killed at least 16 people.
Chinese-made components have previously been found in Russian drones recovered after attacks on Ukraine. However, the newly obtained records reportedly provide the first detailed evidence of a Chinese state-owned company directly exporting essential drone-production materials to Russia.
The Ukrainian Security and Cooperation Centre (USCC), a Kyiv-based think tank, uncovered the documents through Russian sources and subsequently shared them with the governments of the United Kingdom and the United States.
David Albright, founder and president of the Washington-based Institute for Science and International Security, said the records could provide grounds for the US State Department to sanction the Chinese supplier, as they document shipments to the Rosatom subsidiary after it had been sanctioned by several Western countries.
“Rosatom and its enterprises operate in full compliance with applicable laws and regulatory requirements,” said a spokesperson for the Russian state firm. “Any claim to the contrary is false and demonstrates a lack of understanding of how Russia’s customs authorities operate.”
The reported shipments come amid growing scrutiny of Chinese companies accused of supporting Russia’s war effort. The European Union’s diplomatic service has been seeking sanctions against four Chinese companies over their alleged involvement in supporting Russia’s war against Ukraine.
The companies were expected to be included in the EU’s next sanctions package. Officials said their alleged activities included supporting Russia’s shadow fleet, supplying chemicals used by the Russian military, and providing components for the production of attack drones.
The proposed measures were outlined in a May 21 document and formed part of a smaller sanctions package that two EU officials said was expected to be approved by foreign ministers at a meeting in Luxembourg on June 15.

articles.title: Germany plans “Cyberdome” and mobile anti-drone units after Leipzig airport sabotage attempt
articles.body:
Germany’s Interior Ministry is preparing a package of measures to protect the country from Russian drone attacks, computer network intrusions, and acts of sabotage, according to a Bild report citing Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt. The measures are being developed following an attempted attack at Leipzig/Halle Airport in early August, which Berlin has blamed on Russia.
Dobrindt’s plan calls for expanding the federal police mobile anti-drone units. Teams equipped with helicopters and specialized vehicles are expected to be based in Frankfurt, Munich, Hamburg, Berlin, Stuttgart, Düsseldorf, Leipzig, Hanover, and Cologne.
They would be tasked with protecting airports, train stations, and other major transport hubs, along with Berlin’s government district. In addition to intercepting drones, the units would be responsible for defusing bombs and other explosive devices.
Operators of critical infrastructure — including water and energy companies, as well as defense plants — would also be given the authority to counter drones on their own. The proposed powers would allow them not only to detect drones but also to actively repel attacks.
Dobrindt told Bild that Russian hybrid attacks had become an everyday reality. He cited the facts of drones carrying explosives, agent activity, network intrusions, and acts of sabotage.
Another part of the plan would expand the use of artificial intelligence, biometric facial recognition, and video surveillance at train stations and other locations. The technologies would be used to identify people preparing attacks or espionage operations and to automatically detect weapons and suspicious behavior.
To counter cyberattacks, the German authorities plan to create a national system called “Cyberdome,” which Bild described as a network of digital sensors designed to detect and repel attempts to break into government and corporate systems.
In early August, Leipzig/Halle Airport temporarily suspended operations after a drone with a detonator was found near a Ukrainian An-124 transport aircraft. A separate cargo plane was diverted to Hanover due to the closure and struck an unidentified object while still near Leipzig; police found damage to the front of the aircraft after it landed.
Investigators later identified two individuals that it suspects participated in preparations for the attack: a Russian-born man carrying a Latvian passport and a Belarus-born man who holds a Russian passport.
German investigators believe the first man organized logistics and acted as an instructor. The second was identified through traces of DNA found both on the drone and on an antenna near the airport. Three drones, either intact or in pieces, were eventually discovered at the scene.
On Sept. 1, the German government formally accused Russia of organizing the attack, citing the results of its police investigation and intelligence findings. Berlin said that in response to the incident it would close Russia’s consulate general in Bonn effective Sept. 18, terminate an agreement governing the Russian House cultural center in Berlin, and tighten entry controls for Russian citizens.
The Russian authorities rejected the accusations, calling the incident a “provocation.”
On Aug. 28, a collection of European countries bordering the Baltic Sea said they planned to create a task force to counter drones and other hybrid threats. At a meeting in Flensburg, Dobrindt said the group was intended to ensure rapid information sharing. The initiative followed a wider rise in drone sightings near European airports, as well as sabotage incidents involving undersea cables and gas pipelines.

articles.title: Ukrainian AI targeting module placed third among 60-plus entries in NATO contest
articles.body:
A Ukrainian company has placed third in a NATO contest to find ways of keeping an enemy's airfields shut down over time. Its artificial-intelligence targeting module finished among the top three of more than 60 entries in the Persistent Airfield Denial Innovation Challenge, Ukraine's Defense Ministry said.
The challenge was run jointly by NATO Allied Command Transformation and the NATO-Ukraine Joint Analysis, Training and Education Center, the first jointly staffed NATO-Ukraine body. The result shows NATO is building a direct channel for Ukraine's combat-tested technology into its own capability development.
On the NATO side, the finalists' proposals were evaluated by representatives of the Alliance's Commands, as well as the NATO Defense Innovation Accelerator DIANA.
An AI module lands third place
Organizers received more than 60 applications and brought nine finalists to Warsaw. The Ukrainian team took third place with a module designed to enhance the autonomy and accuracy of strike systems. The Ukrainian Defense Ministry did not name the developer.
A Czech firm, LPP Holding, won with a long-range system designed to work with minimal outside control, and a Polish team came second with a plan for the pre-planned destruction of key airfield infrastructure.
JATEC feeds Ukraine's lessons to NATO
Ukrainian experts helped define the problem and judge the entries, including officers from the Air Force Command, the Unmanned Systems Forces, and the National Guard's Omega unit.
The challenge, which carried up to €250,000 in prize funding, was the second of the two bodies to run together, after a 2025 round that fast-tracked European firms to counter Russian glide bombs.
In July 2026, Russian aviation used approximately 8,000 guided aerial bombs against Ukrainian cities.
The winning solutions now move to testing and combat validation, which the Defense Ministry said will show how well they work and whether they can scale.

articles.title: Unpublished audits obtained by The New York Times show Ukraine ignored red flags in defense procurement as the country lost at least $1.2 billion to fraud, waste, and mismanagement in 2024 alone
articles.body:
Unpublished audits obtained by The New York Times show Ukraine ignored red flags in defense procurement as the country lost at least $1.2 billion to fraud, waste, and mismanagement in 2024 alone
The New York Times (1 and 2) obtained previously unpublished audits of the Ukrainian government’s military weapons procurement in 2024 and 2025. Ukraine’s State Audit Service and the Defense Ministry’s internal audit unit reviewed the work of the Defense Procurement Agency. Among other findings, the audits showed that Ukraine lost about $1.2 billion in 2024 alone to fraud, waste, and mismanagement in defense procurement. Here’s what else the documents revealed.
- According to the audit documents, Ukrainian authorities ignore red flags in weapons procurement. Contractors that inflate prices or fail to meet delivery obligations rarely face consequences.
- Companies received contracts without demonstrating that they could deliver the weapons. In some cases, contractors did not even have licenses to deliver them.
- Seven of Ukraine’s 10 largest military contractors received new orders despite open criminal investigations into fraud or failures to fulfill previous contracts, or the arrests of executives on corruption charges.
- In 2024, for example, the Pavlohrad Chemical Plant supplied the military with thousands of defective mortar rounds. The Defense Procurement Agency continued to award the company contracts worth hundreds of millions of dollars even after its director, Leonid Shyman, was implicated in a corruption case.
- Auditors identified 18 companies that received new contracts from Ukrainian authorities despite failing to fulfill earlier agreements. Six had not fulfilled a single contract.
- One company failed to deliver any of the 600 specialized drones it had promised. It then received a new contract for 1,950 more drones but delivered only 50 on time.
- About $126 million was lost because authorities rejected better offers and overpaid for weapons. Contracts were also awarded without sufficient legal justification. In one case, companies remain locked in a dispute over what happened to at least $100 million in advance payments on a deal that ultimately fell through.
- Military contractors around the world — including the world’s largest arms dealer, as well as Ukrainian and American companies — profited from the system, while Ukraine lost about $1.2 billion to corruption and inefficient procurement.
- It is unclear whether the Defense Procurement Agency took any action in response to the audit findings, which were classified and never subjected to public scrutiny. Arsen Zhumadilov, the agency’s director, declined to comment. He resigned on August 31.
- Former Defense Procurement Agency adviser Tamerlan Vahabov told The New York Times that the army is not getting what it needs and that failed deliveries and overpayments shrink the budget, leaving too little money to order more weapons and too little ammunition. He called it “a recurring pattern.”

articles.title: Iran conveyed its ‘conditions’ to US – source
articles.body:
Iran conveyed its ‘conditions’ to US – source
Iran has conveyed its conditions to the US through intermediaries after Washington recently sent new proposals to Tehran, a political source in the Iranian capital has told RT.
The reported contacts come amid renewed regional efforts to revive diplomacy after last week’s flare-up, when the US carried out several rounds of strikes on Iran and Tehran retaliated with missile and drone attacks on American military facilities in Jordan and Bahrain.
“Following the halt of negotiations resulting from US breaches of commitments and its repeated failures in military engagements, the US has recently conveyed proposals to Tehran through mediators,” the source said.
Given Washington’s “repeated violations” and “constant fluctuations in its positions,” Tehran responded by conveying its own conditions to the intermediaries, the source added.
The source did not disclose the details of either the American proposals or the Iranian conditions, but said mediators “continue to talk to both parties.”
Tehran has been pushing Washington to honor the commitments outlined in the June Islamabad Memorandum of Understanding (MoU), but the US is now reportedly seeking a new, broader agreement covering both the Strait of Hormuz and Iran’s nuclear program, the Financial Times reported last week.
Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baqaei said on Monday that US and Israeli attacks on Iranian nuclear facilities were themselves the main obstacle to inspections by the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA), arguing that Washington was responsible for the resulting lack of access while simultaneously using the issue to increase pressure on Tehran.
“The ball has long been in the US court,” Baqaei said, adding that Washington must end its military attacks, economic sanctions and naval blockade if it wants to resolve the confrontation.
“Diplomacy is a dynamic and continuous process,” the spokesman said, noting that delegations from Oman and Pakistan have visited Iran in recent weeks, while Qatari representatives held talks with Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi in Tehran on Sunday.
Qatari Foreign Ministry spokesman Majed al-Ansari told CNN that Doha had put forward several ideas and was exploring different scenarios aimed at addressing the concerns of both sides.
Tehran and Muscat have meanwhile reported significant progress on a separate arrangement for a temporary safe shipping route through the Strait of Hormuz. Iranian officials have stressed, however, that such an agreement would not amount to the full reopening of the strategic waterway, as Washington has claimed.

articles.title: Russia has enough resources to wage war for another 2 years – Ukrainian intelligence agency
articles.body:
Russia has enough resources to wage war for another 2 years – Ukrainian intelligence agency
Defence Intelligence of Ukraine (DIU) has said that Russia has enough resources to continue waging war against Ukraine in 2027 and 2028.
Source: Oleh Ivashchenko, Head of Defence Intelligence of Ukraine, in an interview with Ukrinform
Quote: "Meanwhile, it [Russia] still has sufficient resources to wage war against Ukraine. We do not rule out that these resources could last through both 2027 and 2028."
Details: Ivashchenko said that joint efforts with Ukraine's partners are needed to deprive Russia of these resources.
"Sanctions must actually work. We know which countries supply the Russian Federation with electronic components, machine tools and specialised chemicals. Many intermediary companies are emerging that import into Russia goods which subsequently fuel its war machine against us," he said.
Ivashchenko also believes that public discontent among Russians over the war will grow, although it is difficult to say whether this will develop into sufficiently strong protest potential.
"But more than 60% of people are already against the war. This is a consequence of the economic situation and the enemy's heavy personnel losses. We can say that Russia's contract recruitment model has largely exhausted itself. We see that regional budgets in Russia are no longer able to fund payments for contract recruitment. At the same time, Russian troop losses are increasing. Russia's average daily losses range from 1,200 to 1,400 personnel, sometimes reaching 1,500. This includes those killed and seriously wounded," the DIU chief said.
Background: In early June, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy urged Russian leader Vladimir Putin not to continue the war into 2027 and 2028.

articles.title: Ukraine war briefing: US envoys leave Kyiv without breakthrough on ending war
articles.body:

  US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner have held “encouraging” talks with Volodymyr Zelenskyy in Kyiv in their first official visit to Ukraine but made no breakthrough towards ending the war with Russia. The envoys’ trip followed talks with Vladimir Putin in Moscow on Saturday which a Kremlin aide said were “highly useful” while also giving no indication of a breakthrough. Zelenskyy said at a news conference that his talks with the envoys on Sunday covered air defence needs – including Patriot systems – and a “winter package” of support covering both air defence and energy infrastructure before the colder months. He said Kyiv was seeking “serious volumes” of American support on that front, with backing from European partners as well. It appeared the war would continue into winter, he also said.
- 
  Zelenskyy said Russia had intensified strikes on Ukrainian cities before Russia’s State Duma election later this month, calling the attacks deliberate “terror” against civilians. Ukraine was working with 67 domestic companies developing systems to shoot down Russia’s jet-powered drones at scale. He said the sides agreed to hold a follow-up meeting involving Ukraine, the US and Europe, with a location still to be set.
- 
  The US envoys brought new and “more effective” proposals to Ukraine on ending the war with Russia, according to one senior Ukrainian presidential official. “It’s not the same as it was before. This one now is more effective,” the unnamed offical told Agence France-Presse after the talks with Zelenskyy. “They’re still talking. This is actually the most important part. There are three of them now.” Ukraine’s rail operator announced the envoys’ departure from Kyiv early on Monday.
- 
  Witkoff said earlier that both sides would need to compromise, adding: “We think we have the ingredients to get to that place … and we look forward to continuing this as long as it takes.” Kushner said: “Hopefully this trip has come out with some new ways to advance forward. I think we’ve learned a lot from the trip.”
- 
  In Moscow the US envoys had “discussed substantive plans which will be announced in the coming weeks”, a White House official said. The Kremlin said the Americans had “put forward a number of ideas on possible routes to a settlement”, without elaborating. Witkoff said he was hopeful a new round of US-mediated Ukraine-Russia talks would be announced “in short order”. Putin has repeatedly said Moscow intends to seize the rest of eastern Ukraine while Zelenskyy insists Russia should not be rewarded for its aggression.
- 
  A girl was killed and three other people were wounded in a Ukraine drone attack on the Russia-held Black Sea port city of Sevastopol late on Sunday, the city’s Moscow-appointed governor, Mikhail Razvozhayev, said on Telegram.
- 
  Russian forces struck a Ukrainian cargo vessel in the Black Sea which was carrying military equipment supplied to the Ukrainian army by western countries, Russian news agencies reported the defence ministry as saying on Sunday.
- 
  Kyiv’s forces struck the Ryazan oil refinery – about 480km (300 miles) inside Russia – causing a fire, Ukraine said on Sunday.
- 
  Russia’s foreign minister said Germany’s accusation that Moscow was involved in a drone incident near a Ukrainian cargo plane at Germany’s Leipzig airport were, “by and large, the start of a real war”, state news agency Tass reported. “He is, in effect, declaring war on us,” Sergei Lavrov said of the German chancellor, Friedrich Merz. articles.title: Drones Attack Taganrog Airbase
articles.body:
Ukrainian drones attacked the military airfield in Taganrog.
This is evidenced by data from NASA’s FIRMS monitoring service.
The attack on the airfield took place overnight on September 6–7, 2026. According to the service’s data, a fire was detected at 2:44 a.m. in the aircraft parking lot.
The airfield is located approximately 40 km from Ukraine’s state border, at coordinates 47.2450, 38.8496.
The Russian military actively uses the airbase. The 325th Aviation Repair Plant (military unit 23213), which specializes in renovating transport aircraft and Il-76 units, is located there.
The Taganrog Aviation Plant shares the airfield with a military unit of the 5th Aviation Group.
Due to the facility’s proximity to Ukraine, Ukrainian forces have repeatedly targeted the plant’s territory and the airfield itself.
South of this airbase is the factory airfield of the PJSC Beriev Aircraft Company.
The facility repairs and upgrades A-50U AEW&C aircraft, Il-76 transport aircraft, and Il-38 patrol aircraft. It also upgrades and services aircraft operated by foreign customers.
In December 2024, the aircraft manufacturing and repair plant was targeted in a combined attack.
At the time, reports indicated that the strike took place at around 4 a.m. Some Russian media outlets claimed that ATACMS ballistic missiles and Palianytsia drone-missiles were used in the attack.
The plant had previously been attacked in March 2024.
Militarnyi previously reported that after a drone threat was declared in Russia’s Rostov region, a fire broke out at the Millerovo airbase, where the 31st Fighter Aviation Regiment, operating Su-30SM aircraft, is based.

articles.title: ‘Russophobia a national sport’ – Polish party rallies against push to war (VIDEO)
articles.body:
‘Russophobia a national sport’ – Polish party rallies against push to war (VIDEO)
Polish protesters have accused Warsaw of whipping up anti-Russian hostility and dragging the country toward war as the government continues to arm Ukraine and deepen confrontation with Moscow.
Supporters of the Confederation of the Polish Crown party marched through Gniezno on Sunday behind a banner reading “Poland for Peace,” carrying Polish and party flags.
“They’re trying to turn Russophobia into our national sport. But we won’t give in,” activist Marta Czech told the crowd, urging “prudence” as tensions with Russia continue to rise.
Another speaker, Lukasz Pakulski, accused the authorities of frightening Poles with talk of tanks, nuclear weapons, and a wider conflict. “They are pushing us into war,” he said, declaring that “Poles stand for peace.”
The Crown is a traditionalist, Euroskeptic party founded by MEP Grzegorz Braun. It campaigns for tighter immigration controls, less power for Brussels, and Poland’s withdrawal from the EU, while opposing deeper Polish involvement in the Ukraine conflict.
The protest comes as Prime Minister Donald Tusk’s government has continued to support Kiev, arguing that Ukraine’s security is inseparable from Poland’s own. Warsaw has provided around $6.8 billion in aid to Kiev since 2022, including more than $5 billion in military assistance. Poland also hosts around 961,000 Ukrainians under temporary protection.
However, public enthusiasm for the policy has been fading, with a July poll finding that 52% of Poles opposed accepting more Ukrainian refugees, while another survey showed 67% backed deporting unemployed Ukrainian men of military age.
Another survey found 27% believed Western aid to Ukraine was too large, compared with 22% who wanted more, while opposition to Ukrainian EU membership reached a record 40%.
Relations between Warsaw and Kiev have also recently deteriorated over historical grievances after Vladimir Zelensky named a military unit after the Ukrainian Insurgent Army (UPA), which Poland holds responsible for massacring up to 100,000 ethnic Poles during World War II.
President Karol Nawrocki later stripped Zelensky of Poland’s highest state honor, while other politicians have called for an end to free weapons deliveries to Kiev.
Moscow has consistently accused Warsaw of deliberately stoking anti-Russian sentiment while supporting Kiev’s war effort.
Russian officials have also highlighted the Kiev-Warsaw UPA dispute, arguing that even one of Ukraine’s strongest backers can no longer ignore Kiev’s embrace of neo-Nazi ideology and glorification of figures linked to wartime atrocities.

articles.title: Iran warns South Korea against military role in Persian Gulf
articles.body:
Iran warns South Korea against military role in Persian Gulf
TEHRAN — Iran has warned South Korea against any military involvement in the Persian Gulf or the Strait of Hormuz, while accusing Washington of creating disruption in regional shipping and rejecting Western efforts to revive international pressure over Tehran’s nuclear program.
The warnings, delivered by Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baqaei on Monday, came as Tehran sought to reinforce its position on three increasingly intertwined issues: security in the Strait of Hormuz, the continuing confrontation with the United States and Israel, and international efforts to exert pressure on Iran through the International Atomic Energy Agency and the United Nations.
In a Korean-language post on X, Baqaei highlighted the long-standing relationship between Tehran and Seoul but drew a sharp distinction between economic and diplomatic ties and military cooperation with the United States.
Iran and South Korea have maintained diplomatic relations for more than six decades, he said, adding that Tehran values its traditionally friendly relations with Seoul. But under current circumstances, he warned, any operational military participation by South Korea in the Persian Gulf or the Strait of Hormuz would be viewed by Iran as direct support for an aggressor.
Baqaei argued that Iran is currently defending itself against 'US aggression and attacks on Iranian civilians.' Against that backdrop, he said, the deployment or participation of foreign military forces in the strategic waterway could carry serious consequences.
He also rejected the idea that sovereign states should respond to US pressure by joining military operations against Iran, saying that no responsible government should submit to coercion to participate in aggression.
Baqaei separately accused Washington of attempting to shift responsibility for disruptions to commercial shipping and rising energy prices onto Iran, arguing that the crisis in the Strait of Hormuz was triggered by the US and Israel.
In a post on X, he said the waterway had remained open until February 28, when the United States and Israel launched their military campaign against Iran.
Baqaei said the conflict had disrupted commercial shipping, halted tankers, and contributed to higher energy prices. He accused Washington of attempting to portray the resulting economic consequences as a cost imposed on the international community by Iran.
Iran warns against renewed nuclear pressure
Baqaei also rejected efforts by the United States and Israel to pressure IAEA Director General Rafael Grossi and advance a move to refer Iran's nuclear file to the UN Security Council.
He criticized a draft resolution based on a recent IAEA report, arguing that Western governments had repeatedly turned to nuclear watchdog when they were unable to achieve their political objectives through other means.
He also challenged the legal rationale being advanced by Western governments over the so-called snapback mechanism, under which previous UN Security Council sanctions could potentially be restored.
According to Baqaei, Western governments' current actions contradict their own interpretation of the mechanism and effectively reinforce the position previously taken by Iran, China and Russia that the mechanism is not applicable in the present circumstances.
He also accused the three European powers involved in the process of having lost credibility with Tehran and described some of their demands as unreasonable.
The spokesman placed particular responsibility on Washington for the current impasse over IAEA access to Iranian nuclear facilities. He argued that US and Israeli military actions had created the circumstances that prevented normal cooperation between Iran and the Agency.
Baqaei warned that Tehran would respond to any new action against it, describing the latest diplomatic pressure as evidence of hostile intentions and an effort to further escalate tensions.
Iran accuses US of deliberately targeting civilians
Responding to questions about attacks on civilian sites, Baqaei said Iran would continue to hold the United States accountable for violations of international humanitarian law.
He cited several incidents, including a deadly attack on a wedding ceremony on Iran's Sirik Island, as examples of a broader pattern of attacks against civilians.
Baqaei questioned how US forces, which possess highly accurate weapons, could have failed to identify civilian locations such as a school in Minab, a stadium in Lamerd or the wedding venue in Sirik.
Iran, he said, should not allow such incidents to disappear into history without accountability.
Tehran credits Oman with good faith on Hormuz talks
Against the backdrop of the confrontation over the Strait of Hormuz, Tehran also offered a comparatively positive assessment of Oman's role in recent discussions concerning maritime security.
Baqaei said Oman had acted in good faith during talks with Iran on shipping security and emphasized the importance of the interests of the two littoral states.
Oman, he noted, is a neighboring coastal country with longstanding and close relations with Iran and has played a constructive role throughout the process.
At the same time, Baqaei cautioned that the outcome of the next stages remained uncertain.
He said an understanding between Iran and Oman was necessary for securing shipping routes through the Strait of Hormuz, but by itself would not be sufficient to resolve the broader security crisis.
