articles.title: Russia slams US despatch of missile system to Norway as another blow to idea of arms talks
articles.body:
Russia slams US despatch of missile system to Norway as another blow to idea of arms talks
MOSCOW, Sept 7 - Russia on Monday condemned the U.S. deployment of an advanced missile system to Norway, saying the move dealt a further blow to the prospect of U.S.-Russia talks on strategic nuclear stability.
Russia's Foreign Ministry said in a statement that the deployment in Norway of a missile system based on Mk-41 launchers which can be used to fire a range of missiles, includingTomahawk cruise missiles, posed a threat because missiles fired from them would be capable of reaching a substantial part of European Russia, including Moscow.
"Steps such as the deployment in Europe of U.S. ground-based intermediate range missiles that pose a threat to the Russian Federation 'reset to zero' - to put it mildly - the conditions for constructive dialogue with the US on strategic issues," the ministry said.
It added that Russia would pay "particular attention" to the deployment sites and command-and-control centres of U.S. missile systems and that they would become targets in the event of a military conflict.
U.S. media reports suggested Washington had delivered the new missile launch system to Norway in August.
The Foreign Ministry said dialogue on strategic stability between Moscow and Washington had been curtailed under the previous U.S. administration and described plans by the current administration to pursue multilateral negotiations involving China as "unrealistic." REUTERS

articles.title: Syria’s Assad-era reactor configured for nuclear weapons: IAEA
articles.body:
Syria’s Assad-era reactor configured for nuclear weapons: IAEA
UN watchdog says material now is under IAEA safeguards.
Syria’s Assad-era nuclear facility was configured to produce material for possible use in nuclear weapons, the head of the International Atomic Energy Agency has reported.
The nuclear reactor, which the United Nations nuclear watchdog has been investigating with the cooperation of Syria’s new authorities, would have been able to produce fissile material that could be used for weapons, IAEA Director General Rafael Grossi told a media conference in Vienna on Monday.
“This is a reactor that is very efficient in the production of fissile material that could be used directly for the fabrication of nuclear weapons,” he said.
Grossi’s comments came a week after the UN watchdog revealed in a confidential report that it had visited several sites in Syria in August and carried out verification work.
Based on observations at the Deir Az Zor site, the agency said it confirms “that the cooling infrastructure which has now been uncovered is consistent with that of a nuclear reactor”.
The agency added that it would continue to monitor the activities at the site “as the excavation work progresses”.
Syria was believed to have operated an extensive, undeclared nuclear programme under former President Bashar al-Assad that included a nuclear reactor built by North Korea in Deir Az Zor.
It only became public knowledge after Israeli air strikes in 2007 destroyed the facility. Syria later levelled the site and never responded fully to the IAEA’s questions about it.
Grossi said when the inspectors visited the site in August they had to “tear down walls” and go through “very difficult and narrow passages” to reach the nuclear material that had been hidden. The site had “boxes scattered all over the place,” he said.
Grossi said that “the important thing is that this material now is under safeguards” of the IAEA, adding that agency inspectors had managed to install cameras there.
Israel is believed to have its own undeclared atomic weapons programme, which makes it the only nuclear armed country in the Middle East. Israel neither confirms nor denies having nuclear weapons.
The IAEA has said that the former Syrian authorities had failed to report nuclear material, facilities and activities.
Besides the nuclear reactor at Deir Az Zor, the IAEA listed a fuel fabrication plant, where nuclear fuel for the reactor was manufactured and a store for the nuclear fuel, uranium scrap and waste.
During the visit to Syria last month, an IAEA team also visited a previously undeclared site.
The Syrian administration – made up of the group that overthrew Assad in 2024 – notified the agency of its existence in July and invited the nuclear inspectors to investigate.

articles.title: US missile systems in EU show NATO’s intent to expand strike capabilities against Russia: Moscow
articles.body:
Kanyshai Butun
07 September 2026•Update: 07 September 2026
Russian Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova Monday said the deployment of US missile systems in Norway was another “highly destabilizing” move by NATO and accused the alliance of seeking to expand its capability to launch missile strikes deep into Russian territory.
“We regard the deployment in Europe of US systems capable of launching intermediate- and shorter-range missiles as yet another step in the never-ending series of highly destabilizing actions by NATO countries,” Zakharova said.
She accused NATO of seeking to establish control over key maritime routes in the region, saying the US systems deployed in Norway are based on Mk-41 launch cells capable of firing missiles against targets on land and at sea.
She said the systems can launch long-range Tomahawk cruise missiles and that their deployment in Norway puts a significant portion of European Russia, including Moscow, within range.
“Thus, these missile systems can be used in aggressive actions by NATO countries against our country to solve strategic problems,” she said.
The spokeswoman warned that the US missile systems and their command and support infrastructure in Norway would become a focus of Russia’s strategic deterrence forces, including planning for the use of strike capabilities in the event of an armed conflict.
Regarding strategic stability talks with the US, Zakharova said the dialogue had not stalled but was “unilaterally interrupted” by the administration of former President Joe Biden.
She criticized the current US administration’s calls for multilateral negotiations involving China, saying Beijing had repeatedly made clear it had strong reasons not to participate at this stage.
Zakharova said conditions for substantive and productive strategic stability talks between Moscow and Washington had not been established.
“Steps such as the deployment in Europe of US ground-based intermediate- and shorter-range missile systems that threaten Russia will, to put it mildly, ‘zero out’ the prerequisites for constructive talks with the US on strategic issues,” she said.

articles.title: Satellite images show Russian Ka-52 and Mi-28 helicopters destroyed in Sochi drone attack
articles.body:
Satellite images published Sept. 6 indicate that a Ukrainian attack on Sochi and the nearby federal territory of Sirius that occurred overnight on Sept. 4 destroyed two Russian military helicopters — a Ka-52 and a Mi-28 — at a parking area at Sochi airport, while one Mi-8 was damaged.
The assessment was reported by the Ukrainian open-source intelligence (OSINT) channels Absoliutno Nadiine Dzherelo (lit. “Absolutely Reliable Source”) and Dnipro OSINT ⟨ Harbuz ⟩, which published the satellite imagery. The Russian pro-war Telegram channel Voenny Osvedomitel (lit. “Military Informant”) also agreed with the assessment that two helicopters had been lost.
According to the same OSINT sources, the damage from the raid extended beyond the helicopters. Absoliutno Nadiine Dzherelo reported that two RVS-2000 storage tanks were destroyed at an oil depot near Sochi airport, while four RVS-1000 tanks were damaged (the RVS designations refer to standard Russian vertical steel storage tanks, with the number indicating their approximate capacity in cubic meters).
The channel also published an image of a Russian radar post in the city of Adler and said there had been at least two hits on the radome — the protective radio-transparent dome covering the station.
Another satellite image published by the same channel showed an air defense position in Sirius. The analysts said two launchers and a Pantsir surface-to-air missile and gun system of an unidentified variant had been destroyed there.
The Insider had previously detected a thermal anomaly in the same area — near the Psou River — and reported that an air defense position was located there.
On the night of the attack, Ukrainian drone and missile manufacturer Fire Point said its FP-1 drones had struck several targets in Sochi, including a Lukoil oil depot, fuel infrastructure near Adler airport, and a position belonging to an S-400 air defense system.
Some of the consequences of the raid were already confirmed on Sept. 4. That day, the Krasnodar Region’s operational headquarters said a fire had broken out after drone attacks on Sochi and Sirius. Officials reported no casualties, though windows were shattered in several homes and other buildings.
The Insider then analyzed data from NASA FIRMS and found heat signatures near the airport’s fuel complex and near the aforementioned air defense position by the Psou River in Sirius. Thermal anomalies can indicate fires, explosions, or other intense heat sources, but do not by themselves establish the cause of the heat signature.
Sochi Mayor Andrei Proshunin later warned residents that publishing photographs or video showing the aftermath of the attack was prohibited.
Russia’s Defense Ministry, meanwhile, said 490 Ukrainian drones had been shot down over several Russian regions beginning on the evening of Sept. 3, including over the Krasnodar Region. The ministry did not say how many drones had attacked the Sochi and Sirius area.
Russian authorities did not report any losses of military equipment or damage to the radar post, nor to the airport oil depot or the air defense position.

articles.title: Europe’s biggest nuclear power plant back to normal after weeks in emergency mode
articles.body:
Europe’s biggest nuclear power plant back to normal after weeks in emergency mode
Power supply to the Zaporozhye Nuclear Power Plant (ZNPP) has been restored after more than two weeks in emergency mode, the CEO of the Russian state nuclear energy corporation Rosatom, Aleksey Likhachev, has said.
The main external power line to the plant was cut off back in March following what the Ukrainian authorities described as “damage” to transmission towers. It has never been restored, with no explanations from Kiev.
Since then, the ZNPP has had to rely solely on the backup line – until August 20, when it was shut down by automatic control systems following an unspecified “incident” in territory controlled by Ukraine. That forced the power plant to fall back on emergency diesel-powered generators.
On Monday, Likhachev told journalists that external power supply to the ZNPP had finally been restored, and the facility was now “operating as normal.” The Rosatom chief thanked all the parties involved in establishing a temporary local truce needed for the repair work, including the Russian defense and foreign ministries. He also praised the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) for its “mediation efforts.”
The ZNPP operator also confirmed that external power had been restored. No violations of safety limits were reported, and the radiation situation at the plant and in the surrounding area remained stable and did not exceed natural background levels, it said in a statement. The operator added that the second power supply line has yet to be restored and regular fuel supplies to the station need to be facilitated.
Diesel fuel deliveries to the station were “problematic” because of Ukrainian shelling targeting the roads in the area, the ZNPP communications director, Evgenia Yashina, told Interfax earlier.
Europe’s largest nuclear power plant and the adjacent city of Energodar have been targeted by Ukraine on multiple occasions with artillery and drones since Russia took control of the facility in March 2022.
In July, a Ukrainian drone hit a ZNPP service vehicle on the edge of the plant’s industrial site, killing its chief engineer, Aleksandr Yakovlev, and his driver. Back then, Likhachev called the strike a “deliberate terrorist act.”
According to the Rosatom CEO, more than a dozen employees of the plant have been killed and many others wounded in Ukrainian attacks over the past three months. Kiev’s actions pose the “real danger of a massive nuclear incident” affecting parts of Russia, Ukraine, and the EU, he warned.
Several months ago, the Ukrainian military also started remotely mining the area near the ZNPP and Energodar, where plant employees reside, according to the nuclear chief. In early August, four ZNPP employees were injured by Ukrainian landmines dropped by drones.
Moscow has repeatedly criticized the IAEA, which has experts deployed at the ZNPP, for acknowledging the attacks on the facility but stopping short of blaming Ukraine for them.

articles.title: Chinese state company secretly supplied Russia’s Rosatom with raw materials for producing Shahed-type Geran drones
articles.body:
Chinese state-owned company Jilin Chemical Fiber Group supplied Russia with 46 metric tons of raw material for producing carbon fiber — enough to produce components for roughly 1,300 Geran-type attack drones — according to a joint investigation by Politico and The Telegraph, which based their findings on internal Russian transport and customs documents.
According to the outlets, the supplies went directly to Alabuga-Volokno, a subsidiary of UMATEX — Rosatom’s division for advanced materials and composites that operates a plant in the Alabuga special economic zone in Tatarstan supplying high-strength carbon fiber for the mass production of Russia’s long-range Geran (“geranium”) drones, which are built on the basis of the Iranian Shahed.
The raw material in question is polyacrylonitrile tow, or PAN precursor, an indispensable component for producing lightweight, high-strength carbon fiber. It is used to reinforce the drone’s wing and internal structures, including the fuel tank and engine.
According to David Albright, founder of the Washington-based Institute for Science and International Security, the volume of PAN precursor supplied is enough to produce carbon fiber for roughly 1,300 Russian-made suicide drones. “You can’t build the airframe without it,” Albright explains.
The documents also indicate that the shipment may have been deliberately disguised, as it was filed under a customs code that is used for civilian synthetic fibers like nylon and polyester. Under the correct classification, the shipment should have gone through as a dual-use good, Albright says.
Kerri Bitsoff, a former U.S. Treasury official who worked on sanctions against Russian arms procurement networks, concurred that the use of a different customs code could indicate an attempt to conceal the sensitive nature of the shipment.
Ukraine’s Center for Security and Cooperation (USCC) obtained the paperwork from Russian sources and shared it with the U.S. and UK governments. The U.S. House Select Committee on China reviewed the documents and found them to be authentic, an American official said. Their authenticity was also confirmed by the Ukrainian government.
USCC says it has identified at least eight tenders since 2022 for container shipments of PAN precursor from Jilin Chemical Fiber Group to Alabuga-Volokno.
Alabuga-Volokno and UMATEX have been under Western sanctions since 2023. Jilin Chemical Fiber Group is not currently under Western sanctions, and the company did not respond to reporters’ requests for comment. Meanwhile, Rosatom stated the parent company and its enterprises operate “in full compliance with applicable laws and regulations,” and called claims to the contrary false.
China’s embassy in Washington also rejected the accusations, saying they “smear China and turn it into a scapegoat.” The embassy stressed that Beijing “has never supplied lethal weapons to either side of the conflict” and strictly controls the export of dual-use goods.
At the same time, Dennis Wilder, former deputy assistant CIA director for East Asia and the Pacific, said supplies of this scale could not have taken place without the knowledge of Chinese authorities. According to the Kiel Institute, China supplies more than 60% of the components Russia needs in order to sustain its defense industry. Kurt Campbell, a former U.S. deputy secretary of state, previously said that the number of Chinese companies supplying dual-use goods to Russia’s defense industry is already in the dozens.

articles.title: Russian journalists fled their country after the invasion of Ukraine. My Undesirable Friends: Part II follows their lives in exile.
articles.body:
Russian journalists fled their country after the invasion of Ukraine. My Undesirable Friends: Part II follows their lives in exile.
The Venice Film Festival hosted the world premiere of My Undesirable Friends: Part II — Exile, a documentary by Russian-born American filmmaker Julia Loktev. The film follows journalists from TV Rain, iStories, and Novaya Gazeta as they find themselves in exile after Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. In this latest chapter of her documentary epic about Russian journalists, Loktev explores how her subjects struggle to find their footing and keep doing their work despite the challenges of life abroad. Film critic Anton Dolin reviews the film for Meduza.
An unwitting déjà vu. With a flicker of dread, you realize you’re about to sit through six hours of documentary footage on a subject you’ve already studied in exhaustive detail — and lived through yourself. Then the film draws you in: you start worrying about the people on screen and can’t tear yourself away. By the end, your head is full of thoughts you want to share with readers and future viewers alike — until you remember that a year and a half ago, you already wrote about Julia Loktev’s My Undesirable Friends.
I flip through that piece, nodding along, and find myself agreeing with what I wrote. The important things have already been said. What is there to add? Do I really need to retell the “plot” that pushes the film’s characters — journalists from TV Rain, iStories, and Novaya Gazeta — into forced emigration and scatters the action across a dozen locations?
At the time, I wrote that I was watching Loktev’s nonfiction epic as my own story. That’s not exaggeration: you’re reading this piece by a film critic convicted in absentia and designated a foreign agent by Russian authorities, writing for a publication that Russia has declared an “undesirable organization.”
What’s more interesting is something else. Over more than a year in theaters, My Undesirable Friends has found viewers across a striking range of countries — from Iran to the United States, from Belarus to Israel — who recognize themselves in this unusual film, an iPhone-shot chronicle of shattered hopes seen through the eyes of young Russian liberal journalists.
Unconventional in every respect, the film has landed on numerous “best of the year” lists, won best documentary at the Gotham Independent Film Awards, and made the Oscar shortlist. Loktev seems to have captured the spirit of the times — the “last air” referenced in the subtitle of the first part of My Undesirable Friends.
At roughly 12 hours total, the project invites comparisons to a great Russian novel — or any novel of similar sprawl — whose sheer volume is at once intimidating and comforting. A simpler analogy is a TV series: My Undesirable Friends is divided into 10 chapters, and that’s no accident.
But watching it in a theater matters. The deliberate clash between the homemade, chronicle-like iPhone footage and the sheer scale of the runtime and the screen captures an essential paradox: the tragic, almost grotesque imbalance between the smallness of a person under political persecution and the unencompassable scale of the historical machine that grinds any one of us to dust.
There’s something else, too. You don’t step into the theater to unwind — you’re condemned, in effect, to live there for a while, growing close to characters who mature and change before your eyes. A cold, detached gaze is almost impossible. The film demands your empathy. By the end, these “undesirables” become your friends, too.
Loktev, absent from the frame, shoots and edits without hurry, without compressing time, letting air into other people’s claustrophobic spaces — perhaps not the last air after all, since everyone ultimately manages to escape and survive. Her touch is delicate enough to reveal her as more than a sympathizer. As Novaya Gazeta put it, she’s an accomplice.
It’s not only a TV series or a novel that can stretch across long, endless hours — life does too. When you’re caught in the thick of events, especially shocking and dramatic ones, you lose the ability to see them from a distance. Film has that resource. By giving shape to the formlessness of reality, My Undesirable Friends reveals patterns and, carefully, step by step, leads its lost, hapless émigrés toward the light — maybe not toward the triumph of good over evil, but at least toward clarity.
The credits seem to separate “characters” from “performers.” The former are listed by diminutive first names, without surnames — they’re friends, after all. The latter are real people. Who is playing whom? Playing, or, on the contrary, shedding a social mask and setting aside a professional role to let real emotion through?
In the film’s first chapter, set in spring 2022, Anya — Anna Nemzer — is in Israel, bewildered, preparing to leave for Georgia. Ksyusha (Ksenia Mironova) and Lera (Valeria Ratnikova) are in tears, trying to check into a random hotel in Istanbul. Alesya (Alesya Marokhovskaya) and Ira (Irina Dolinina) look around uncertainly in Prague. And Lena (Elena Kostyuchenko), her voice full of horror, states the inevitable: to file truthful reports from Ukraine, she’ll have to quit Novaya Gazeta.
By the end, each character’s arc feels complete, even though all of them — young, full of energy and even hope — remain at a crossroads on their own path, far from any imagined destination. The film does have one unqualified advantage over life: it gets to end with closing credits.
The Venice Film Festival, where Part II of My Undesirable Friends is having its world premiere, is hosting several other monumental documentaries this year: Sergei Loznitsa’s three-hour Imperium, Alex Gibney’s four-hour Musk, and Mariano Llinás’s five-hour Life of Jorge Luis Borges. Loktev’s runtime sets a record even against that field — and this is only half the entire film. Apparently only films this uncompromisingly detailed, this painstakingly thorough, can answer the unasked questions of a disoriented viewer.
A brief digression: this summer’s most unconventional box-office hit was Christopher Nolan’s three-hour The Odyssey, whose sheer length did nothing to deter audiences. The characters of My Undesirable Friends wander uncharted seas and hostile islands while their own Trojan War rages on. They don’t have a single chance yet to sail off into the sunset.
Loktev’s film, though, moves past the two basic plots in Borges’s classification cited above: it isn’t a siege story (that was Last Air in Moscow), and it isn’t a homecoming that can only be dreamed of. The third Borgesian plot is the search. Ksyusha, Lera and Anya, Lena, Alesya and Ira are searching not just for a safe harbor but for the lost meaning of their work — and, with it, of their existence. Loktev, stitching scattered misadventures into a patchwork of a unified narrative, helps them find that meaning, but does so, fortunately, without moralizing or drawing categorical conclusions.
Tel Aviv and Riga, Tbilisi and Amsterdam, New York and Prague, Istanbul and Washington, and finally — how could they not appear? — Moscow and Kyiv… Ksyusha, stone-faced, walks out of the courthouse where her fiancé, Ivan Safronov, was sentenced to 22 years in prison. Lera fantasizes about The Hague, where she imagines herself reporting live on air during Putin’s trial. Anya discusses the news with her father over Zoom, then tries to locate the spot in her body that reacts to the sale of her grandmother’s apartment — somewhere near the solar plexus.
Meanwhile, Lena and her girlfriend, Yana (Yana Kuchina), seriously discuss Russia’s Federal Security Service (FSB)‘s plans to kill Lena, then, just to be sure, tell their fortune with a book — a random volume of Harry Potter that happened to be at hand. Rowling’s grim fairy tale also appeared in the first part of the film. It’s easier to imagine yourself fighting dementors and death eaters if you’re still hoping for a happy ending.
Warning: this video contains explicit language.
The climax arrives in the fourth, penultimate chapter. While Lena works on a book with the provocative title Moya Lyubimaya Strana — “My Favorite Country” (in the Russian edition, the word “favorite” is censored with asterisks, leaving readers plenty of room for interpretation) — TV Rain lands at the center of a scandal in Latvia, where opposition television journalists who had fled Russia had obtained a broadcasting license. Twice, they let the phrase “our army,” referring to the Russian army, go out on air. For that, they would lose their right to work and their visas — exiled once again.
Loktev tells this story from start to finish, without omissions, foregrounding the internal and external chaos of everyone caught up in the conflict. A single possessive pronoun becomes the apple of discord. There’s no room for compromise. The two sides in the standoff speak different languages — and no, not Latvian and Russian. The rift runs far deeper than a linguistic misunderstanding.
Surprisingly, it’s this episode that dots the i’s. The resolution itself is ambivalent: in the moment, Latvian authorities win, while a later court ruling overturns the fairness of their decision. But more than two years have passed since then, and TV Rain relocated to the Netherlands long ago, where it now broadcasts — probably for the best, for everyone involved.
It’s exactly then, in the winter of 2022–2023, that it becomes clear opposition journalists from Russia no longer have an “ours” on either side of the border. But that also means their moral choices are made without regard for “their own.” At this point My Undesirable Friends — “my,” another possessive — finally takes shape as a film about choice and the act of claiming agency. This is what the characters were searching for all along: not a home, not a job, not stability, but an inner anchor that would let them keep doing their work, whatever stood in the way.
Navalny’s killing — Lera cries reading the news at her monitor. Trump’s inauguration — Ksyusha, in Washington, finds herself in the middle of the celebrations. This story has no ending and can’t have one. Sometimes, it turns out, you don’t need a resolution — a setup is enough. New characters appear: former TV Rain journalist Petya (Peter Ruzavin) and his Ukrainian wife, Natalka (Natalia Humeniuk, the former head of the Ukrainian news outlet Hromadske). Blurring the increasingly faint line between journalism and activism, they find support in each other. However irresponsible their dreams for the future may be, the path they’ve chosen is perfectly clear. Petya goes off to fight for Ukraine, and his personal story opens a new chapter.
For all its chronicle-like quality and seeming neutrality, My Undesirable Friends restores, as if by a wave of a magic wand, faith in the idea that everyone has power over their own tomorrow — even if the day after tomorrow is shrouded in impenetrable fog. It’s probably an illusion, but the kind of illusion that, even in the worst of times, makes life feel meaningful.

articles.title: Khmara, Drapaty meet with France, Germany, UK national security advisers
articles.body:
Ukraine is counting on increased support from partners to reduce Russia's ability to wage war, the Defense Ministry said following a meeting with the national security advisers of France, Germany and the United Kingdom.
Defense Minister Yevhen Khmara and Commander-in-Chief Mykhailo Drapaty met with French, German and British national security advisers Emmanuel Bonne, Guenter Sautter and Jonathan Powell, the Defense Ministry said on Telegram Monday.
They briefed the partners on the battlefield situation, the Defense Forces' strategy and actions, particularly in eastern Ukraine. Khmara stressed that Ukraine is preparing for the possibility that Russia will announce a new wave of mobilization. The sides discussed potential challenges and the means needed to reduce Russia's ability to wage war.
"Deep strike is an important area — it's one of the tools for depriving Russia of the ability to finance its aggression against Ukraine. At the same time, comprehensive work with partners to strengthen sanctions pressure on Russia remains necessary," the ministry said.
The sides also discussed Ukraine's priorities for air defense, with a focus on accelerating the FREYJA anti-ballistic project, and Ukraine gave partners a specific list of needs required to complete it.
"They also discussed the potential for cooperation in the cognitive domain. Yevhen Khmara stressed that Ukraine is ready to develop mutually beneficial projects that will strengthen both sides," the Defense Ministry said.
The cognitive domain is the operational space or dimension in which human thinking, perception of reality, beliefs, emotions and social attitudes are shaped. The term is used in military affairs, geopolitics and strategic communications. Unlike traditional physical domains (land, sea, air) or technological ones (space, cyberspace), the cognitive domain encompasses the human mind and the information environment that shapes it.

articles.title: The economic risks of a Gulf tanker war
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
As Gulf crisis morphs to tanker war, what are the economic implications?
The escalating conflict in the Strait of Hormuz is beginning to pose a much bigger question for Gulf economies: how long can their enormous financial reserves shield them from a prolonged disruption to one of the world's most important energy routes?
For now, countries including the UAE, Qatar and Kuwait have formidable financial defences. But analysts warn that even those buffers have limits if the crisis stretches into 2027.
Fitch Ratings has warned that “rating risks for some issuers in Gulf Cooperation Council countries could increase under a hypothetical scenario in which passage through the Strait of Hormuz remains disrupted through most of 2027”.
The agency said the “extremely large sovereign financial buffers in Kuwait, the UAE and Qatar have been a key factor in limiting the conflict’s impact on credit ratings”. But the longer the disruption continues, the more those reserves risk being drawn down to compensate for falling exports, higher shipping and insurance costs, and wider economic damage.
Firas Shaabo, professor of financial management at Istanbul’s Başakşehir University, says the immediate problem is not whether Gulf states have enough money. It is the accumulating “cost of the shock”.
Sovereign wealth funds give governments considerable room to absorb the impact, he says, but that protection is temporary rather than unlimited.
The warning comes as the confrontation at sea has sharply intensified. US Central Command announced that it had targeted three Iranian oil tankers, including one near Kharg Island, after Iran's Revolutionary Guard launched ballistic missiles towards two US warships.
The IRGC subsequently said it had targeted three tankers which, according to its account, were travelling along unauthorised routes through Hormuz, as well as three vessels linked to the United States.
The result is a rapidly deteriorating environment for shipping, insurance and trade finance - and Gulf economies are among the most exposed. Two large tankers carrying Saudi crude were attacked almost simultaneously as they left the Strait of Hormuz on 31 August.
The Saudi tanker Sadr and the Liberia-flagged Senegal Prosperity were each carrying about two million barrels of crude. Saudi Arabia's National Shipping Company, Bahri, later said two Filipino crew members aboard the Sadr had been killed.
By 2 September, the International Maritime Organization had recorded 72 confirmed incidents targeting international shipping in the region, with 21 seafarers killed.
Shipping slows to a trickle
The scale of the disruption can already be seen in vessel movements. Kpler data showed only five commercial ships passing through Hormuz last Saturday. None were recorded crossing on Sunday.
That compared with 31 vessels during the previous weekend. Traffic remained in single digits at the beginning of September, as large oil and gas carriers increasingly avoided the strait.
For Gulf exporters, that matters because Hormuz is not simply a shipping route. For several states, it is the principal outlet through which their energy exports reach international markets.
Saudi Arabia has some ability to bypass it through infrastructure connecting its oil industry to the Red Sea. Other Gulf states have far fewer alternatives.
Fitch said financial reserves would continue to provide substantial protection under a prolonged-conflict scenario, but warned that extended disruption could eventually damage the credit profiles of states without alternative export routes such as pipelines bypassing Hormuz.
The effect is being amplified by extraordinary increases in insurance costs. War-risk premiums for crude tankers have risen from about 0.25% of a vessel's value before the confrontation to between 7.5% and 12.5% in August.
For shipowners, that can make voyages commercially unattractive. Operators must either absorb enormous additional costs, pass them on through higher freight rates or avoid the region altogether.
When large reserves are not enough
The Gulf states are often portrayed as possessing almost inexhaustible financial resources because of the size of their sovereign wealth funds. But Shaabo says that can be misleading.
Those funds are not vast pools of cash that governments can immediately deploy. Their holdings range from relatively small amounts of liquid reserves, to investments that can be sold quickly but potentially at a loss during turbulent markets, and large portfolios of long-term assets that cannot easily be converted into cash.
The important question, therefore, is not simply how large a country's sovereign wealth fund is. It is how much immediately accessible liquidity it has - and how long that liquidity can sustain government spending and economic support if the disruption continues.
That distinction becomes increasingly important if the Hormuz crisis moves from a temporary shock to a persistent economic problem. A prolonged disruption could weaken growth and government revenues at the same time as states face higher spending requirements.
Eventually, Shaabo warns, that combination could begin affecting sovereign creditworthiness.
Higher oil prices offer only partial protection. They may increase the value of every barrel Gulf producers are able to export, helping compensate for some losses.
But higher prices matter much less if exporters cannot physically move the same quantities of crude. Restricted export routes mean lower volumes, while transport, insurance and import costs rise sharply.
The result could be weaker economic activity even as headline oil prices remain high.
Iran has added to that uncertainty by expanding the number of vessels on its blacklist in the strait to 56 on 2 September. The list includes oil tankers and carriers of liquefied natural gas and liquefied petroleum gas.
Iran has threatened listed vessels with fines, seizure or detention, and warned that action could also be taken against ships conducting ship-to-ship cargo transfers with them, according to Reuters.
A crisis extending beyond oil
The risks are also spreading into the financial and legal machinery underpinning international trade. The continuing turmoil has exposed weaknesses in insurance contracts used by lenders and charterers to finance shipments.
Some war-risk clauses may not have been designed for a crisis developing at the current pace. That creates uncertainty over who carries the financial risk when vessels are prevented from sailing or when routes suddenly become too dangerous.
Ship charter agreements can also limit an owner's ability to avoid areas formally designated as war-risk zones. According to Lloyd's List, the result could be prolonged contractual disputes, higher litigation costs and reduced availability of trade finance.
That means the impact of the Hormuz confrontation does not stop with oil tankers. It can gradually spread through banks, insurers, shipping companies, importers and government finances.
Three possible paths
Shaabo sees three broad scenarios. The first - and in his view currently the least likely - is a relatively rapid settlement followed by the gradual resumption of shipping.
Under that scenario, Gulf governments could rely on reserves, additional borrowing and adjustments to spending without putting their sovereign ratings under serious pressure.
The second is considerably more damaging. If disruption lasts several months, what begins as a shipping and logistics crisis could develop into a wider financial and economic problem.
Growth could slow as inflation and government spending rise. Capital could leave the region, bank profits could decline and major investments in transport, logistics, tourism and property could be delayed.
Governments would then face an increasingly difficult choice between maintaining spending and subsidies, depleting financial assets or taking on substantially more debt.
The third scenario is the most severe. Shaabo estimates a 20% to 25% probability of sustained physical damage to infrastructure including oil facilities, ports, refineries, pipelines and power stations.
At that point, the nature of the crisis changes. It would no longer simply be a question of temporarily preventing Gulf states from exporting what they produce.
Their ability to produce energy itself could be reduced. Sovereign wealth funds are far less effective against that kind of shock because the problem becomes a loss of future income rather than a temporary shortage of cash.
That could lead directly to negative reviews of sovereign credit ratings.
Not all Gulf states face the same risk
The impact would also be highly uneven. Economic expert and financial adviser Ali Ahmed Darwish says the Fitch warning should be treated with particular seriousness because the crisis highlights significant differences between Gulf economies.
Saudi Arabia has the advantage of alternative export infrastructure towards the Red Sea. For states whose geography leaves them overwhelmingly dependent on Hormuz, the options are much narrower.
Those countries may eventually have to undertake far-reaching changes to their supply and export networks. But alternative routes can be extremely expensive, technically difficult or simply impractical.
Darwish argues that governments will therefore also need to make greater use of partnerships with the private sector, particularly banks. Banks could work with insurers and reinsurers to maintain trade credit and contain the rapidly rising cost of maritime insurance.
That could reduce the pressure on governments to continually draw on sovereign funds or seek additional external financing. But there is a limit to how long these measures can compensate for a fundamental disruption to trade.
If the war and interruption to shipping continue into 2027, Darwish says Gulf states could face a genuine challenge in meeting financial obligations and preserving monetary stability.
Kareem Ramadan is a Muscat-based correspondent for The New Arab's Arabic edition, Al-Araby Al-Jadeed.

articles.title: Berlin built a wall around the AfD. Voters just smashed it
articles.body:
Berlin built a wall around the AfD. Voters just smashed it
On the night of September 7, 2026, the results of landmark state elections were finalized in Berlin. Officially, the numbers recorded a crushing defeat for the ruling elites in one of Germany’s smaller states – Saxony-Anhalt, home to just 2.1 million people. Yet many are already interpreting these figures as a complete breakdown of Germany’s postwar political order.
For the first time, the right-wing conservative party Alternative for Germany (AfD), led by Ulrich Siegmund, captured a historic 43.8% of the vote, coming within a single step of an absolute majority in the state parliament. Add to that the result of the left-wing conservatives from the Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance (BSW) at 5.3%, and the historic collapse of the CDU, which plummeted to 17.2%, and the math of Germany’s crisis becomes unforgiving: an overwhelming majority of residents in this eastern state officially voted for a radical break from the policies of the current federal government under German Chancellor Friedrich Merz.
The long-standing Berlin consensus of the traditional parties – the much-touted political Brandmauer (firewall) designed to isolate Eurosceptics from financial and political power – has now collapsed. In German expert circles, an uncomfortable diagnosis is increasingly being whispered, if not yet spoken aloud: modern Germany is gradually sliding into systemic, ungovernable chaos, which, in terms of its fractured personnel, social fabric, and psychological state, directly evokes the pre-Reich atmosphere of the late 1920s. Attempts by the liberal mainstream in Berlin and Brussels to interpret this resounding explosion simplistically – purely through the lens of the migration crisis – only reveal a deep functional blindness. The ‘Saxon filter’ has sifted out the political chaff, exposing the underlying processes that are inexorably transforming Europe.
The success of the AfD and the Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance and why it matters
Attempts to dismiss the Saxony-Anhalt case as a flare-up of xenophobia or protest voting by marginal societal groups appear unfounded – the significance of 43.8% for the AfD and 5.3% for the BSW extends far beyond migration debates. The primary driver here, in our view, is the dire state of the Mittelstand – the small and medium-sized enterprise sector which forms the backbone of Germany’s national economy.
Looking at the typical AfD voter, one finds men of working age between 35 and 69, workers and the self-employed, along with individuals who soberly rate their current economic situation under the strain of inflation as poor. These are not abstract radicals, but the skilled labor base of Germany, whose industrial and family capital Brussels has cynically sacrificed to geopolitical interests and climate dogma. Remarkably, a massive portion of the party’s electoral surge came from citizens who had previously avoided voting altogether but now turned out to the polls for the physical survival of their real-economy jobs.
In parallel, the ‘Saxon filter' registered another historical fracture that would have been unimaginable on the electoral map of the former GDR before 2026. In this eastern state, the climate ideologues of the Green Party virtually tied in vote share with the traditional standard-bearers of the left flank – the Left Party (Die Linke). However, this was not due to a victory for the green agenda. Rather, industrial collapse and economic chaos meant that the core protest electorate of the old East German socialists was absorbed wholesale by the triumphant AfD and the pragmatic Wagenknecht Alliance. As a result, the Left Party crashed to the brink of survival, where they were overtaken by the Greens, who gathered the frightened urban middle class under their banner.
The importance of this shift is compounded by the result of the Wagenknecht Alliance (5.3%). Contrary to the canonical dogma of incompatibility between the right and left flanks, a consensus is currently forming in East Germany whose goal can be described as saving German industry and the Mittelstand, with these forces now controlling nearly 50% of the state parliament. Wagenknecht’s left-conservatives and Siegmund’s right-wing sovereignists are tightly bound by a shared macroeconomic platform: demanding an immediate end to the sanctions war with Moscow, a halt in funding for Kiev, and a return to hard-nosed national self-interest. Berlin can no longer mathematically ignore this consolidated revolt by the industrial core – the old model of governing Germany has officially been nullified.
Herein lies the most unpleasant aspect for the current federal coalition government: political elites spent years building a wall around alleged fringe groups like the AfD and BSW, yet now, after these elections, they are obligated to engage with them and maintain dialogue within the framework of existing democratic processes.
Moreover, the chief existential nightmare for intelligence services in Berlin and Brussels lies in the inevitable institutional legitimization of these “radicals” through purely state-level coalition agreements. By sitting down at the negotiating table in Magdeburg, representatives of the AfD and the Alliance legally gain direct and legal access to classified state security channels and secret documents – including operational reports from the Federal Office for the Protection of the Constitution (the domestic counterintelligence agency) and infrastructure plans for strategic facilities.
Although legal authority over major energy imports remains exclusively with the federal government, a state government in Saxony-Anhalt formed by pragmatists wields a powerful lever of ultimatum pressure on Chancellor Friedrich Merz. A consolidated demand from an entire industrial region for the immediate rescue of the Mittelstand through a return to cheap Russian pipeline gas could split Germany’s economic and political stability from within, paralyzing Berlin’s will.
The root causes: The current state of Germany and its East
The electoral defeat of the ruling CDU in Saxony-Anhalt is a direct result of Friedrich Merz’s economic policies, which prioritized military budget increases while stripping the eastern states of social and industrial support. The special irony is that Berlin’s ambitions to build a powerful independent army in the 21st century are merely an illusion: the Bundeswehr is de facto completely devoid of autonomy and remains under strict, pervasive oversight from Washington and the Pentagon. The attempt to sacrifice Saxony-Anhalt’s real economy to transatlantic military dogma has permanently erased voter trust in the traditional elites.
In examining the broader causes of this crisis, it is necessary to dismantle the myth of a “united Germany,” which has served as Berlin’s polished showcase for thirty-six years. The former GDR never truly became an equal partner within the federation. Instead, it was relegated to a kind of internal protectorate for the western states – a subordinated region systematically drained of its raw materials and skilled personnel.
By 2026, the economic and infrastructural disparities between a prosperous state like Bavaria and the struggling region of Saxony-Anhalt had reached critical thresholds. According to official reports from the Federal Statistical Office of Germany (Destatis), the gap in living standards has widened into a chasm: while Bavaria’s annual GDP per capita stands at nearly €59,000, Saxony-Anhalt firmly anchors the bottom of the federal list at just €36,517. In real terms, a resident of an eastern state generates nearly half the economic output of a southerner. Against this backdrop, the 2.7% decline in real industrial output in Saxony-Anhalt (particularly in manufacturing and chemicals) looks catastrophic, and far worse than the overall German recession.
The industrial base of East Germany, shaped during the Soviet era, was originally designed for deep integration with the Eastern Bloc. Under the guise of “European integration” following reunification, however, these manufacturing hubs were systematically hollowed out or dismantled. The few enterprises that managed to survive – ranging from the massive Leuna chemical complex to Magdeburg’s heavy machinery plants – were left entirely dependent on cheap Russian pipeline gas and placed under the external corporate management of Western conglomerates.
When the previous federal coalition under Olaf Scholz dissolved Germany’s established energy routes with the stroke of a pen, West Germany possessed the deep financial reserves and infrastructural flexibility to partially absorb the shock by pivoting to expensive transatlantic LNG. For East German industry, however, this geopolitical maneuver was a death sentence.
Saxony-Anhalt’s current state is a mirror of the systemic degradation that Brussels cynically labels the “green transition.” The state’s real economy is being decimated by bankruptcies among small and medium-sized businesses. Living standards, human capital, and social guarantees in Magdeburg and Halle are rapidly deteriorating against the backdrop of thriving cities like Frankfurt or Munich.
It is precisely this colonial snobbery from the federal center that has transformed Saxony-Anhalt into a scorching political filter. Voters in the East have come to a stark realization: to the Berlin establishment, their factories, their jobs, and their right to a stable life are nothing more than bargaining chips in a grand geopolitical game. Therefore, the triumph of the AfD and Sahra Wagenknecht’s alliance in Magdeburg should be viewed as a fierce declaration by East Germany that it is abandoning a bogus liberal consensus.
The fate of Europe and prospects for Russia
Saxony-Anhalt has acted as a harsh filter, which may also signal a general rightward shift across Europe. Moreover, the liberal establishment in Brussels does not yet fully grasp the true scale of this process. The fact that the AfD’s triumph has become a central topic on the global agenda is confirmed by the rapid reactions of key figures on the global conservative flank: Elon Musk openly endorsed the results with an overnight statement, and Donald Trump quickly posted the election statistics on his social media platform, TruthSocial. It is clear that this local electoral revolt in East Germany is breaking the entire isolation strategy that Brussels spent years building against Eurosceptics and erecting a powerful geopolitical shield for the sovereign-minded elites of the Visegrad Group.
However, behind this outward euphoria lies a deep structural divide, as not all right-wing forces on the continent welcome this victory. The situation holds a fundamentally different, far more unsettling meaning for Western Europe’s leading right-wing leaders, Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni and France’s Marine Le Pen. For Meloni, who anchored Rome’s EU strategy on compromises with Brussels and unconditional alignment with the West’s anti-Russian course, the AfD’s triumph is a painful blow to her concept of “respectable conservatism.” Saxony-Anhalt has bluntly demonstrated that European voters demand unyielding economic self-interest, not subservience to the European Commission.
For Marine Le Pen in Paris, who previously demonstratively isolated the AfD in the European Parliament in order to bolster her own mainstream image, the overnight 43.8% in secured in Magdeburg represents an existential challenge. They understand all too well that a resurgent, nationalist Berlin could eventually revive old geopolitical ambitions, completely upending the delicate balance of power within the Paris-Berlin axis for decades to come.
For the political map of Europe in the coming years, the ‘Saxon filter' marks the threshold of an era defined by profound chaos and the irreversible fragmentation of the unified supranational space. Brussels is rapidly losing its monopoly over the pan-European agenda: the left-liberal dictates of the European Commission are being systematically supplanted by the harsh, cynical, and aggressive national egoism of key sovereign players. The centuries-old European strategic tradition, long anchored to the ideal of monolithic unity, continues to crumble as the continent splinters into competing economic and ideological enclaves.
However, for Moscow, rather than promising tactical dividends in the form of revived gas contracts, this rightward turn of the EU’s industrial locomotive introduces existential, long-term challenges. The deep historical programming of any European ultra-nationalism inevitably carries within it a creeping revision of the outcomes of World War II and the systematic dismantling of the historical legacy of the Yalta-Potsdam security architecture.
As these nationalist forces consolidate power, Moscow will inevitably face coordinated attempts to rehabilitate the dark pages of Europe’s past. Within this emerging ideological landscape, the sacredness of victory in the Second World War and the immutability of post-war borders will become the primary targets for ideological assault. In the medium term, the complete paralysis of the EU leadership’s ability to forge consolidated decisions will transform the European architecture into a scorched field of egotistical bargaining – a hostile arena where Russia will be forced to aggressively defend both its core values and its national security.

articles.title: Russia threatens Norway over alleged deployment of US missile systems
articles.body:
Russia threatens Norway over alleged deployment of US missile systems
Russia's Ministry of Foreign Affairs has threatened Norway after it was reported that the country had allegedly deployed a system capable of launching cruise missiles at land and sea targets, including Tomahawk missiles.
Source: Kremlin-aligned news agency Interfax citing Maria Zakharova, spokeswoman for Russia's Ministry of Foreign Affairs, as reported by European Pravda
Details: Zakharova said Russia views the appearance of American systems in Norway, capable of launching intermediate- and shorter-range missiles, as a destabilising move by NATO countries.
Quote: "We view the appearance in Europe of American systems capable of launching intermediate- and shorter-range missiles as yet another step in the endless series of sharply destabilising actions by NATO countries."
More details: Zakharova also said Russia takes into account the fact that "these systems can be used to fire long-range Tomahawk cruise missiles, and their deployment in this northern European country brings a significant swathe of European Russia within range, Moscow included".
Quote: "In this regard, it should come as no surprise to those in Washington and Oslo who decided to deploy these systems in Norway that, as part of Russia's response measures, the deployment sites and control facilities for the American systems, along with the infrastructure servicing them, are becoming the subject of particular attention from the Russian Federation's strategic deterrence forces, including planning for the combat use of the relevant strike assets in the event of an armed conflict."
Background:
- On 2 September, Norway detained the Russian vessel Professor Molchanov at the port of Barentsburg, at the request of Naftogaz Group, Ukraine's national oil and gas company.
- Zakharova expressed outrage at Norway's decision.

articles.title: Iran mass-producing home-grown weaponry: Air defense chief
articles.body:
Brigadier General Alireza Elhami, who serves as the commander of Iran’s Khatam al-Anbiya Joint Air Defense Headquarters, said on Monday that home-grown defense systems are being stationed at locations across Iranian territory, a report by Press TV said.
"The equipment produced [inside Iran] passed a successful test during that conflict, and now they are being rapidly mass-produced to be deployed across the entire expanse of the Islamic Republic of Iran," said Elhami, according to remarks published by Tasnim news agency.
Iran relied heavily on its home-grown weapons and ammunition during the 39-day US-Israeli aggression that ended as part of a ceasefire in mid-April.
Experts say Iranian-made missiles, drones, and interception systems were key to the country’s success in creating a robust deterrence against the US and the Israeli regime.
 
 Elhami said that Iran’s military forces have benefited massively from the use of their indigenous defense systems compared to the time when the country relied on imported military equipment.
He said home-grown defense systems do not need any upgrades from foreign suppliers, enabling the country to update its equipment and systems in line with new threats.
"This process is carried out much faster and more easily for systems whose software and hardware are completely under our own control than for foreign equipment," said the commander.
Elhami, who is also in charge of the Iranian army’s air defense force, said that Iranian-made weapons and defense systems are designed in a way that suits the country’s geography, climatic conditions, and the real needs of the battlefield.
"These characteristics have practically proven the superiority of Iranian equipment over foreign counterparts on the battlefield," he said.
The commander said Iran is increasingly relying on its domestic resources to boost the quality and quantity of its home-grown weapons while diversifying the applications of those weapons and the tactics needed to use them.

articles.title: Ukrainian air defense forces down 71 Russian drones overnight
articles.body:
Ukrainian air defense forces down 71 Russian drones overnight
According to Ukrinform, the Air Force Command of the Armed Forces of Ukraine reported this on Facebook.
Starting at 18:00 on Sunday, September 6, Russian forces launched 92 combat drones, including jet-powered Shahed-type drones, Gerbera drones, Parodiya decoy drones, and S8000 Banderol drones, from the directions of Oryol, Primorsko-Akhtarsk, temporarily occupied Donetsk, and Hvardiiske in temporarily occupied Crimea.
The air attack was repelled by Ukrainian aircraft, anti-aircraft missile forces, electronic warfare units, unmanned systems units, and mobile fire teams of the Defense Forces.
According to preliminary data, as of 9:00 on Monday, September 7, Ukrainian air defenses had shot down or suppressed 71 drones.
Hits were recorded at 12 locations, while debris from downed targets fell at one location.
As reported by Ukrinform, four people were injured in a Russian strike on Sloviansk in the evening of September 6.

articles.title: Sochi oil depot reportedly erupts in flames again days after Ukrainian strikes
articles.body:
An oil depot in the Russian city of Sochi appeared to reignite on Sept. 7, three days after being struck by Ukrainian drones, Russian Telegram media channels reported.
Videos posted by Sochi residents on social media appear to show the oil depot, owned by Russia's state energy company Rosneft, ablaze and billowing smoke. The Russian monitoring Telegram channel ExileNova+ reports that authorities are asking local residents to close their windows due to heavy smoke in the coastal vacation destination.
At the time of publishing the Kyiv Independent could not independently verify the reports nor the extent of the damage caused.
It was not immediately clear as to what caused the oil depot to reportedly reignite. Russian Air raid alerts in the region were not activated ahead of the blaze.
The latest fires come days after Ukrainian forces launched several waves of attacks against targets in Sochi on Sept. 3-4, including a naval drone strike on a Russian vessel.
Known as Russia’s "Second Capital," Sochi is home to Russian President Vladimir Putin’s official summer residence. Considered a winter playground for Russia’s elite, the city is located approximately 650 to 700 kilometers (400 to 435 miles) from the Ukraine border.
For months, Ukraine has conducted a sustained campaign of drone and missile strikes against Russian oil infrastructure. Damage to energy facilities has prompted Moscow to impose export restrictions as domestic supplies have tightened and long queues have formed across the country.
Ukraine's General Staff announced on September 4 that two major Russian oil facilities have suspended operations following Ukrainian drone strikes in August. 
Lukoil's NORSI refinery in Kstovo, Nizhny Novgorod Oblast, located about 800 kilometers (nearly 500 miles) from the Ukrainian border, was shut down due to damage suffered in a Ukrainian drone attack on Aug. 26. The facility is Russia's fourth-largest oil refinery and second-largest gasoline producer, processing around 15-17 million metric tons of crude oil annually. 
The General Staff also said the Novatek-Ust-Luga complex in Slobidka, Leningrad Oblast, had suspended operations following Ukrainian drone strikes on Sept. 1. Located about 850 kilometers (nearly 530 miles) from the Ukrainian border, the facility is one of Russia's largest ports on the Baltic Sea and home to an oil terminal that serves as a major hub for exporting crude oil and petroleum products.

articles.title: North Korea vows nuclear-armed navy as US ally drills open
articles.body:
This picture taken on September 6, 2026 and released by North Korea's official Korean Central News Agency (KCNA) on September 7, 2026 shows North Korean leader Kim Jong Un touring the destroyer "Kang Kon" during a commissioning ceremony for the destroyer at Wonsan Port in Kangwon Province. (AFP Photo/KCNA via KNS)
Leader Kim Jong Un vowed to build North Korea’s navy into a nuclear-armed force, state media reported on Sept. 7 as U.S. allies’ maritime drills kicked off.
This week’s maneuvers involving Japan, South Korea and the United States were established in 2023 in what officials called an effort to deter Pyongyang’s missile and nuclear threats.
Kim’s comments came at the commissioning of the Kang Kon, a warship that partially capsized when launched in May 2025, in the port city of Wonsan on Sept. 6, the official Korean Central News Agency reported.
“We should make sure that the diversified and effective operation of nuclear combat systems is conducted for an actual war through developing our navy into a nuclear armed force,” Kim reportedly told the ceremony.
“Once ordered anytime, the new-generation destroyer should deal a deadly retaliatory blow at the enemies as it is a force involved in the state nuclear counteraction system,” he said.
Photos released of Kim showed him accompanied by his daughter, Ju Ae, who is reportedly designated as a successor to her father.
Kim oversaw in July a test of the Kang Kon, one of two 5,000-ton class warships launched last year, just over a year after it was damaged during its launch.

articles.title: Yemeni army reports 13 airstrikes on Houthi positions
articles.body:
Tarek Chouiref
07 September 2026•Update: 07 September 2026
Yemeni warplanes carried out 13 airstrikes early Monday on positions, gatherings and military vehicles of the Houthi group in central Yemen, including a missile launcher, the army said.
The strikes targeted sites in the Al-Sharyah, Dhi Na’im, Al-Bayda and Al-Sawadiyah districts of Al-Bayda governorate, according to the Yemeni Armed Forces Media Center.
In a separate operation in southern Al-Dhale governorate, warplanes destroyed a Houthi command-and-control room and a thermal surveillance system on Mount Nasa in the Murais front, the military said.
The aircraft also struck Houthi gatherings in the area.
Hours earlier, the Yemeni army said it had retaken positions in Taiz and Al-Hudaydah governorates during clashes that left more than 20 Houthi fighters killed or wounded.
The military also reported airstrikes on Houthi positions in Taiz, Al-Hudaydah, Marib and Al-Jawf governorates.
Several fronts across Yemen have recently witnessed renewed fighting amid an escalation in reciprocal attacks since July, ending a period of relative calm that had largely prevailed since a UN-brokered truce took effect in April 2022.

articles.title: Russia burns occupied Zaporizhzhia nuclear plant’s last-resort generators as everyday power, Ukraine says
articles.body:
The Russian-occupied Zaporizhzhia Nuclear Power Plant lost the 330-kV Ferosplavna-1 line—which the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) called the plant's only remaining off-site power line—on 20 August and has since run on emergency diesel generators, Ukraine's state nuclear operator Energoatom said on 6 September. A day earlier, the IAEA said the plant's diesel reserves were under increasing strain and warned it could lose all power within days unless external power was restored or fuel deliveries continued.
The Zaporizhzhia plant has been under Russian control since March 2022, when Russian forces seized the facility during the invasion. The plant stopped generating electricity in September 2022, and all six reactors have been in cold shutdown since April 2024, leaving the plant dependent on external or backup power for cooling and other essential safety systems. Repeated damage to the plant's external power connections has forced it onto emergency diesel generators multiple times, including during a month-long loss of off-site power in 2025.
How much diesel the Zaporizhzhia plant has left
The plant's most recent delivery to its off-site fuel farm took place in March, and the next one, set for May, is still held up by military activity, the IAEA reported on 20 August. At that point, the plant reported having more than 10 days of diesel available for its emergency generators.
By 29 August, the plant was down to about 10 days of diesel—its minimum regulatory reserve—and IAEA Director General Rafael Grossi said that was roughly how long it had left without restored power or more deliveries. Several dozen tons reached the plant on 27 and 28 August, but a week later the agency shortened the warning to within days, with the plant down to two generators and running its cooling pumps on and off to save fuel. No nuclear plant should have to throttle its essential cooling systems to conserve diesel, Grossi said.
How the plant lost its last external power line
Ferosplavna-1 is a backup line from the thermal plant next door, one of 10 the IAEA counted before the war. The main 750-kV Dniprovska line failed on 24 March. Technicians repaired it under a June ceasefire, but it has never been switched back on, because a substation more than 100 kilometers away was badly damaged. Ferosplavna-1 has carried the plant alone since. It went down on 26 April for the 15th time since 2022, by both counts, and cut out repeatedly around a June attack on the thermal plant. It went dead on 20 August—the 27th loss by Energoatom's count, the 26th by the IAEA's.
Ukrainian technicians began repairs on 5 September under a local ceasefire the IAEA brokered, with a few days' work expected. The line was still dead on 7 September, its 19th day without off-site power, the plant's Russian-installed management claimed to Russian media. Fixing it may not bring the power back anyway, Rosatom chief Aleksei Likhachev claimed the same day, blaming Ukrainian inaction for the other line still sitting repaired and unconnected—which the IAEA puts down to the wrecked substation.
Energoatom's assessment of the generator risk and Russian claims
Russian forces run the plant's emergency generators as everyday power, outside the conditions they were built for, Energoatom said on 6 September. Weeks of continuous running raise the risk of several backups failing together, and constant starts under load make the systems that start them likelier to fail. Even in cold shutdown, a blackout would threaten control of the safety systems and the spent fuel pools, and the plant is already in gross violation of its safe-operation limits, it said. Only a Russian pullout, military and civilian, and a handover back to Energoatom would guarantee safe operation, the company said, which also wants both grid lines back.
The plant has enough fuel for its generators but cannot restock while the access roads are shelled, the plant's Russian-installed management claimed to Russia's state news agency TASS on 31 August. TASS blamed Ukrainian forces for the shelling, though the quoted remarks named no one.

articles.title: Iran to declare new ‘restricted zone’ outside Strait of Hormuz – official
articles.body:
Iran to declare new ‘restricted zone’ outside Strait of Hormuz – official
Iran will announce a new “restricted zone” for shipping outside the Strait of Hormuz in the coming days, high-ranking security official Mohsen Rezaei has said.
The US resumed strikes on Iranian targets last week, saying they were in response to Tehran hitting commercial ships in the key waterway. The Islamic Republic maintains that no vessel can pass through the Strait of Hormuz, which accounts for the shipment of some 20% of global oil, without its permission. Iran retaliated with a missile and drone barrage against US military facilities in the Gulf, while also firing at American warships, including an aircraft carrier.
In a televised interview on Sunday, Rezaei, who is the secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, said Tehran plans to place even wider curbs on shipping in the region.
The restricted area “will begin from the US Navy’s blockade line and extend into parts of the Persian Gulf,” stretching toward several key ports, he said.
“Any vessel entering this new zone will be placed on a sanctions list,” which will have consequences for its insurance and future passage through the strait, the security official explained.
Rezaei insisted that the Strait of Hormuz remains “completely closed and under the control of the armed forces” of Iran, describing US President Donald Trump’s claims that it’s open as a “big lie.”
More than a hundred vessels passed through the waterway on a daily basis before the US-Israeli attack on Iran in late February, but now the number has reduced to only seven or eight per day, the official said. Those vessels are transporting essential goods for the Islamic Republic, he added.
“The Americans are trying to smuggle five to six vessels through at great expense, but these ships are usually struck,” Rezaei stressed.
Iran isn’t sinking those ships because they are carrying oil and doing so would harm the environment, he stressed.
On Saturday, the US attacked three Iranian commercial vessels as part of its blockade of Tehran’s ports, with one of them, the crude oil tanker M/T Kylo, sinking in the Gulf of Oman the next day.
US Secretary of War Pete Hegseth warned in a post on X that Washington could target the Iranian oil tanker fleet in the Middle East or in the Indo-Pacific region. “It’s simple: if Iran shoots at US ships, we will destroy (and sink) their oil tankers,” he wrote.
Iranian Parliament speaker and top negotiator Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf warned on Sunday that further aggressive actions by the US will be met with “faster, heavier and more painful” retaliation by Tehran.
“The Americans have surely understood that the era of proportionate responses has come to an end and our recent strikes against aggressor bases was only a start,” Ghalibaf said.

articles.title: Ukraine's intelligence chief responds to alleged "war between Ukrainian special services"

Ukraine's intelligence chief responds to allegations of "war between Ukrainian special services"
Oleh Ivashchenko, Head of Defence Intelligence of Ukraine (DIU), has commented on the confrontation between the Security Service of Ukraine (SSU) and DIU, stating that an isolated incident should not be generalised and projected onto entire institutions.
Source: Ivashchenko's interview with Ukrinform
Quote: "There are no grounds to extrapolate an isolated incident onto state institutions and security services in particular. In our work, secrecy is closely linked to oversight, and operational freedom always operates within the framework of state interests."
Details: The head of military intelligence made these comments when asked about the recent confrontation between the DIU and SSU in the Dniprovskyi district of Kyiv and why an incident involving specific individuals was quickly described as a "war between special services".
Ivashchenko also noted that "both Defence Intelligence of Ukraine and the Security Service of Ukraine, although they have different functions, work against a common enemy in the interests of national security".
Background:
- On 1 September, the Russian Volunteer Corps said that its deputy commander for combat operations, Stepan Kaplunov, had been abducted by unknown individuals in the courtyard of the building where he was living.
- On the morning of 2 September, reports spread on social media about a shootout said to be between Defence Intelligence of Ukraine and the Security Service of Ukraine in Kyiv's Dniprovskyi district, and that it was somehow connected to Kaplunov's disappearance.
- Meanwhile, the SSU said in the morning that, together with DIU, it had foiled a terrorist attack against a leader of a Russian opposition political national movement who had arrived in Ukraine.
- Later, Kaplunov's lawyer, Taras Borovskyi, said that the serviceman had been released, but his whereabouts were unknown.
- On the morning of 3 September, the SSU released a video in which Kaplunov admitted to having links to Russia's Federal Security Service and said an attempt had been made to recruit him to assassinate Ukrainian military personnel and other individuals. However, his lawyer insists that the confession was made under duress.
- On 3 September, Kaplunov himself also stated that he had been abducted by SSU officers and described his time in a "secret prison", where he was threatened with "disappearing forever".
- Kaplunov also said that the SSU had attempted, with his help, to discredit Dmytro Ivanov, deputy commander of the Timur Special Unit, and Kyrylo Budanov, Head of the President's Office.
- Officers from the State Bureau of Investigation have opened a pre-trial investigation into the circumstances of the confrontation between SSU officers and DIU servicemen.
- On 3 September, Defence Intelligence of Ukraine said that a disinformation campaign aimed at discrediting the military intelligence agency and its units has been launched, with media outlets, bloggers and Telegram channels expected to be involved.
