articles.title: Germany’s democracy rests on one party’s choice
articles.body:
Germany’s democracy rests on one party’s choice
The Ukraine conflict has exposed a German establishment more willing to defend its commitments to Kiev than to consider their cost to Germany. Saxony-Anhalt has delivered its verdict: an overwhelming win for the AfD (Alternative for Germany).
Now the parties it defeated may try to preserve their power through the establishment’s political firewall, while the BSW (Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance) must decide whether it will help restore political independence and relations with Russia or become the anti-Russian establishment’s last line of defense.
The war in Ukraine has posed a very basic question: whose interests should the German government serve? Kiev has its objectives. Germany has its own responsibilities, resources, and limits. The two cannot simply be declared identical. The AfD deserves credit for challenging this confusion. It has insisted that German interests are paramount and that Russia cannot be treated as a permanent enemy without serious costs to Europe. Its proposals include reducing financial and military assistance to pressure Kiev into peace negotiations, offering partial sanctions relief to encourage talks, and lifting sanctions fully once a peace agreement is reached. These are subjects for practical diplomacy. They recognize that Russia will remain a major European power whatever German ministers say about it, and that a durable settlement must be negotiated with Moscow. The AfD’s parliamentary proposal gives negotiations and the restoration of relations a place in policy that endless establishment declarations of “resolve” cannot supply.
The BSW’s opposition to arms deliveries to Ukraine and its demand for diplomacy give it substantial common ground with the AfD. This is one reason to welcome its presence in parliament. Thus, in Saxony-Anhalt, the immediate opportunity belongs to the AfD and BSW: together, they could turn their rejection of the present course into a governing coalition.
Supporters of military assistance argue that weapons strengthen Ukraine’s negotiating position. In reality, it merely prolongs the fighting and delays the inevitable defeat of Ukraine. Kiev cannot reasonably expect foreign taxpayers to shoulder indefinite financial burdens while facing economic hardship at home, especially without clear limits or a realistic plan for peace. Germany should also take Russia’s stated security concerns seriously enough to examine them in negotiations. Taking those concerns into account does not oblige Berlin to accept every Russian demand. It means recognizing that a settlement requires terms the parties will observe, rather than a declaration written for the satisfaction of only one side.
Saxony-Anhalt has now given that challenge political weight. The AfD won 43.8% and 39 seats. The CDU (Christian Democratic Union, Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s party) received 17.2% and 15 seats. The BSW entered parliament with 5.3% and five seats. Together, the AfD and BSW would hold 44 of the 83 seats, exceeding the 42 needed for a majority. The CDU, SPD (Social Democratic Party), Greens, and Left have only 39 between them. An alternative majority excluding the AfD would therefore require the BSW. The reported seat allocation presents the BSW with a clear choice: negotiate a change of government with the election winner or help its opponents keep it out.
The AfD fell short of an absolute majority, but has still earned the strongest political claim to lead coalition negotiations, even though it has no automatic right to govern. The establishment’s firewall exists to prevent that claim from being tested through ordinary bargaining. Before demands are presented, before compromises are considered, before a common program is examined, the answer is already supposed to be no. The establishment then describes this refusal as a “defense of democracy.” It might more honestly describe it as a defense of its own exclusive right to supply the government.
No party is legally obliged to cooperate with the AfD. Equally, no party is entitled to escape criticism for refusing. The defenders of the firewall like to recite the first point as though it settles the second. It does not. Parties make choices, and voters are entitled to judge them. If the CDU can contemplate arrangements involving the Greens and the Left (both radical, socially destructive, and truly extremist), it must explain why differences in those directions can be managed while differences with the AfD prohibit even a discussion. Saying “we will not cooperate with the AfD because of the firewall” does not explain why cooperation would be wrong.
The CDU’s position is especially contemptuous of the conservative voters whose support it continues to solicit. During the campaign, their concerns are important. After the campaign, those concerns must wait while the party protects the firewall. What is such a party conserving? Increasingly, the answer appears to be its own place in government. Its failure to mount a serious challenge to the woke cultural agenda prevalent across German institutions makes it, in practice, a party of the left wearing a conservative label. Its clearest commitment is to keep the AfD out of power, even when that means preserving the policies its own voters want changed.
This is the practical meaning of the uniparty. The Greens and the Left openly advance the left-liberal agenda, the SPD supports it, and the CDU helps preserve it while calling itself conservative. Their campaign quarrels offer voters the illusion of choice without a real change of direction. When the AfD threatens to overturn that agenda, they unite to keep it out of government and call their cooperation “democratic responsibility.” Ministers can be replaced and coalition partners reshuffled, but the same political course survives. The firewall protects the established parties from the consequence elections should make possible: losing power to an opposition that intends to govern differently.
The firewall lets the established parties lose voters without losing power. Instead of defeating the AfD through better government and stronger arguments, they can gather enough coalition partners to keep it out. Parties rejected at the ballot box then present their survival in office as a “victory for democracy.” This gives force to the AfD’s accusation that opposition is welcome only while it cannot govern. Every additional party recruited to keep the AfD out makes the arrangement harder to disguise: the established parties are protecting their own hold on power.
The BSW should understand this danger better than most. It was founded to challenge policies that the established parties treated as beyond debate. It deserves sympathy for reopening arguments about war, economic interests, and the costs imposed on ordinary people. Its call for normal relations with Russia offers a necessary alternative to permanent confrontation, and its willingness to defend that position under political pressure deserves credit. However, if the BSW refuses to enter into a coalition with the AfD, it accepts an establishment veto over its own political freedom. It may still speak against the system, but the established parties will have allowed the BSW to criticize their policies while preventing it from forming a government that could change them.
The BSW’s refusal even to consider a coalition with the AfD amounts to surrender before negotiations begin. It gives up a possible majority without discovering which of its demands the AfD would accept. The BSW should put its policies on the table and negotiate hard. If agreement proves impossible, it can explain what prevented it. But refusing talks in advance means obeying the establishment’s command that the AfD must never govern. A party elected to oppose the old parties would then be helping keep them in office. Its voters would have supplied the seats; the establishment would collect the benefit.
Supporting individual AfD proposals is better than rejecting them on principle, but it can become an excuse for avoiding the real contest over power. The BSW could claim influence through occasional votes while leaving the government and its priorities in other hands. A government in Saxony-Anhalt cannot stop Germany’s weapons deliveries to Ukraine or negotiate peace with Russia; those decisions belong to the federal government. An AfD-BSW coalition would need an agreement on matters it could directly influence, such as schools, policing, and state spending. If it governed well, it would give voters concrete evidence that cooperation between the two parties can work. That would weaken the argument for keeping the AfD out of office. The established parties would then have to defend their record against an actual AfD-led government. The firewall spares them that comparison.
The statements, views and opinions expressed in this column are solely those of the author and do not necessarily represent those of RT.

articles.title: China Updates Defense Mobilization Law to Enable Rapid Transition to Martial Law
articles.body:
China has revised its national defense mobilization law, allowing Beijing to transition the country from peacetime to wartime more quickly in the event of a serious threat.
The Ministry of National Defense of the People’s Republic of China announced this.
The law will take effect on October 1, 2026.
The Standing Committee of the National People’s Congress approved the amendments on August 28. The document sets out procedures for mobilizing military and civilian resources in the event of a threat to China’s sovereignty, territorial integrity, and security.
The new rules may primarily apply to a potential conflict over Taiwan. At the same time, they could also be invoked in the event of a war with other countries with which China has territorial disputes, including the Philippines, India, and Japan.
China already has a law allowing the use of “non-peaceful means” against supporters of Taiwan independence. The new rules supplement this legal framework with mechanisms for mobilizing the country’s resources.
One of the main changes concerns civilian resources. The new law allows the state not only to requisition property but also to expropriate it.
In the event of mobilization, the authorities will be able to set priorities for the financial system, transportation, information networks, energy, and water supply. These resources may be directed toward the needs of China’s People’s Liberation Army.
The new rules may also allow the state to mobilize resources from government institutions, companies, organizations, and private individuals during wartime call to arms.
In early July 2026, Militarnyi reported that President of China Xi Jinping outlined a vision for China’s future that calls for strengthening the country’s military capabilities, expanding its international influence, and shaping a new global order.
Military power was one of the central themes of his speech. The Chinese leader linked the country’s future to the continued development of its armed forces.
According to Xi Jinping, China should strengthen political control over the military, pursue military reforms, develop defense technologies, strengthen personnel capabilities, and improve its military management system.

articles.title: Ukraine eliminates suspected killer of military intelligence General Shapoval in occupied Donetsk – media
articles.body:
Ukraine eliminates suspected killer of military intelligence General Shapoval in occupied Donetsk – media
Sources in the Ukrainian intelligence services told LB.ua, according to Ukrinform. They also provided photographs that they said showed surveillance of Shutov and his elimination.
According to the publication’s sources, the operation was carried out by Ukrainian intelligence services in the occupied territory. Shutov was reportedly killed after an improvised explosive device was planted in his Subaru and detonated when he arrived at the Dynamo sports complex in Donetsk’s Leninskyi district in the evening of July 27.
Local occupation-affiliated information resources reported the incident as a “nighttime UAV attack that injured the head of the sports wrestling federation.” However, according to LB.ua’s sources, Shutov was killed in a car explosion.
According to the sources, information about Shutov’s elimination was not released immediately after the operation for security reasons, until the intelligence and combat group had returned to Ukrainian-controlled territory.
Oleh Shutov was president of the so-called DPR Judo and Sambo Association and an operational officer with the special operations center of the so-called DPR Ministry of State Security, which was controlled by Russian intelligence services. In April 2024, Russian occupation authorities abolished the so-called DPR Ministry of State Security and transferred its functions to the local FSB directorate.
Then-SSU chief Vasyl Hrytsak was the first to publicly identify Shutov’s involvement on April 19, 2019. “Shutov Oleg Nikolaevich, born March 9, 1966, a resident of Donetsk. It was this individual who planted an explosive device under the car of Ukrainian military intelligence general Maksym Shapoval on June 26, 2017. Today, for the first time, we are making public information about the perpetrator of this terrorist attack,” Hrytsak said at the time.
According to Hrytsak, Shutov had rented an apartment in the building where Shapoval lived, as well as a parking space near the location where the general parked his car.
On June 27, 2017, Maksym Shapoval was killed when a car bomb exploded in Kyiv’s Solomianskyi district.
According to Hrytsak, about an hour after carrying out the attack, Shutov packed his belongings from the rented apartment and left Kyiv, traveling to Russia and then to Donbas.
Shutov was also implicated in the bombing of the car of SSU Colonel Oleksandr Kharaberiush in Mariupol on March 31, 2017.
According to the SSU, the organizers of both killings of Ukrainian officers were Russian FSB Lieutenant General Dmitry Minayev, head of the FSB department for counterintelligence operations, and his subordinate, Vasily Yevdokimov, head of the so-called DPR Ministry of State Security special operations center, known by the nickname Lenin.
In April 2019, the SSU announced the detention of seven members of a Russian sabotage and reconnaissance group, two of whom were career officers of the Russian intelligence services. SSU operatives also established a connection between the group and Oleg Shutov. The group had planned to assassinate a military intelligence officer; one of the saboteurs was killed when an explosive device detonated while it was being planted under the officer’s car.

What North Korea’s new warship reveals about Kim’s moves to secure surrounding waters
Kim’s promised ‘important plans’ that will deepen the ‘concerns of the enemies’ are likely to be nuclear, observers say
“The nuclearisation of our navy is being realised, making it increasingly suited, diversified and practical for the use of our deterrent,” Kim said while commissioning the Kang Kon in the southeastern port of Wonsan on Sunday.
“We must make the practical operation of our nuclear combat systems more diverse and effective, and our military activities for maritime defence and war deterrence more explicit, by making our powerful and reliable nuclear war deterrent more clear,” he said. “Concerns of the enemies will be surely deepened.”

articles.title: ‘If you f**k, f**k a queen’: Surveillance points to power players behind Ukraine’s scam centers
articles.body:
‘If you f**k, f**k a queen’: Ukraine’s scam-call center revelations take down prosecutor general
Vladimir Zelensky’s government was hit by another corruption scandal over the weekend after Western-backed investigators accused the head of the cybercrime unit at the Ukrainian Prosecutor General’s Office of extorting payments from the very criminals he was supposed to prosecute.
Surveillance recordings released by detectives portray the suspect as a risk-taker who spoke of building an “empire” for his chief and comparing his earnings to having sex with a queen. Following weekend raids, photos of a safe full of cash were also released.
Ukrainian Prosecutor General Ruslan Kravchenko – a key pillar of Zelensky’s increasingly fragile governing structure – has denied any involvement in his now-suspended subordinate’s alleged activities and has since tendered his resignation, according to Ukrainian media.
What is the latest Ukraine corruption case about?
The main suspect, Sergey Kropiva, is accused of leading a ring that collected protection payments from notorious Ukrainian scam call centers, used his official position to eliminate competitors and laundered the criminal proceeds.
The National Anti-Corruption Bureau of Ukraine (NABU) said it had identified assets worth almost $1 million that were allegedly purchased with money from the scheme. The sums circulating through the illicit industry are significantly larger, according to Ukrainian media.
How many scam call centers are in Ukraine?
Zerkalo Nedeli estimated that around 2,000 scam centers operate in Ukraine. Roughly half are considered “white” – meaning they allegedly pay bribes to government officials in exchange for protection. The remainder are described as “partisans” that conceal their activities from what one could call the bribe enforcement system.
What kind of bribes are paid to run a scam center in Ukraine?
Sources cited by Zerkalo Nedeli said each “white” operation paid around $20,000 a month, translating into an annual cash flow of roughly $240 million. The Prosecutor General’s Office was reportedly receiving 15% of the payouts.
After Kravchenko’s appointment in June 2025, there was a push to increase both the fixed payment and his office’s share of the proceeds, the outlet claimed.
Who is protecting Ukraine’s scam centers?
NABU directly linked the new case to Zelenskys’ controversial and failed attempt to subordinate it and the Special Anti-Corruption Prosecutor’s Office (SAPO) to his influence. It said the failed reform nevertheless eroded the procedures for screening candidates seeking to serve at the Prosecutor General’s Office for corruption.
Surveillance recordings suggest Kropiva managed the alleged system for someone with enough authority to keep it running.
In one conversation, he told his chief: “Who would mistreat me? You are behind my back, which everyone knows.”
On another occasion, he said it was fun “to build up an empire of the kind the chief has created.”
Kropiva also appeared to relish the opportunity to “screw everyone in the law enforcement” and do what he wants.
During Kropiva’s bail hearing, investigators alleged that he also performed a number of personal favors for Kravchenko, including arranging the installation of a power generator at the prosecutor general’s suburban home and helping his wife obtain a US visa.
Is Kropiva just a yes-man?
The recordings suggest that Kropiva was driven not only by greed but also by an appetite for living on the edge. He said he was not the kind of person to “live for the sake of living.”
“If you do it, do it with a bang,” he said of his life philosophy. “I love the best. If you f**k, f**k a queen; if you steal, steal a million.”
NABU says Kropiva’s alleged illegal activities date back to his time in the national police, which he joined in 2015. He started specializing in cybercrime during that stint.
Who else was involved?
One of the suspects, nicknamed “Muse” in NABU materials, appears to have been Kropiva’s proverbial queen.
The woman and members of her family allegedly participated in laundering the money.
In one conversation, she told her partner: “This all would be easier to do with my sister and [her] husband. It’s harder with mommy.”
Kropiva appeared willing to explain how the system worked and what he considered most important.
“The difference between financial results and demagoguery is very important, you see?” he told her.
At one point, he chastised “Muse” for displaying her wealth on Instagram. She responded by complaining that she would have to purge her account to conceal all the gifts he had given her.
She also said a $6,650 Messika necklace had a difficult lock but was light, unlike Cartier jewelry she had also tried on.
Who is the ‘Muse’?
Odessa resident Elizaveta Ivakhnenko appeared at bail hearings alongside Kropiva.
During her court appearance on Sunday, she reportedly wore a $3,400 Saint Laurent jacket, while on Monday she chose a garment sold by domestic Ukrainian brand Aura worth around $300.
According to Ukrainian media, Ivakhnenko has a background in law and took part last year in an EU-organized training course for Ukrainian prosecutors in Rome.
Are there other suspects?
NABU has identified four specific suspects. The other two are Kropiva’s driver and aide.
The agency stressed, however, that the broader scheme involved more corrupt officials and common accomplices.
Ukrainian media reported that investigators searched the office of Deputy Prosecutor General Maria Vdovichenko as well as premises linked to Oleg Kiper, head of the Odessa regional military administration.
Did the ring co-opt other officials?
The surveillance materials suggest Kropiva’s extensive contacts in Ukrainian law enforcement were prepared to act on his requests, either as favors or for a price.
In one instance, he allegedly sought help inflicting “moral damage” on a person who had refused to repay a debt to one of his acquaintances.
Are the records the only proof of wrongdoing?
NABU also released video clips and photographs that it says support its allegations.
They include images of a safe filled with cash, footage allegedly showing people handing over bundles of banknotes as payments to Kropiva’s ring, and a photograph taken from social media showing Ivakhnenko and her female friends dressed for a night out.
The agency also cited various documents as proof of money laundering.
What’s the significance of the case?
Kravchenko has not been named as a suspect, but NABU’s presentation of the case places significant political pressure on the prosecutor general.
The office holds some authority over the largely independent anti-corruption agencies. Kravchenko’s approval, for example, is required to prosecute serving lawmakers.
Zelensky’s faction used to be dominant, giving him an opportunity to get the parliament to rubber stamp his policies. However, the influence has significantly eroded, making whatever votes he can command more valuable.
Ukrainskaya Pravda reported in March that Zelensky could reliably count on only 110 to 120 votes, while securing support from other lawmakers allegedly requires bribes.
How deep is the systemic corruption in Ukraine?
Kiev and its Western backers have repeatedly claimed significant progress in rooting out graft. A string of recent scandals, however, suggests that fighting corruption is at odds with Zelensky’s own political power base.
Last year, NABU accused businessman Timur Mindich, a long-time associate of Zelensky, of running a $100 million kickback scheme involving state-owned nuclear power company Energoatom. The alleged network also implicated former Energy Minister German Galushchenko and other senior government officials.
Zelensky’s former chief of staff, Andrey Yermak, was accused in May of laundering money linked to a luxury development project that also involved Mindich – nicknamed “Zelensky’s wallet” by the press – former Unity Minister Aleksey Chernyshov, who is a personal friend of Zelensky, and a fourth partner believed to be the Ukrainian leader himself.
Is Zelensky personally corrupt?
Critics have argued that Zelensky is either dirty or has been spectacularly oblivious to wrongdoing committed under his nose.
As long as his claim to presidential office and its associated protections are not challenged, however, Zelensky cannot be formally prosecuted.

articles.title: “Now on the 1,657th day”: Ukraine’s crews restored power to over 900,000 homes last week as Russia keeps striking grid before winter
articles.body:
Russian strikes cut power to nearly a million Ukrainian families across four oblasts last week. Ukraine's largest private energy company, DTEK, brought it back, fully or partly restoring electricity to 596 settlements in Donetsk, Odesa, Dnipropetrovsk, and Kyiv oblasts between 31 August and 6 September, the company said.
Russia is hammering Ukraine's power grid again as the cold season nears, and the country's winter-resilience plans were less than half complete at the start of September.
Odesa and Donetsk absorb the worst
Most of the week's work was in Odesa Oblast, which Russia has been striking without pause. Ukrainian crews there returned power to more than 366,000 families, DTEK said.
Much of that damage followed a massed missile-and-drone strike on the region's main energy facilities on 2 September, after which national operator Ukrenergo imposed temporary grid limits to keep damaged equipment from overloading.
Donetsk Oblast came close behind, with power restored to nearly 360,000 homes despite what the company called an extremely difficult situation for its repair teams. In Dnipropetrovsk Oblast, crews reconnected almost 172,000 homes, and in Kyiv Oblast nearly 9,000 more.
Strikes keep cutting the grid
The reconnections are happening under continued fire. Russia keeps attacking energy sites in Odesa and Dnipropetrovsk oblasts, damaging lines faster than they can be fully secured. DTEK crews can only begin repairs once the military and emergency services have cleared access to the damaged equipment.
"Russia keeps attacking our energy system. Despite everything, we keep working and restoring power — now on the 1,657th day," said Alina Bondarenko, chief executive of DTEK Grids.
Winter sharpens the threat
The timing is the danger. Ukraine has until the heating season to shore up a grid that Russia has spent the war trying to break.
This year's attacks have again concentrated on the energy system as temperatures start to fall.

articles.title: What we know about Iran's planned restricted zone around Hormuz
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
What we know about Iran's planned restricted zone around Hormuz
Iran has announced plans to establish a new restricted zone in the Gulf in the coming days, saying it will also publish maps for a new shipping corridor through the Strait of Hormuz.
The move appears to be part of Tehran's efforts to increase pressure on Washington in response to the US blockade, as renewed attacks on shipping have pushed oil prices higher.
But where will Iran's new restricted zone be, what could happen to ships entering it and what does the move mean for the already heavily restricted Strait of Hormuz?
Where will Iran's restricted zone be?
The new restricted zone, where Iran says action could be taken against passing ships, would begin where the US blockade of Iran starts and extend into parts of the Gulf.
According to Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council, it would stretch from an area near the Gulf of Oman and Arabian Sea, through the Strait of Hormuz and into Gulf waters to the north.
Iran has not yet revealed detailed boundaries for the planned zone.
Rezaei said maps would be published showing the shipping routes through the strait that Tehran intends to adopt.
"The maps of the new international corridor, which lies in Iranian and Omani waters and which Iran will manage, have been agreed upon and are due to be signed in the coming days," he said.
Iran and Oman had already agreed in August on a temporary maritime route through the Strait of Hormuz.
Tehran has also previously sought to determine which routes ships can use through the strait. It published a map of approved navigation routes in April, directing vessels closer to the Iranian coast.
Oman, working with the International Maritime Organization, subsequently established a separate southern corridor closer to Oman. Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps objected to that route, insisting the Iranian route was the only authorised passage.
The latest Iran-Oman agreement could therefore establish a new recognised route through the strait.
Rezaei's comments suggest that once the agreed corridor is announced, ships travelling through areas outside it could face Iranian sanctions.
What could happen to ships outside the agreed route?
Iran has not yet explained exactly what those sanctions would involve.
Rezaei said any ship entering the new zone could be placed on a sanctions list.
"From now on, if ships are moving on the western or eastern side of the Strait of Hormuz, but stop or commit a violation, we will put them on the sanctions list," he said.
He claimed sanctioned ships could encounter problems obtaining insurance and could face consequences if they attempted to pass through the area again.
"The Strait of Hormuz will become a sanctions zone," Rezaei said.
He did not explicitly say that Iran would militarily attack ships that breached the restrictions.
However, he appeared to hint at the military risks involved, claiming that Iran had tested an anti-destroyer missile over a US warship days earlier.
"This special missile created hell for the Americans, so they fled," Rezaei claimed.
Why is Iran introducing the restricted zone?
Iran says it has been forced to adopt a new strategy on both the war and negotiations following US President Donald Trump's withdrawal from what Rezaei called the "Islamabad understanding".
"After Trump's withdrawal from the understanding, we concluded that we needed to adopt a new strategy regarding the war and negotiations," Rezaei said.
"We considered the US withdrawal from the understanding as putting us on a new path."
The move comes as Washington intensifies its economic pressure on Iran, seeking to restrict the country's oil exports and prevent Tehran from circumventing sanctions.
Iran has increasingly signalled that it could retaliate by targeting US economic and military interests and threatening shipping through the Gulf.
What about the Strait of Hormuz, which Iran says is virtually closed?
Rezaei said Iran would not commit to fully reopening the Strait of Hormuz until the US stopped "sabotage, threats and attacks on Iran".
He claimed the strait was currently effectively closed and described US assertions that it remained open as "completely false".
Before the war, billions of dollars in trade and millions of barrels of oil passed through the waterway each day.
Rezaei claimed that only around seven or eight ships carrying food were now crossing.
He acknowledged that some vessels were still passing through, claiming the US was attempting to move five or six ships at a time near Oman with their tracking systems switched off.
However, independent and Western figures indicate that more ships are still passing through the strait, although traffic remains sharply below pre-war levels.
The UK Maritime Trade Operations centre said on Sunday that 59 ships had crossed the Strait of Hormuz during the previous 48 hours.
Marine analytics firm Kpler, meanwhile, said on Monday that an average of 10 commodity ships per day had crossed over the previous 10 days, the lowest level since May.
Before the US and Israel launched the war on Iran on 28 February, more than 130 ships passed through the strait each day.
The competing figures underline the dispute between Tehran and Washington over how much control Iran currently exercises over the waterway.
How did the conflict reach this point?
The latest developments come around seven months after the United States and Israel launched their war on Iran on 28 February.
A 60-day memorandum of understanding signed in June temporarily halted months of military hostilities, but the arrangement expired last month amid disputes over control of the Strait of Hormuz.
Under the agreement, the US was to end its naval blockade within 30 days, while Iran agreed to clear mines from the strait and allow ships to pass without charge for 60 days.
After a relative pause in military operations during much of August, attacks have resumed.
US Central Command recently said it targeted three Iranian tankers, including one off Kharg Island on Saturday, in response to Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps firing ballistic missiles towards two US Navy vessels.
Tehran has demonstrated that it retains the ability to threaten US interests and severely disrupt oil flows through the Strait of Hormuz.
Before the war, around 20% of the world's oil supplies passed through the waterway, making any disruption a significant risk to global energy markets.
Shipping data released on Monday showed an average of just 10 commodity vessels a day passing through the strait over the previous 10 days, the lowest level since May.
Is economic pressure pushing Iran towards tougher measures?
Iran has said it will step up efforts to deal with the economic impact of US sanctions and the blockade.
Three senior Iranian sources told Reuters that it had become increasingly difficult for Tehran to withstand Washington's campaign to choke the Iranian economy by restricting oil exports and preventing sanctions evasion.
Iranian parliament speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf said on Sunday that the US should understand "before it is too late" that the rules of the conflict had changed.
"From now on, any aggression against Iran's interests and security will be met with a faster, harsher and more painful response," he said.
Ghalibaf said Iran's main struggle, alongside the military front, was now centred on production and people's livelihoods.
He pointed to sharp currency fluctuations, inflation, unemployment and market management as major challenges, saying Iranians could endure hardship but would not tolerate mismanagement or government inaction.
Against that backdrop, Iran's proposed restricted zone appears to be another pressure tool against Washington, linking Tehran's ability to disrupt one of the world's most important shipping routes to the wider military, diplomatic and economic confrontation with the US.

articles.title: US Envoys Say Putin Talks Were “Very Constructive,” Sees Opening for Trilateral Format
articles.body:
- Category
- War in Ukraine
US Envoys Say Putin Talks Were “Very Constructive,” Sees Opening for Trilateral Format
US President Donald Trump's envoys, Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, met Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy in Kyiv, outlining a pathway toward renewed peace talks and expressing hope for a trilateral format soon.
The two envoys outlined their assessment during remarks in Kyiv, a day after meeting the Russian leader, Vladimir Putin, in Moscow, according to a UNITED24 Media correspondent on September 6.
Kushner told reporters that Washington had consulted both sides about reviving three-way negotiations. "One thing Steve and I really thought would be productive is to go back to the trilateral format," he explained. "We've spoken with both parties, and so hopefully we'll have progress on that very soon."
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Witkoff stated that Trump, Vice President JD Vance, and Secretary of State Marco Rubio had dispatched the pair to reopen talks. "The President asked Jared and me to come here and to restart conversations, negotiations, because this is so important to him," he noted.
Kushner characterized the Moscow talks as constructive and substantive, with both delegations posing questions about the elements of a durable settlement.
Witkoff, who has made about eight visits to the Russian capital to meet Putin, emphasized the role of personal ties in ending the war. He and Kushner have traveled there together at least three times. "Relationships are critical in terms of solving conflicts like this," Witkoff declared.
The envoys met Putin first to gauge Moscow's position and briefed Zelenskyy's team on the discussion. Witkoff stated that their task is to bring the two sides together, narrow the issues between them, and build reliable communication channels.
He described the previous 48 hours as a constructive start and expressed confidence in an eventual resolution.
The Kyiv visit was the envoys' first trip to the Ukrainian capital, which they reached by train after their aircraft landed in Poland. Ukraine had readied its airports to receive the delegation by air, but Russian strikes ruled out a direct landing.
At the railway station, they were met by senior Ukrainian officials, including presidential office chief Kyrylo Budanov, his deputy Serhii Kyslytsia, and parliamentary faction leader Davyd Arakhamia.
The timing carries added weight as winter nears, with Moscow calculating that Ukrainian resolve will weaken through the cold months and that Putin's willingness to negotiate will fade until the season ends in mid-March.
The Kyiv talks followed directly from a marathon session in Moscow the previous day. There, Witkoff and Kushner spent more than three hours with Putin—three hours and 10 minutes in all—focused primarily on approaches to ending the war in Ukraine.
Officials on both sides framed the exchange as substantive and unusually frank, and the delegation was reported to have arrived with a range of settlement proposals. The discussions extended beyond Ukraine to potential large-scale US-Russian economic projects.
The Moscow visit unfolded under a temporary arrangement on strikes. Putin had ordered Russian forces to refrain from hitting Kyiv for three days from midnight on September 5, and Zelenskyy signaled Ukraine's readiness to observe a matching halt on cities tied to the negotiations.

articles.title: Ukraine peace talks – full of symbolism, but differences of opinion remain
articles.body:
The peace talks in Kyiv were full of symbolism, as US President Donald Trump’s envoys set foot on Ukrainian soil for the first time since the start of the full-scale invasion, writes the BBC.
The American negotiators had to travel to Kyiv by train to avoid attacks by Russian drones – weapons launched at the behest of Russian dictator Putin, and just hours earlier the US envoys were sitting at his table in Moscow. It was also symbolic that Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky welcomed Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner to Kyiv’s Saint Sophia Cathedral, which is not only a monument to Ukrainian history but also lies just a few meters from the headquarters of the state security services, which was attacked by Russian drones on the 4th of September.
The two sides spent several hours in talks, and later the Ukrainians and Americans were joined by security advisers from several European countries, including Britain’s Jonathan Powell. The negotiators then spoke favorably of the important discussions that had taken place and expressed hope that trilateral talks could be resumed, involving both the Americans and the Europeans.
However, fundamental differences of opinion remain. The US envoys had come straight from Moscow, where Putin had told them that Russia was making “tangible progress” on the battlefield. In Ukraine, Americans heard a different story. Ukrainian officials said that more territory had been regained than lost since August, and that the number of casualties on the Russian side had reached 42,000.
Putin told Witkoff and Kushner that the root causes of the conflict must be addressed,
including his demand for territory that belongs to Ukraine, Kyiv’s rejection of the idea of joining NATO, and the significant reduction of the Ukrainian army. Zelensky said after the talks that Ukraine needed firm and clear security guarantees, including a strong army. He also made it clear that he would not give up Ukrainian land in the east of the country to the Russians.
Meanwhile, Witkoff insisted that progress had been made and that everything was in place to reach an agreement. At the same time, he also acknowledged that there are serious disagreements between the parties involved, and a compromise is needed, but it is currently difficult to predict how this might happen.
For now, Kyiv is preparing for the continuation of hostilities, and expects a harsh winter ahead. Some diplomats talk about a window of opportunity next spring, while others are much more pessimistic.
Zelensky thanked the US envoys for their visit, as the brief pause in attacks has given the people of Kyiv a much-needed respite, but few believe it will last.

articles.title: Poland’s anti-Ukrainian turn spills into violence
articles.body:
WARSAW — Poland’s nationalist right is turning hostility toward the country’s roughly 1.5 million Ukrainians into a potent political issue, tapping into local resentment over social benefits and wartime history just over a year before a pivotal parliamentary election.
During Poland’s 2025 presidential campaign, politicians began portraying Ukrainians in Poland as freeloaders straining the country’s public finances.
This summer, Polish President Karol Nawrocki stripped his Ukrainian counterpart, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, of Poland’s highest honor, the Order of the White Eagle, in reaction to Zelenskyy’s decision to name a military unit after the World War II-era Ukrainian Insurgent Army, or UPA. The group murdered tens of thousands of Poles during an ethnic-cleansing campaign in 1943-1945, although it also fought against the Soviet Union.
Advertisement
Warsaw has been one of Kyiv’s strongest supporters against Russia since the full-scale invasion of Ukraine began in 2022. But the nationalist camp, which Nawrocki seeks to lead, has sought to capitalize on tensions over the Ukrainian presence in Poland and the wartime massacres.
Anti-Ukrainian rhetoric is already intensifying ahead of the fall 2027 parliamentary election, when Prime Minister Donald Tusk’s broadly pro-Ukraine coalition will face the nationalist Law and Justice party and two other far-right parties. Polls show Tusk is far from certain of victory.
The libertarian Confederation party denounced Ukrainians getting social welfare, while Gregorz Braun, the European Parliament member who leads the far-right Confederation of the Polish Crown party, said: “The Kyiv regime is neither our ally nor our friend, it is our enemy,” during a summer gathering commemorating the wartime killing of Polish civilians by Ukrainians.
Przemysław Czarnek, the candidate for prime minister from the Law and Justice party, said July: “Military aid to Ukraine must be suspended until that country changes its historical policy.”
Rafał Pankowski, a sociology professor at Warsaw’s Civitas University and co-founder of the Polish anti-racism group Never Again, believes that while the Polish population is broadly supportive of Ukraine, fissures are beginning to show.
“Solidarity with Ukrainians remains strong among many Poles, but populist anti-Ukrainian rhetoric has created fertile ground for attacks, turning a large and visible minority into a target and helping verbal hostility spill into violence. Russian propaganda seized on the opportunity, too,” he said.
Advertisement
Ukrainian Ambassador to Poland Vasyl Bodnar is worried about politicians using Ukraine as a wedge issue.
“Part of Poland’s political class is trying to exploit the Ukrainian issue for political gain. Some focus on developments in Ukraine, others on the behavior of Ukrainians living here. One way or another, Ukraine features in the narrative of every political group — it is simply packaged differently,” he told POLITICO.
In the line of fire
The latest Polish-Ukrainian row might have faded from the headlines, but the fear it helped instill has not.
Vasyl Bodnar is worried about politicians using Ukraine as a wedge issue. | Adem Altan/AFP via Getty Images
“I’ve lived in Poland for about 10 years. I came here to study and stayed,” said Olena, a guide at a Warsaw cultural institution whose name POLITICO changed at her request because she feared for her safety.
“It took me quite a while to integrate, but I have never felt as alienated as I have over the past year. I have become afraid to speak Ukrainian in public, and I have started worrying about my friends and loved ones who live here or come to Poland to visit,” she said.
Opinion polls show a decided shift against Ukrainians.
Advertisement
In an annual survey by the state-run pollster CBOS, sympathy among Poles toward Ukrainians fell from 51 percent in 2023 to 29 percent in January 2026, while antipathy rose from 38 percent to 43 percent over the last year.
Another CBOS poll found that 45.4 percent of those polled attributed the deterioration to disputes over the wartime massacres and historical policy, with social benefits for Ukrainians in second place at 36.4 percent.
Ivan, a Ukrainian national who works at the University of Warsaw and asked to only be identified by his first name, said a neighbor confronted him over Zelenskyy’s decision to name a military unit after the UPA.
“We were in the elevator. My neighbor started yelling at me, telling me to go back to Ukraine and explain to Zelenskyy that he shouldn’t have done that. It was absurd,” Ivan said.
Olena recalled a Polish woman following the group she was guiding and complaining that hearing her speak Polish was “an embarrassment” to her as a Pole.
“I said loudly that Polish was not my native language, that I came from Ukraine,” Olena said.
Advertisement
For Ivan and Olena, the hostility remained verbal. For other Ukrainians, it has turned violent.
In July, two men were arrested after two Ukrainians, Anastazja, 20, and her 21-year-old partner Maksym, were beaten outside a Wrocław grocery store. The attack was denounced by Poland’s Interior Minister Marcin Kierwiński. Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha thanked the police for the arrests.
Earlier that month, an off-duty employee of Bielsko-Biała’s municipal bus company hurled nationality-based abuse at three Ukrainians, including two 11-year-old schoolgirls, on a bus.
Donald Tusk attends a ceremony in London on May 27, 2026. | Pool photo by Jack Taylor via WPA/Getty Images
In August, a Ukrainian man was attacked on a tram in Poznań.
The Polish police recorded 180 reports of ethnically motivated crimes against Ukrainians in the first half of this year, a 30 percent increase over the same period last year, reported the Rzeczpospolita newspaper.
The Polish government — which has tightened Ukrainians’ access to welfare, even though their collective contribution to Poland’s economy far exceeds public spending on them — set up 50 specialist prosecution teams in early 2026 to investigate hate crimes.
Advertisement
Between February and June, Polish prosecutors sent 283 cases to court. Ukrainians were the victims in more than 80 percent of such cases, up from 4 percent in 2014 and 74 percent in 2023.
Tusk said in July that attackers had become bolder because they believed they enjoyed political protection and called on Nawrocki to speak out on the matter.
“I am appealing directly to the president to stop remaining silent on this matter,” Tusk said. “We must wage a decisive fight against this violence, because the bandits, the hooligans, this violent pathology has gained courage and audacity because it has also received political patronage.”
The Roman Catholic Church has also weighed in, issuing an appeal “not to fuel nationalistic sentiments.”
Ambassador Bodnar hopes politicians will stop inflaming relations between the two countries.
“The best response will be effective communication — from politicians, the media, and, of course, government officials — who would communicate in a positive manner and resolve those issues that are painful or important to both sides,” Bodnar said.
Advertisement
For Ivan, the change in tone is making him more wary of drawing attention to himself in Poland.
“I still speak Ukrainian, and I wear a pin with the Polish and Ukrainian flags. What has changed is the way I feel about potential conflicts. I used to not be afraid to speak up and stand up for myself if someone attacked me because I’m Ukrainian,” he said. “Now I’m afraid no one would help me and that I would be accused of violating some law and simply deported, even though I’ve already built my life in Poland.”
The government’s policy is to deport Ukrainians even for minor offenses — one Ukrainian 18-year-old was kicked out of Poland for jumping a barrier at a concert.

articles.title: Zelensky mistaken about chances of stopping Russia — media
articles.body:
LONDON, September 8. /TASS/. Vladimir Zelensky is mistaken about Ukraine’s chances of defeating Russia, Owen Matthews, a columnist for The Spectator, argued.
Matthews also described Zelensky’s belief that Kiev can halt the slow but steady advance of Russian troops as another delusion. As winter approaches, Ukraine is about to run out of "not only Patriot missiles and men for the front lines, but money to fight on," he wrote.
Matthews also noted that Vladimir Zelensky faces a "perfect political storm" at home. He cited a series of corruption scandals, investigations into members of Zelensky’s inner circle, a conflict involving a shoot-out between the Security Service of Ukraine (SBU) and the Ukrainian Defense Ministry’s Main Intelligence Directorate (GUR), and fraud, waste and mismanagement in defense procurement.

articles.title: Ukraine Strikes Crimea Rail Bridge Supplying Russia’s Southern Front Military Logistics
articles.body:

Ukraine Strikes Crimea Rail Bridge Supplying Russia’s Southern Front Military Logistics
Ukraine's Defense Forces struck a railway bridge over the North Crimean Canal near Vladyslavivka in temporarily occupied Crimea on September 6 and overnight into September 7.
The General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine reported the strike on its official Telegram channel, describing the bridge as a route Russian forces rely on for military logistics.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
"The extent of the damage inflicted is being clarified," the General Staff stated, adding that operations against key enemy military targets continue.
Ukrainian forces struck several other positions across occupied territory during the same operation, according to the General Staff:
- Command posts of Russian units near Nyzhniy Naholchik and Dovzhanske in Luhansk region, and near Azovske in Zaporizhzhia region;
- An automated technical reconnaissance post known as "Grenadier" in Perekop, in occupied Crimea;
- An ammunition depot near Teple in the Luhansk region.
The "Grenadier" is an automated technical-reconnaissance post that scans for movement and incursions along Russia's occupation lines.
Such posts form part of a layered detection network in Crimea, and their loss opens gaps that leave nearby command posts and depots more exposed to follow-up strikes.
The strike extends a sustained Ukrainian effort to sever the rail links sustaining Russia's hold on Crimea.
On August 1, Ukrainian forces hit the Syvash railway bridge near Chonhar and a second railway bridge near Vladyslavivka, both used to move personnel, equipment, and ammunition between the occupied peninsula and Russian-held areas of southern Ukraine.
Days before that, strikes on July 27 and overnight into July 28 targeted a logistics warehouse and a fuel and lubricants depot near Ichki in occupied Crimea, alongside a drone storage warehouse near Chervonopopivka in Luhansk region.

articles.title: Iran will protect its nuclear facilities: Ex-diplomat
articles.body:
Mohsen Pakaein, Iran's former ambassador to Azerbaijan, told Mehr News Agency that U.S. threats against Iran's nuclear programme have no legal or international basis, especially given Iran's membership in the Non-Proliferation Treaty.
He said the threats continued because of the silence of the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) in the face of U.S. pressure and the inability of the UN Security Council to confront Washington's threats.
Pakaein said Iran has repeatedly stated that its nuclear programme is peaceful and that Tehran is not seeking to build a nuclear bomb, a point confirmed by the IAEA. "Any American action would be met with a decisive response from Iran," he said.
He said Washington's actions had neither rational logic nor any international legal basis. If attacks on nuclear centres became a practice, he noted, it was the United States and the Israeli regime that would suffer, because both possess nuclear weapons and such actions could have dangerous consequences for regional and international security.
Pakaein said every action the Americans had taken so far had ultimately turned against them. Iran, he added, has repeatedly stated there are no nuclear facilities or programmes at Kuh-e Kolang, and such claims are based on false information spread by the Americans.

articles.title: NATO jets scrambled multiple times over Baltic region in one week
articles.body:
NATO fighter jets were scrambled three times between Aug. 31 and Sept. 6 in response to Russian military aircraft operating near the Baltic states, according to data from Lithuania's Defense Ministry.
On Aug. 31, NATO jets identified a Russian Il-20 reconnaissance aircraft flying through international airspace from mainland Russia toward the Kaliningrad region without its transponder switched on or a filed flight plan, though the crew maintained radio contact with air traffic controllers.
A day later, NATO fighters were dispatched to identify and intercept an object that entered Estonian airspace from Russia before conducting patrols along the Estonian-Russian border.
On Sept. 5, 12 NATO air-policing fighter jets were deployed to identify another Russian Il-20 traveling toward Kaliningrad, which was also flying without an active transponder or flight plan.
The incidents come amid heightened tensions in the region, as the Baltic governments have accused Russia of cyberattacks, sabotage, attempts to influence public opinion, and aerial incursions.
Officials in Estonia and Latvia stated on Aug. 27 that they remained vigilant but had not changed their overall assessments of the threat posed by Russia, with Latvian Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs saying the risk of a direct military invasion remained low.

articles.title: Taiz again emerges as battlefield of choice in Yemen renewed war
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Taiz again emerges as battlefield of choice in Yemen renewed war
The latest fighting around Taiz has revived fears of another major battle for one of Yemen's biggest cities.
But military analysts say the Houthis may have little interest in actually storming it.
Instead, they argue, the group's more achievable objective is to cut the roads keeping Taiz connected to the rest of government-held Yemen - and gradually make the city harder to sustain.
"The real danger does not lie in a direct attack, but in the Houthis succeeding in cutting the supply arteries and turning the siege into a permanent reality," military and security affairs researcher Assem al-Mujahid told The New Arab.
"Accordingly, the western front remains the key to the battle for Taiz: if the supply routes remain open and the forces retain the ability to manoeuvre, the strangulation project will remain obstructed, while cutting this corridor would mean subjugating the city without the need for a comprehensive assault."
That helps explain the pattern of the latest escalation.
The Houthis have launched intense attacks west of Taiz, using ballistic missiles and drones and temporarily breaking through government lines. But around the city itself, their strategy has largely involved pressure on roads and supply routes rather than an attempt to seize its densely populated neighbourhoods.
Al-Mujahid said: "The forces defending the city have accumulated extensive field experience in urban and mountain warfare, which has pushed the Houthis to favour a strategy of strangulation and attrition rather than entering a direct battle to storm the city."
Why Taiz matters
Taiz is Yemen's most populous governorate, with close to four million inhabitants.
Its importance is also strategic. To the west lie the port of Mocha and the approaches to the Bab al-Mandab Strait, one of the world's most important shipping routes.
Control of the governorate is divided among several anti-Houthi forces as well as the Houthis.
The internationally recognised government controls much of Taiz city and large parts of the governorate. On the western coast, the National Resistance forces of Tariq Saleh - an anti-Houthi commander who sits on Yemen's Presidential Leadership Council - control Mocha and other coastal districts.
The Houthis control much of the north and east, including the economically important al-Hawban area north-east of the city.
Al-Hawban contains major factories, trading companies and markets, giving the Houthis access to substantial revenues while most of densely populated Taiz city remains under their opponents' administration.
That makes the current division of the city economically useful to the group: it can extract revenue without assuming the full cost of governing Taiz.
The battle for the roads
The latest offensive began early last Thursday after the Houthis fired 14 ballistic missiles as well as drones, followed by fighting that lasted around 15 hours.
They temporarily reached strategic positions including Jabal Nu'man in Jabal Habashi district, before government and allied forces counter-attacked and recovered many of them.
At al-Kadha, an important link between Taiz and the western coast, anti-Houthi forces also repelled the attack.
Reinforcements have since arrived from the Giants Brigades, a powerful southern anti-Houthi force, and Nation's Shield, another military force aligned with Yemen's internationally recognised authorities.
The significance of the fighting lies in two crucial roads.
One connects Taiz with Mocha and the western coast. Another runs south-west towards Aden, the interim seat of Yemen's government.
For residents, they are not simply military supply routes. They are among the main arteries carrying civilians, food and commercial goods into and out of the city.
The Houthis have also targeted al-Wazi'iyah bridge, an important route between Taiz and the western coast.
"The Houthis understand that controlling the supply routes would give them the ability to gradually strangle the city and recreate the siege model of the early years of the war," al-Mujahid said.
"The Houthi objective at the current stage is focused on exhausting Taiz until it reaches a point where it loses its ability to withstand pressure, with the aim of draining the government and blackmailing it politically and militarily."
The consequences of cutting those routes could include higher prices, disruption to trade and further displacement among a population that has already endured years of war.
It could also give the Houthis greater leverage in future political negotiations.
Why not simply capture the city?
Taking Taiz would be extremely difficult.
The city consists of densely packed neighbourhoods surrounded by mountainous terrain, including Jabal Sabir, which provides defenders with a powerful natural position.
Government forces and local fighters have also accumulated more than a decade of experience in urban and mountain warfare.
Al-Mujahid said: "Taiz's rugged geography, the high ground surrounding it, and the complex nature of fighting inside residential areas make any large-scale attack a military adventure with uncertain results."
Military analyst Colonel Sarhan al-Muhaya argues that years of fortification have made the city's defences significantly stronger.
"The positions of the National Army inside Taiz have become literally impregnable, thanks to strong engineering fortifications combined with the rugged geography and innovative obstacles, alongside the precise implementation of concealment and camouflage principles. All of this has created a firm conviction among the Houthis that achieving any breakthrough is impossible, regardless of how long the war lasts or the intensity of firepower, meaning that the attacks result in human and material losses for them."
Even a successful assault would carry substantial costs.
The Houthis would have to fight through a hostile and heavily damaged city, then take responsibility for services and infrastructure serving a large civilian population.
By contrast, their current position around Taiz allows them to retain economic influence and military pressure without bearing those costs.
"The Houthis' dreams of controlling the al-Dhabab road and the Taiz-Mocha road, and closing the remaining corridors under the control of government forces, are unattainable, and Houthi forces will not be able to achieve them."
He added: "It has been proven theoretically and practically that the Houthi forces are unable to retake any territory they have lost in Taiz governorate despite their repeated attempts."
Fakhr al-Azb is a Yemeni journalist based in Taiz. Writes for Al-Araby Al-Jadeed, The New Arab's Arabic-language sister edition.

articles.title: Germany seeks to quash Gaza genocide case at top UN court
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Germany seeks to quash Gaza genocide case at top UN court
Germany will Monday ask the top United Nations court to toss out a case brought against it by Nicaragua, which has accused Berlin of "facilitating genocide" with its support of Israel.
Lawyers for Germany will kick off four days of hearings at the International Court of Justice (ICJ), the court based in The Hague that rules on disputes between countries.
The case dates back to 2024, following the start of Israel's offensive in Gaza. Nicaragua urged ICJ judges to impose emergency measures to force Berlin to halt all aid to Israel, in particular military equipment.
The court threw out Nicaragua's request in April of that year, saying "the circumstances, as they now present themselves" did not justify emergency orders.
The case is nevertheless ongoing and Germany is now seeking to have it removed, either by persuading judges they do not have the power to rule in the case or that Nicaragua's argument does not stack up.
Berlin has filed so-called "preliminary objections to the jurisdiction of the Court and to the admissibility of certain claims" presented by Nicaragua, according to an ICJ statement.
The detail of Berlin's case has not yet been made public.
Genocide claim
After Germany presents its case on Monday, Nicaragua will respond before both countries get another chance to address the court on Wednesday and Thursday.
It takes on average six months for the court to hand down a ruling in such cases.
The court could either side with Germany and throw out the case completely or rule against Berlin, meaning the case would then be considered "on the merits" in more detail.
During hearings at the court in April 2024, Nicaragua said Germany was "pathetic" to provide aid to Gaza while also simultaneously furnishing Israel with weapons.
Nicaragua's ambassador to the Netherlands, Carlos Jose Arguello Gomez, told the court: "Germany seems not to be able to differentiate between self-defence and genocide."
Germany retorted that Nicaragua's case was "grossly biased", strongly denying the accusations that it was in breach of the 1948 UN Genocide Convention.
Israel launched its offensive in Gaza following the October 7, 2023 attacks against it by Hamas.
Due to its Nazi past, Germany has placed Israel's security "at the core" of its foreign policy, its representative told the court in the 2024 hearings.
Germany has been a staunch supporter of Israel for decades and is the second-largest supplier of arms to Israel after the United States.
Germany said its arms trade with Israel was subject to "detailed scrutiny... that far exceeds the requirements of international law".
Last year, Germany stopped authorizing any exports of military equipment to Israel that could be used in Gaza but later lifted those restrictions.
This procedure is separate from a high-profile case also before the ICJ, in which South Africa has accused Israel of perpetrating genocide in Gaza, which Israel denies.
Both South Africa’s case against Israel and Nicaragua’s case against Germany allege violations of the 1948 Convention on the Prevention and Punishment of the Crime of Genocide. The convention was drawn up in the wake of the Holocaust to codify a new crime: genocide.
In January 2024, judges at the ICJ ordered Israel to do all it can to prevent death, destruction and any acts of genocide in Gaza. Two months later, the court told Israel to take measures to improve the humanitarian situation in Gaza, including opening more land crossings to allow food, water, fuel and other supplies.
South Africa says that Israel largely ignored those orders.
A team of independent experts commissioned by the United Nations’ Human Rights Council and the largest professional organization of scholars studying genocide have both concluded that Israel is violating the treaty.
The ICJ's rulings are binding but it has no power to enforce them.
For example, it has ordered Russia to stop its invasion of Ukraine, a demand that has fallen on deaf ears in the Kremlin.
The proceedings are the latest legal attempt to rein in Israel’s military campaign by a country with historic ties to the Palestinian people, after South Africa accused Israel of genocide at the same court in 2023.
South Africa says that Israel largely ignored those orders.
Proceedings at the ICJ can take a long time to conclude
Both South Africa’s case against Israel and Nicaragua’s case against Germany allege violations of the 1948 Convention on the Prevention and Punishment of the Crime of Genocide. The convention was drawn up in the wake of the Holocaust to codify a new crime: genocide.
A team of independent experts commissioned by the United Nations’ Human Rights Council and the largest professional organization of scholars studying genocide have both concluded that Israel is violating the treaty but only an international court can make a legal determination.
Proceedings at the ICJ can drag on for years. In 2007, the court ruled that Serbia “violated the obligation to prevent genocide” in the 1995 Srebrenica massacre, when Bosnian Serb forces rounded up and murdered some 8,000 mostly Muslim men and boys in eastern Bosnia.
In May, the court set a November 2027 deadline for South Africa to file its written pleadings and gave Israel until May 2029 to reply. Hearings on the core question of the case — whether Israel committed genocide in Gaza — likely won’t be heard until late 2029 at the earliest.
In separate proceedings at the International Criminal Court, also in The Hague, which tries cases against individuals rather than between nations, judges have issued arrest warrants for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his former Defense Minister Yoav Gallant in connection with the conflict.
The pair are charged with crimes against humanity, not genocide. The court said it found that there was reason to believe they used “starvation as a method of warfare” by restricting humanitarian aid and intentionally targeted civilians in Israel’s campaign against Hamas in Gaza — charges Israeli officials deny.
In response, the United States has issued sanctions against many senior court staff, including nine of the ICC’s 18 judges.

articles.title: Billions for space defence under new national strategy
articles.body:
The government has published a new UK Space Strategy backed by £7.8 billion until 2030, with more than £3 billion of it directed at defence capabilities in orbit, the Department for Business, Innovation, Science and Trade stated.
The strategy brings government space investment and activity under a single plan covering growth, defence and national security, and formally replaces the National Space Strategy published in 2021.
Wes Streeting, the Defence Secretary, said: “This space strategy recognises that our national security depends on our freedom of action in space and, if necessary, the ability to protect UK and allied space assets. As threats in orbit grow more sophisticated, so must our ability to detect and respond to them, ensuring we protect the interests of the UK and allies while fuelling economic growth along the way.
“Backed by the Defence Investment Plan, we’re investing more than £3 billion to ensure our defence capabilities in space keep pace with the threats we face, supporting reindustrialisation and creating opportunities here in the UK.”
The largest single defence line is £880 million towards space control and intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance capabilities, funding technologies the department says can track military activity on the ground and potential attacks on satellites.
A further £2.8 billion goes towards connectivity, including the Connectivity in Low Earth Orbit and SKYNET defence communications programmes, which the department says play a pivotal role in keeping the armed forces connected wherever they are in the world. The same investment is expected to improve rural connectivity and reduce mobile signal dropouts on trains.
Space domain awareness, meaning the monitoring of satellites, rockets and debris in orbit, receives £149 million for the European Space Agency’s Vigil mission and £85 million for the National Space Operations Centre. According to the department, that funding will allow British technology to provide earlier warning of potential satellite collisions, hostile activity and solar storms.
Launch and industry
The strategy commits £148 million to European rocket programmes and £30 million to SaxaVord Spaceport in Shetland, which the government says will allow Britain and its partners to launch satellites without relying on countries further afield.
Douglas Alexander, the Scottish Secretary, said: “The UK Space Strategy is a huge vote of confidence in Scotland’s Space Sector. Scotland already builds more satellites than anywhere else in Europe, and with a £30 million UK Government investment boost, SaxaVord is now poised to deliver up to three-quarters of the continent’s orbital launch slots.
“This UK Space Strategy has defence, security and economic growth at its heart, creating skilled jobs right across Scotland, showing what we can achieve when government, industry and ambition come together.”
Jonathan Reynolds, the Business, Innovation, Science and Trade Secretary, said: “As space becomes a new frontier of economic and military competition, this plan will help keep Britain secure by strengthening our ability to launch satellites, detect threats and protect the services people rely on every day.
“At the same time, this plan will enable our excellent UK industry to seize the boundless opportunities of this new age in space, creating skilled jobs, driving growth and improving connectivity for all of us.”
A further £40 million supports in-orbit servicing, assembly and manufacturing, which the department says will help repair and maintain satellites damaged by debris, solar storms or hostile interference, and clear dangerous objects from orbit. The strategy also allocates £163 million to space science and exploration missions including the Rosalind Franklin Mars Rover built at Stevenage, £190 million from UK Research and Innovation for astronomy and space science research, £57 million from the Department for Transport for rail connectivity and £9 million from the Met Office for space weather forecasting.
For the first time, the department says, government will take a single approach to buying and developing space technology, beginning with satellite communications, which it argues will help British firms win more work and deliver capabilities faster.
Industry response
Kevin Craven, chief executive of the ADS Group, said: “We welcome the publication of the new space strategy, and the sustained effort to bring a cross-government perspective to space capability delivery. It is important that government maintains an open, transparent and ambitious partnership with industry to realise its national security and growth goals.
“Certainty allows the sector to operate at pace and for its industrial base to make long-term strategic and commercial commitments. It is also a vital signal of intent to our international partners for trade and collaboration.”
Doug Liddle, chair of the trade association UKspace, said: “UKspace welcomes the publication of the government’s new UK Space Strategy. It sets out a constructive path towards a refreshed approach to space in the UK, which we hope will result in a stronger emphasis on open, inclusive cross-sector dialogue. The new, focussed strategy offers a valuable opportunity to create a more streamlined framework, strengthen collaboration and deliver greater impact across the UK space sector.”
Professors Anna Hogg and Mark Sims, co-chairs of the Space Academic Network, said: “SPAN welcomes the new cross-Government space strategy and its integrated delivery plan. We look forward to seeing the detail of the strategy and delivery plan, which will be critical in enabling academia and industry to plan, invest and work together to deliver the UK’s ambitions for space. Sustained investment across academia and industry is crucial to creating the cutting-edge technologies, capabilities, talent and growth of the future.”
The department puts the value of the UK space sector at £18.6 billion supporting more than 55,000 skilled jobs. Alongside the strategy, the government is reforming space regulation with the stated aim of reducing costs and rewarding responsible operators.

articles.title: Burnham and Kristersson discuss Joint Expeditionary Force
articles.body:
Prime Minister Andy Burnham spoke to his Swedish counterpart Ulf Kristersson on the morning of Sunday 7 September, with the two leaders discussing the importance of the relationship between the two countries both bilaterally and through the Joint Expeditionary Force and NATO in order to protect shared interests, according to a readout issued by Downing Street.
The leaders agreed that Russian aggression, both in Ukraine and through hybrid attacks in Europe, emphasised the importance of that close relationship. Burnham reflected on his recent visit to Ukraine and thanked Prime Minister Kristersson for Sweden’s strong support, particularly as Russia has stepped up what the readout described as egregious attacks.
The Joint Expeditionary Force is a British-led grouping of ten northern European nations, bringing together the United Kingdom with Denmark, Estonia, Finland, Iceland, Latvia, Lithuania, the Netherlands, Norway and Sweden. It is designed to operate either independently or alongside NATO and other partners, with a focus on the High North, the North Atlantic and the Baltic Sea region, and it has been used in recent years to coordinate activity around the protection of undersea cables and pipelines and the monitoring of shadow fleet tanker movements.
Sweden’s participation in that grouping predates its accession to NATO, which it completed in March 2024 after abandoning a policy of military non-alignment that had held for two centuries. Swedish membership, alongside that of Finland, has substantially altered the alliance’s position in the Baltic and has drawn Stockholm into closer planning arrangements with London on questions of northern European security.
The call also covered economic matters with a defence and energy dimension. The leaders discussed opportunities to drive growth between the two countries, including through Rolls-Royce’s delivery of Swedish small modular reactors. The Prime Minister said the programme was a good example of how both countries could work together to deliver highly skilled jobs and support Sweden’s plans to deliver clean, reliable and secure power.
Rolls-Royce SMR, the company established to develop and build the British small modular reactor design, has been selected by the Swedish state-owned utility Vattenfall to supply reactors at the Ringhals site on the country’s west coast. The same design has been chosen for the British small modular reactor programme, and the company has pursued export orders on the basis of a factory-built approach intended to reduce the cost and construction time associated with conventional nuclear plants.
Turning to Europe more broadly, the leaders discussed the British ambition to move closer to the European Union. The Prime Minister said he was focused on driving a closer relationship that delivered for people in both the United Kingdom and Europe, increasing security, boosting opportunity and supporting growth. The two leaders said they looked forward to meeting soon.
